Kenny Beats — [Vocal Template](https://youtu.be/X_iDENABLmk) · [New Vocal Chain 2022](https://youtu.be/-SvBNOBWJ_8) · [Recording Vocals the Right Way](https://youtu.be/3Nw1d37nluo) · [Recording Without Latency](https://youtu.be/Gj4_IvHFn6g) · [Auto-Tune Process](https://youtu.be/dyr6F9DLG7c) — Disclosure — [Help Me Lose My Mind](https://youtu.be/FPgLRkgKoMU) · [ENERGY Release Party](https://youtu.be/fMqPuf1UVzI) · [Ultimatum](https://youtu.be/uWe3UvI4KlU) (1073→LA-2A→Maag lineage) — Illangelo — [How Illangelo mixes The Weeknd's vocals](https://youtube.com/shorts/fG2s168La_E?is=dN4ixQppvlexuZOz) · Mix with the Masters, Producing The Weeknd's vocals with Illangelo — Mix with the Masters (070 Shake & Dave) — [Behind the Track｜'Elephant' by 070 Shake](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OKBT8-0l9AI) — Mix with the Masters (Benny Blanco & Selena Gomez) — [Behind the Track｜'Younger And Hotter Than Me' by Selena Gomez & benny blanco](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rkJ-LaoArUY) — Mix with the Masters (Ben Baptie) — Julian Casablancas' vocal sound with Ben Baptie — Mix with the Masters (Kuk Harrell) — Radio-ready vocal effects with Kuk Harrell — Mix with the Masters (Stuart White) — Mixing vocals in the box with Stuart White — Mix with the Masters (Andrés Torres and Mauricio Rengifo) — Vocal production with Andrés Torres and Mauricio Rengifo — Mix with the Masters (Greg Wells) — Bringing vocals out of the speakers with Greg Wells — pages in `20 Music/YouTube Notes/`

chains.title: Backup Vocals Group
chains.routing: [Backup Vocal tracks] → Backup Vocals Group → Vocal Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Sums all backup/ad-lib tracks into one wide, controlled element that never steps on the lead.

## Chain overview
Carve → glue harder than the main group → widen slightly → duck under the lead.

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Carve
- HPF the summed group again (150–200 Hz) · dip the lead's presence band (3–5 kHz) −1 to −2 dB.

### 2. Glue Compressor — Glue
- **Ratio 4:1** (②) · **Attack 20 ms** (③) · **Release Auto** (④) · **Threshold set for 3 dB GR** (① — read the GR meter, not the number) · **Range 8 dB** safety cap (⑥) · **Makeup** to match bypassed level (⑤) · **Dry/Wet 100%** (⑦)
- **Why:** Backups can take real bus compression (harder than the lead) — it fuses multiple takes into one solid block. 4:1 + 20 ms is firm enough to glue without killing consonant transients.

### 3. S1 Imager — Width
- **Width +15%** (①) — slight increase; **check mono compatibility** (⑤)
- **Why:** Backups live at the sides; the lead owns the center.

### 4. Pro-C 2 — Duck (sidechain from lead vocal)
- External sidechain keyed from [Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) · 2:1 · **1–2 dB GR** only when the lead sings · slow release
- **Why:** Automatic priority — backups bloom in the gaps and tuck when the lead speaks.

## Send FX
- Backups feed the **same shared vocal send bank** as the mains (dialed on [Main Vocal Group](#/chain/main-vocal-group)) — one delay/reverb space for every vocal lane. Backups typically run the delay **hotter** than the lead (throws + wetter tails are on-brand), sidechain-ducked to the lead → Sidechaining.
- **Ad-lib word throws are inserts, not sends** — a dedicated throw track (loud EchoBoy, high-end cut, subdivision), per [Backup Vocal Track](#/chain/backup-vocal-track) §6. Cohesion → shared group send · moment → insert.

## Variations
- **Call-and-response arrangements:** skip the duck — the parts already alternate.
- **Huge hook stacks:** swap S1 Imager push for [Width Send](#/chain/width-send) so the width is blendable.

## From videos

- **De-ess doubles noticeably harder than the lead — the ear can't discern multiple simultaneous S sounds unless they land out of time — and repurpose a redundant double (EQ out the low end, compress hard) into a distinct "breathy" high-frequency lift instead of muting it.** Tony Maserati, on K.Flay's "Dreamers": two main doubles carry body, a repurposed third carries breathy energy. Vary the blend section-to-section (a phrase before the chorus, or the end of a chorus) rather than repeating the same treatment every time, specifically to hold listener attention. → De-essing, RX De-ess, Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Layering and Stacking — Tony Maserati (Mix with the Masters), Background Vocals  - Tony Maserati
- **The Disclosure stack-bus chain** — per track: Tube-Tech-style EQ (lows out) + de-esser; on the GROUP: **overdrive (saturate in) → stereo 1176 (LA-3A auditioned for group vocals, passed) → EQ → Decapitator → de-ess AGAIN** ("a lot of S's as a group"). De-ess before AND after the group color — Disclosure, [Remix Stems Stream](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8) → Compression Staging

chains.title: Ensemble Stack Group
chains.routing: [Ensemble Stack layers — flexible count] → Ensemble Stack Group → Vocal Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Sums a self-stacked vocal ensemble — **however many layers you built** — into one cohesive element, and holds the *arrangement* (which layer-roles are present) plus the glue, cohesion, shared space, and width treatments. The per-layer prep already locked pitch/time/level on [Ensemble Stack Track](#/chain/ensemble-stack-track); the group makes the layers read as one. Distinct from [Main Vocal Group](#/chain/main-vocal-group) (which balances a lead against its layers) — here the stack is the instrument.

## Two ways to run it (choose per song)
- **Fused ensemble (no lead)** — every core layer level-matched so nothing wins; one shared space; tightest fusion. *Bon Iver "Holocene", Imogen Heap, gospel self-stacks.*
- **Lead + support stack** — a front vocal with the other roles tucked underneath (doubles just under, octaves ~−8 to −12 dB, harmonies below the lead); the standard pop stack.
Same building blocks either way — only the **level relationship** changes. Everything below applies to both.

## Layer roles — the modular stack (add blocks as the section needs)

There is **no fixed take count.** Build from these roles; a sparse verse might be Core only, a final chorus might stack all of them. Record doubles as **L/R pairs** and harmonies **doubled per part**.

| Role | Job | Typical count | Pan | Level | Double it? | Band-limit (track §4.3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core / Unison** | the body of the ensemble — your main "approaches," sung different ways | 1–several | center → near-center | reference | it's its own role (see Doubles) | HPF 80–120 Hz |
| **Doubles** (of each core layer) | width + thickness; the main stereo image | 2–8, in **L/R pairs** | tight ±20–30% (verse) → wide ±60–100% (chorus/hook) | just under their source | — align each to its source | HPF 80–120 Hz, softer sibilance |
| **Octave-down anchor** ("low one in the middle") | weight + gravity, *felt not heard* | 1, **not doubled** | **center** | ~−8 to −12 dB under core | no | HPF low (~40–60 Hz), keep weight |
| **Octave-up / air** | sheen + lift on top | 1 (optionally doubled) | center or slight ± | low, felt not heard | optional | HPF high (~150–300 Hz) |
| **Harmonies** (3rd/5th/6th/7th) | color; don't harmonize every note | each part doubled | wide ±60% (high one side, low the other) | under core/lead | yes | HPF ~120 Hz+ |
| **Whisper / air texture** | ear candy | doubled | ±L/R | subtle | yes | HPF high, consistent mic distance |
| **Gang / choir** | anthemic size | 6–20 takes, varied tone/accent | spread around the field | balance to taste | — | vary per take |

**Build order:** Core → Doubles (width) → Octave-down (weight) → Octave-up / Harmonies / Whisper / Gang as wanted. **Panning principle:** the stereo field is a *stage* — keep the Core and Octave-down anchor **centered** and get width from the doubles/harmonies/air. Don't hard-pan *everything* or you carve a hole in the middle and the stack disconnects from the mix — [Synchro Arts](https://www.synchroarts.com/posts/vocal-layering).

### This song's config (worked example — 5 layers, expandable)
Two approaches sung different ways = **Core A + Core B** ▸ **each doubled** (A + A-double L/R pair, B + B-double L/R pair) ▸ **+ Octave-down anchor, centered**. Add more later by dropping in blocks from the table (an air layer up top, a harmony pair, etc.) — the group chain and width variants don't change, they just have more to fuse.

## Harmony layer (turning the stack into a chord)

Everything above stacks the *same note* (unison + octaves). Adding **harmonies** turns the ensemble from a thick single note into a **chord sung by one voice** — the biggest expansion move available. It's an optional layer-role, but arrange it deliberately:

- **Intervals — start with 3rds and 6ths** above and/or below the melody (the **3rd is the "money note"** — most color per layer). Add **5ths** for openness and **7ths / octaves** for a fuller, choir-like spread. Match the interval to the underlying chord so the harmony spells the actual harmony, not just a parallel line.
- **Don't harmonize every note.** Bring harmonies in on **hooks, phrase-ends, and transitions**; harmony that's on the whole time loses its lift. Subtraction is the arrangement (Arrangement and Song Form).
- **Double each harmony part** (L/R pair) and **pan wide (~±60%)** — high harmony one side, low harmony the other — so the chord **opens up around the centered Core + octave anchor**. This is what makes a self-stack read as a *group* rather than one fat note.
- **Register / EQ:** HPF each harmony **~120 Hz+** so they sit above and around the core without stacking mud; keep them a touch **under** the core/lead in level (color, not competition).
- **Tuning:** harmonies follow the **harmony line, not the melody** — set them in Auto-Tune Pro to the right scale, and run them slightly *more* tuned than the leads to lock the chord tight. For a Beatles/block-harmony blend instead, back the tune off (retune 40+) and let the takes blend (see [Harmony Vocal Track](#/chain/harmony-vocal-track) Variations).
- **Fused vs lead:** in a **fused ensemble** the harmonies blend as equal chord tones; in a **lead + support** stack they tuck under the lead as color. Same parts, different balance.
- **Per-part processing** (band-limit, wetter delay/reverb, texture-split between harmony layers) lives on the dedicated [Harmony Vocal Track](#/chain/harmony-vocal-track) — route those tracks into this group so they share the glue, de-ess, and one space.

## Chain overview
Carve → glue-comp (one comp over the whole stack) → light saturate → de-ess the composite → one shared space. **Unify-then-glue:** the single most important group move is *one* slow comp riding every layer together, and *one* ambience they all share.

> **What the group does NOT do (inherited downstream):** program leveling (UAD Teletronix LA-2A), broad tone EQ, final de-ess, resonance (Soothe2 — kept as *one* instance on the bus, not per-track), and air all come from the [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus) this group routes into — don't duplicate them here. Track prep + this group + the bus together = the full chain the lead runs, just distributed (see [Ensemble Stack Track](#/chain/ensemble-stack-track) §4).

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Composite carve
- Subtractive EQ on the **summed** stack, not each layer: HPF cleanup if the sum still has mud, tame resonances that only poke out when everything's up (2–4 kHz harshness, 200–400 Hz box). Broad, gentle. Carve the vocal's lane against the *other* groups here rather than boosting.
- **Why:** Stacked layers pile up low-mid and sibilant energy; carve the composite so the glue comp isn't fighting buildup.

### 2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — Glue compression (slow opto)
- Compress mode · **2–4 dB GR** on the loudest phrases · gain to unity. Optical, soft-knee, longer release for cohesion — [Sage Audio](https://www.sageaudio.com/articles/how-to-stack-vocals). UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII is an equally good opto here; Ableton Glue Comp or Pro-C 2 in an opto style stands in fine.
- **Why:** **One comp moving the whole stack together** is the biggest part of the single-source illusion — it makes the layers breathe as one voice. Slow opto so there's no audible pumping.

### 3. Decapitator — Saturation for cohesion
- Style A (tape-ish) · Drive 2–4 · Mix 20–35% · Punish off. A UAD Pultec EQP-1A / UAD Neve 1073 tone pass is an alternate flavor.
- **Why:** A touch of *shared* harmonic drive fuses stacked voices more than almost anything — common harmonics read as one source. Post-glue so drive level is consistent.

### 4. Pro-DS — De-ess the composite
- Split-band, sidechain framed on the S region (~4–8 kHz), range 4–6 dB. De-ess background layers **harder** than a lead.
- **Why:** Many stacked "s"es get harsh fast — de-ess the **sum**, not each layer (per-layer de-essing over-processes and dulls the performances).

### 5. ValhallaVintageVerb — One shared space (reverb)
- A single short room/plate, low-to-medium mix. For depth, a short plate to glue + a longer hall/chamber to push some layers back.
- **Why:** Putting every layer in **the same ambience** is what makes them read as one performance in one room. Never give individual layers their own reverb — separate spaces re-separate the voices.

## Delay / echo — where it goes

Same principle as reverb: **cohesion lives on the group, moments live on a throw track.**
- **Ambient / glue delay** (slap, 1/8, 1/4 that places the *whole ensemble* in a space) → a **shared group send** to [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) / [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other) (one setting, varied only by subdivision, band-limited via EchoBoy's internal hi/lo cut). One delay across the whole stack reinforces the single-source illusion; a per-layer delay pulls the voices apart the way per-layer reverb does. **Sidechain-duck the delay returns to the stack** so tails tuck under words and bloom in the gaps — Sidechaining.
- **A specific word / phrase throw** (last word repeats, a catch on one line) → **not the group.** Drag that word to a dedicated effects/throw track with a **loud EchoBoy insert**, high end cut, subdivision per throw ("spotlight throws are an insert, not a send"). This is a *per-layer* move and lives on the track — see [Ensemble Stack Track](#/chain/ensemble-stack-track) §5.
- **Rule of thumb:** cohesion → group send · moment → individual insert.

### Routing
**Ensemble Stack Group → [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)** — the vocal-dedicated delay/reverb returns output **into the [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus)** (so bus glue melts wet into dry and riding the bus fader carries the space with the voice), not straight to master. Keep this group about fusing the stack.

## Variations — width treatments (driven by which layers are present)

- **A — Thick & Centered** *(Bon Iver "Holocene"; intimate lead-stack)* — one big voice: tightest VocAlign Project 5 AU alignment; core + doubles near center (±0–15%); octave-down anchor doing the weight; Little MicroShift off/low; short, mono-leaning ValhallaVintageVerb; glue comp a touch firmer.
- **B — Wide Ensemble / Choir** *(Imogen Heap, HAIM, gospel)* — a choir-of-yourself: looser alignment (keep the natural timing spread); pan the double/harmony pairs across the field (e.g. ±100 / ±60 / ±25%); Little MicroShift for extra spread; wider/stereo verb; slightly *less* glue so they breathe. Core + octave-down still centered.
  - 🎬 *From video:* a minimal from-scratch version of this exact variation — 4 layers (main/low/high/mid-different-tone) instead of a full role menu, with Little AlterBoy doing the pitch/formant differentiation per layer (main formant-down-slightly; a second layer octave-up + formant-down, paired to the main's reverb; a third layer same pitch/formant setting but a longer, heavier reverb since it reads more exposed) and the low layer getting Decapitator crunch instead of pitch shifting — see Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs § From videos for the full breakdown.
- **C — Hybrid: Center Core + Wide Halo** *(modern produced pop)* — focused center in a big bloom: the Core layers + octave-down anchor tight-center; the doubles/harmonies/air spread wide with Little MicroShift as the halo; center marginally louder but no single "lead"; HPF the halo a little higher so it sits *under* the core; big surrounding bloom.
  - 🎬 Optional moving element: one halo layer on PanMan drifting between the wide pair (static width + one moving voice) — the trick [Backup Vocal Track](#/chain/backup-vocal-track) §2 cites for ad-libs.

## From videos

- **A minimal 4-layer "choir from one voice" build (Variation B in miniature) — main/low/high/mid-different-tone, no external singers, pitch/formant + reverb doing all the differentiation instead of the full tune/align/glue chain above.** Little AlterBoy set differently per layer (main: formant down slightly + short reverb; second: octave-up + formant-down, same short reverb as main to fuse the pair; third: same pitch/formant setting but a longer, heavier reverb since it reads more open/exposed); low layer skips AlterBoy for EQ (cut lows) + Decapitator crunch + heavy reverb. All four bounced to one stem. A useful low-overhead reference point against this note's full role-based system — worth reaching for when a quick choir texture is needed without tracking a full ensemble menu. → Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Little AlterBoy, Decapitator — loner, [making a soulful/emotional gospel sample for lil durk & lil baby (turning my vocals into a choir)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nHBEE-uvq4M)

## Sources

Layering best practice (researched 2026-07-17): [Sage Audio — How to Stack Vocals](https://www.sageaudio.com/articles/how-to-stack-vocals), [Twisby — 7 Layers You Need to Record](https://twisbyrecords.com/post/how-to-layer-vocals-like-a-pro/), [Synchro Arts — Vocal Layering](https://www.synchroarts.com/posts/vocal-layering), [Singing Success — 5 Industry-Standard Vocal Layers](https://singingsuccess.com/5-industry-standard-vocal-layers/). Kuk-Harrell stack discipline via [FX Chain System](#/chains/system). Style references — thick-centered: Bon Iver "Holocene"; wide choir: Imogen Heap, HAIM, gospel self-stacks. Spec: `spec-131-ensemble-vocal-stack-chains`.

chains.title: Main Vocal Group
chains.routing: [Main Vocal, Main Vocal (high), Double Vocal, Harmony Vocal] → Main Vocal Group → Vocal Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Sums the lead + its layers (high, doubles, harmonies) into one balanced element. Group-stage work is about the *relationship between the layers* and carving against the rest of the mix — the heavy lifting already happened on the tracks, and the [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus) does the final polish. Keep this lean.

## Chain overview
Carve EQ → gentle glue. Balance between layers is faders/automation, not more processing.

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Group carve
- EQ *against the other groups*: find where the vocal masks or is masked (usually 1–5 kHz vs guitars/synths, 200–400 Hz vs everything)
- Cut the offending band in the *other* group's chain first — boost here only if the vocal still needs it
- Dynamic node dip on this group only if a layer resonance pokes out when the stack is summed
- **Why:** Step 4 of the process — pick what stands out, EQ the interference out of the *other* tracks so the vocal wins its lane without being boosted into harshness.

### 2. LALA — Layer glue
- **Peak Reduction for ~1.5 dB GR** (① — slow/gentle) · **Comp mode** (③) · **HPF engaged** (④) · **Mix 100%** (⑤) · **Gain to unity** (②)
- **Why:** An LA-2A-style leveler melts the layers into one voice without audible pumping; the real leveling already happened per-track.

## Send FX (the shared vocal space)

One send bank, shared by **every** vocal lane (mains and ad-libs through the *same* returns) — that's what makes the stack sit in one room. Dialed here at group level; full recipes live in the send chain notes. Architecture per [Kenny Beats Vocal Chain](#/chain/kenny-beats-vocal-chain):

**Return routing:** the vocal-dedicated returns ([Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap), [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other), [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long)) output **into [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus)**, not master — the bus glue melts wet into dry, and riding the bus fader carries the space with the voice. Mix-wide returns ([Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room), [Width Send](#/chain/width-send), [Saturation Send](#/chain/saturation-send)) stay → master.

- **Delays — all EchoBoy:** 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, slap, 1/2 returns share one setting varied only by subdivision, band-limited with EchoBoy's internal high/low cut (no EQ after) → [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap), [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other)
- **Delay returns sidechain-duck to the lead** — tails tuck under words, bloom in the gaps → Sidechaining
- **Reverb tiers:** short = Pro-R 2 "Vocal Backings Bright" (body only; preset originates on the older Pro-R) · long/super-long = ValhallaVintageVerb → [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room), [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long)
- **[Width Send](#/chain/width-send)** on hooks · **[Saturation Send](#/chain/saturation-send)** for attitude sections
- **Spotlight throws are an insert, not a send** — dedicated "effects track": loud EchoBoy insert, high end cut, subdivision per throw, long-verb ducked under the ad-libs

## Variations
- **Dense stack sections:** automate the group fader, not the layers — the internal balance is already set.
- **If backups fight the lead:** the duck belongs on [Backup Vocals Group](#/chain/backup-vocals-group), not here.

## From videos

- **A gated-distant-mic alternative to a plugin reverb send, driven by the vocal's own dynamics** — David Bowie's "Heroes," Tony Visconti: three mics at increasing distance from the singer, with a Gate on the two farther mics thresholded so only louder singing opens them — quiet phrases stay dry, loud phrases progressively open the more reverberant, more distant mics. In-the-box equivalent: send the vocal to a room-verb return and gate that return's input off the vocal's own level, rather than automating a send fader by hand. → Gate — David Bennett Music Theory, 15 facts you didn't know about classic songs
- **"The group has the chain"** — Kenny's mantra (via Alex Tumay's Young Thug template, ~150 released songs): every comp/verse/hook track stays 100% empty, the one chain lives here on the group, so takes punched in 30 minutes apart sound identical and every settings change happens in exactly one place. Exception: Auto-Tune Pro goes on individual tracks when parts need different keys/retunes — Kenny Beats, [Vocal Template](https://youtu.be/X_iDENABLmk) + [New Vocal Chain 2022](https://youtu.be/-SvBNOBWJ_8)

chains.title: Vocal Bus
chains.routing: [Main Vocal Group, Backup Vocals Group, vocal FX returns (Delay Send Slap, Delay Send Other, Reverb Send Long)] → Vocal Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Final polish on *all* vocals summed — the "vocal master." This is your current working chain, kept as the default with researched starting points.

**Vocal FX returns feed this bus** — [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap), [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other), [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) output here (not master), so the glue melts tails into the dry voice and a bus fader ride moves voice + space together. Safe because the GR here is gentle (1–3 dB — heavy bus compression would pump the tails). Mix-wide returns ([Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room), [Width Send](#/chain/width-send), [Saturation Send](#/chain/saturation-send)) stay → master. If a hook wash ever turns murky, the Decapitator/Inflator densifying the tails is the suspect — trim the return level, don't re-route.

🎬 *From video:* the reason THIS bus exists as a separate, dedicated bus rather than sitting inside a general vocal group — with the lead routed here and every OTHER instrument (including backing vocals/doubles/harmonies) summed into a separate instrumental bus, LUFS meters on both buses let you measure and match the two: in the majority of popular mixes the lead vocal reads at roughly the SAME loudness as the instrumental. Once matched, push the vocal slightly below that reading to sit "in" the mix, or slightly above to sit "on top of" it. → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain), Referencing and Translation — Sage Audio, [The 5 MOST IMPORTANT Vocal Mixing Tips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXk1lvT6AhU)

## Chain overview
Slow leveler → saturation → broad tone → density → de-ess → resonance cleanup. The logic: glue the level first so every later stage sees a steady signal; add color; then the last three stages *clean up what the color added*. De-ess and soothe sit at the end because saturation and Inflator both regenerate harshness.

**Bus philosophy:** by the time audio hits a bus, moves should be broad and gentle — 1–3 dB, wide Qs, low mix knobs. If you're reaching for surgery here, the fix belongs on a track or group.

## Chain

### 1. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — Program leveling
- Compress mode (Limit rarely sounds good on vocals) · **1–3 dB GR** on the loudest phrases (up to ~5 on dense material) · gain to match unity
- **Why:** The LA-2A's optical release "stomps on the brakes" — fast at first, slowing as it approaches zero — so it rides the performance like a fader without audible letting-go. With the CL 1B as the opto leveler on the way in, the chain now rides gently at *both* ends — CL 1B in, LA-2A on the bus — and the fast peak-precision work sits in the middle on Pro-C 2 (§4.3 of the track chains). Two smooth opto stages bracketing one fast stage: no single comp does all the work, which is the point. Three gentle stages always beat one deep one — an LA-2A asked to do all the work alone clamps hard on peaks and recovers too slowly.
- 🎬 *From video:* the point of a leveler here is to **glue a stacked vocal** (one lead + doubles) into one voice; Disclosure follow it with a character pass (even a flat Neve, "not done unless it's been through a Neve"). A subtle OTT at ~23% can stand in for the glue and "sounds like a G-bus comp" — Disclosure, [You've Got To Let Go](https://youtu.be/1iRPvK1gaOI) & [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).

### 2. Decapitator — Saturation
- Style A (tape-ish) or E (aggressive) · Drive 2–4 · Mix 20–35% · Punish off
- **Why:** Harmonic density on the summed stack reads as loudness and presence without EQ boost. Post-leveler = consistent drive; parallel mix keeps the transients honest.

### 3. Pro-Q 4 — Broad tone
- HPF 80–100 Hz on the sum · wide presence lift +1–1.5 dB @ 3–4 kHz if needed · air shelf +1 dB @ 10 kHz+
- **Why:** One broad tonal statement for the whole vocal picture. Cuts the saturation's low-mid buildup too (check 200–300 Hz).

### 4. Oxford Inflator — Density
- Gentle bus use: Effect 20–40% · Curve 0 · watch output — keep unity
- Sonnox's intended full workflow (for when you want more): **Effect 100%, ride the input fader up until the clip lights flicker, then pull the output down to match the bypassed peak level** — that's the honest way to hear only the effect, not extra volume
- **Curve meaning:** −50 = subtle richness/depth · 0 = balanced valve warmth (default) · +50 = fat, mid-forward, eats subtle dynamics
- **Why:** Perceived loudness/fullness without GR (it's psychoacoustic, not compression — it can even make full-level white noise sound louder). The "make it sound finished" stage. Always level-match when judging it.

### 5. Pro-DS — De-ess
- Split-band · range 3–6 dB
- **Why:** Decapitator + Inflator both push sibilance back up — catch it after them, not before.
- 🎬 *From video:* on a committed track, **manual de-essing beats this** — chop and lower each harsh S by hand to dodge the lisp/phasing a de-esser adds; a bus de-esser is the safety net, not the whole job. And add air *before* the harshness stages with a boost-type de-esser (Gem Dopamine) so the top stays breathy — Disclosure, [Higher Than Ever Before](https://youtu.be/9XkHSronZck) & [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).

### 6. Soothe2 — Final resonance tame
- Depth moderate (start ~30%, raise until audible, back off) · sharpness medium-high · focus 1–8 kHz
- **Why:** The last safety net: dynamic, frequency-specific control over whatever harshness survived — far more transparent than carving static EQ dips.
- 🎬 *From video:* keep **one Soothe on the bus rather than per track** — it's CPU-heavy and one instance on the sum tames harshness across the whole stack. Same plugin also works keyed off the vocal to duck *other* instruments out of its way (see Sidechaining) — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ) & [Looking For Love](https://youtu.be/NlJt0pCptGk).

## Meters & gain staging
Meter sandwich per [FX Chain System](#/chains/system) — ~0 VU in, unity out. Every device's output gain set so bypassing it doesn't change level (otherwise "louder = better" fools you on every knob).

## Variations
- **Trap/hip hop:** Decapitator Style E, Drive 4–5, Mix up to 40% — modern rap vocal density.
- **Ballad/acoustic:** drop Decapitator mix to ~10–15%, Inflator to ~15% — keep the dynamics breathing.
- **If the bus feels overworked:** soothe2 earlier (before Decapitator) so the saturator gets cleaner input — try both, keep the one where 3–4 kHz stays sweet.

## From videos

- **The "sound-good-izer" stays OFF until the song is done** — Kenny's chain ends in a CLA Vocals-style lift (bass module a touch + light compress) that he never enables while tracking: it adds latency, adds character artists get used to, and hides real problems. Owned lane: treat Oxford Inflator/Saturn 2 here the same way — toggle on when the record is finished, then re-trim levels — Kenny Beats, [Vocal Template](https://youtu.be/X_iDENABLmk)
General tips pulled from production breakdowns (via `/music-enrich`), newest-first.

- **Subtle OTT (~23% depth) glues a stack like a G-bus comp** without the pumped sound — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8)
- **One Soothe2 on the bus** (CPU-heavy) tames harshness across the whole stack; **Gem Dopamine** adds air while de-essing at the front — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ) & [Higher Than Ever Before](https://youtu.be/9XkHSronZck)
- **Manual de-essing beats a bus de-esser** once committed — chop and lower each harsh S by hand to avoid the lisp/phasing — Disclosure, [Higher Than Ever Before](https://youtu.be/9XkHSronZck) & [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8)
- **Glue-comp a 3-vocal stack**, then character (even a flat Neve for "it's been through a Neve") — Disclosure, [You've Got To Let Go](https://youtu.be/1iRPvK1gaOI)

chains.title: Arlo Parks Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Arlo Parks / Baird — *Ambiguous Desire* (Senses, Jetta, Heaven)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a deliberately restrained, un-fussed vocal system — a small saved insert chain ("Really Really Basic Vocal Chain") plus a handful of named, characterful parallel sends, wrapped around a lead performance built on trained, punch-in-free doubling accuracy rather than comp-and-align editing. The whole approach mirrors the record's production philosophy: keep the moving parts to the minimum that still lets the vocal feel embedded in the track rather than sitting dry and in-front.

**Signal source:** Shure SM7, used for the entire *Ambiguous Desire* album (documented, not owned — see Shure SM7) — "that's the microphone we used for the entire project... I've tried so many other mics that are fancier or whatever and I just... I'm a creature of habit."

## Chain overview

Track (SM7, full album) → doubled/tripled/quadrupled full takes, no comping, no punch-ins → insert chain "Really Really Basic Vocal Chain" (tune → EQ → compressor → slapback delay → touch-up EQ) → parallel sends ("Underwater Space" reverb, a doubler, a plate reverb, a delay automated on/off per section).

## Step 1 — Tracking: trained doubling accuracy, no comping

- Arlo sings every take **start to finish, never punching in**, and doubles/triples/quadruples the vocal by singing the whole song again from scratch rather than comping sections together — described by Baird as "extremely precise," landing in near-alignment without correction tools. The skill traces back to not knowing comping was an option as a teenager, so every home recording had to be perfect start to finish — a constraint that became a trained ability. → Vocal Comping and Takes
- On Senses, the guide vocal was recorded as a wordless freestyle over the instrumental first (no lyrics yet, just a repeating "dulled my senses" motif), with real lyrics written afterward around that emotional/lyrical center. → Creative Process and Idea Capture

## Step 2 — Insert chain: "Really Really Basic Vocal Chain" (saved preset)

A small saved preset used as a starting point on most vocals:
1. **Tune** — light pitch correction, "a little tune."
2. **EQ** — a first EQ pass.
3. **Compressor** — "a little compressor."
4. **Slapback delay** — originally added just to make the tracking process feel more fun/inspiring in the room, but sometimes left on in the final mix rather than removed.
5. **A second, touch-up EQ** at the end of the chain.

## Step 3 — Parallel sends (named, characterful — not generic reverb/delay)

- **"Underwater Space"** — a named send bus described as giving the vocal a "watery texture"; several elements are routed to it at once rather than it being a single insert.
- **A doubler** — width/thickening send, separate from the literal doubled vocal takes in Step 1.
- **A plate reverb** send.
- **A delay**, automated on/off per section rather than left running throughout — turned on only where the arrangement calls for it.

## Notes / variations

- **The goal stated explicitly is embedding, not front-and-center clarity:** "I always enjoy when my vocal feels like it's kind of embedded into the tapestry of the music but also still having that definition" — a deliberate move away from the drier, more up-front vocal treatment on Arlo's earlier records, part of this album's wider electronic/nocturnal palette shift.
- **Vocal-as-percussion is a second, separate technique layered on top of this chain, not a replacement for it** — on Jetta and Heaven, short chopped slices of the SAME lead vocal are used rhythmically/percussively alongside the sung lead. → Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Sampling and Sound Selection
- **This chain is a starting point, not a fixed formula** — the send balance and which effects are active are described as "kind of different for every song."

**Source:** Tape Notes, TN 183 Arlo Parks & Baird - Full Video Episode ([watch](https://www.patreon.com/posts/160593609)) — real subtitles, high confidence.

chains.title: Billie Eilish Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Billie Eilish / Finneas (Ocean Eyes, when the party's over, everything i wanted, BIRDS OF A FEATHER)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** ASMR-close whisper singing over enormous negative space — the quietest vocal presented the loudest. The technique is 80% **capture + editing**: sing genuinely soft inches from the mic, comp obsessively, crossfade between every word to kill the noise floor, then stack quiet harmonies until the whisper becomes a choir.
**Signal source:** Neumann TLM 102 (her mic is the TLM 103 — same family), often **handheld**, 1–3" away. Bedroom, not booth.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — clean, generous gain (whispers need it; watch the noise floor)
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 1–2 dB
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — bypass
- **The real step 1 is takes + comping:** many full takes, something usable in each; Finneas: *"crossfade into silence between every word she sings"* — the between-word editing IS the noise-floor control. ([Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) Step 1.5 discipline, doubled.)

## Chain overview
Comp/edit → de-pop the proximity → gentle level → de-ess soft → intimate space. Every stage tiny — the whisper must never sound *processed*, only impossibly close.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Proximity manage
- HPF 60–80 · **tame the proximity boom 150–250 Hz** dynamically (handheld distance varies) · zero air boost — her top end is breath already.

### 2. Pro-C 2 — Even the whisper
- Vocal style, 3–4 dB, slow-ish release — whispers have tiny dynamics; this is about consistency, not control.

### 3. Pro-DS — Soft-S
- Whisper sibilance is huge relative to tone — range 6–8 dB but *listen*: S's are part of the ASMR aesthetic; tame, don't remove.

### 4. Saturn 2 — Warmth
- Warm tape, mix 10–20% — body for a voice with almost no chest.

## Step 3 — Effects (sends)
- **Space as an instrument, per song:** dead dry ("bad guy") vs cathedral ("when the party's over" — [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) hot, ducked). Pick one identity per song, don't blend.
- **Harmony stacks are the sound:** quiet 3–5 part harmonies ([Harmony Vocal Track](#/chain/harmony-vocal-track) rules but *softer than the lead*), sometimes pitched layers (Little AlterBoy octave-down whisper tucked).
- [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) rarely; [Width Send](#/chain/width-send) on stack blooms.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | one whisper, dead center, **no double** | nothing — the negative space is the arrangement |
| Pre / lift | same whisper | a single quiet harmony a third up |
| Hook | whisper, unchanged | 6–10 whispered harmony layers, all low |
| Ad-libs | breaths, consonants, mouth noise, panned wide |

**The move — the choir is built from whispers, never from volume.** Every layer is tracked at the same soft dynamic inches off the mic; the hook gets bigger by *count*, not by anyone singing harder. The lead never changes across the whole song.

**Stack count: 1 → 10, all quiet.** The dynamic contrast is entirely arrangement, which is why the capture-and-edit discipline above matters so much — ten whispers only stack cleanly if each one's noise floor was crossfaded out.

## Notes / variations
- **Handheld capture confirmed directly by Finneas, from an early writing-session verse take:** Billie tracked a verse vocal on a TLM 103 while physically holding it in her hand, at a house Finneas lived in in Highland Park — not a booth, not on a stand. Corroborates this chain's "handheld, 1–3" away, bedroom not booth" signal-source note above from the writer/producer's own account. → Neumann TLM 102 (owned equivalent), Vocal Mic Technique — Mix with the Masters (Finneas), Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas
- **Gain-automate a naturally quiet ad-lib by a large, specific amount to make it pop, rather than re-recording it louder.** A laugh Billie did on that same verse take was a genuinely quiet, natural laugh they liked — instead of asking for a louder take, they rode the gain up **+27 dB** on that single moment "just so that it would pop out in the mix." A concrete, quantified example of the ad-lib treatment hierarchy: automation rescuing a good quiet performance instead of discarding it. → Automation, Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Gain Staging — Mix with the Masters (Finneas), Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas
- **The loudness trick:** the vocal sits far above the sparse track — intimacy = vocal loud + arrangement quiet, never vocal effects.
- **Distorted lane ("you should see me in a crown"):** parallel [Saturation Send](#/chain/saturation-send) under the whisper — clean center, dirty edges.
- Requires a *quiet room* more than any other chain here — the Shure SM57 lane works when the TLM hears too much house.

**Sources:** [MusicRadar — Billie/Finneas vocal sound](https://www.musicradar.com/how-to/billie-eilish-vocals) · [Mixing A Band — Finneas vocal production breakdown](https://mixingaband.com/vocal-production-for-billie-eilish-by-finneas) · Mix with the Masters (Finneas), Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas

chains.title: Bryson Tiller Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Bryson Tiller (Trap Soul — Exchange; Anniversary — Next to You; Outside), producer Foreartec
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** present-but-filtered, moody, chopped-down R&B — the vocal stays up front in the mix (not buried the way a straight lo-fi vocal would be), but a lo-fi/filter pass at the end gives it a "muffled through something" character that's the genre's signature. Three lanes depending on era/song: a light-touch **present + filtered** lane (Exchange), a light-touch **present, layered** lane (Next to You), and a heavier **chopped and screwed** lane (Outside).
**Signal source:** built from scratch in this breakdown rather than pulled from a real session — the general shape (pitch tool → space → time-based FX → a character/lo-fi finishing stage) is the reusable part, not exact settings.

## Lane 1 — Present + filtered (Exchange, *Trap Soul*)

1. **Little AlterBoy** — pitch shifted up a touch; kept subtle, this is not a full character/robot effect, just enough lift to sit the vocal in its slot.
2. **Reverb → EQ → Delay** — standard placement/space stage (source didn't specify exact plugin per stage; on this vault, ValhallaRoom for the reverb and Pro-Q 4 for the EQ are the natural first calls).
3. **kHs Bitcrush — Quantize (sample-rate) reduction as the finishing stage.** Bounce the whole processed vocal and drop the **Quantize** knob down until the top end reads as muffled/"filtered out" rather than clean-hi-fi, while staying present in the mix — this is the signature Exchange-era Tiller vocal texture. Source used Edison's sample-rate control; kHs Bitcrush's Quantize knob is the owned equivalent.

*Why:* the vocal is the main melodic element of the sample (per the source, "the most important part"), so it can't be washed out the way a background layer would be — the filtering has to land after everything else, as a final color pass, not as an upfront processing choice.

## Lane 2 — Present, layered (Next to You, *Anniversary*)

1. **Little AlterBoy → Reverb → EQ → Delay** — identical light-touch chain to Lane 1's steps 1–2, but **no** bitcrush/filter finishing stage this time — this song's vocal stays cleaner.
2. **A second vocal layer, chopped from a separate recording** (not a duplicate/double of the lead take) — layered under/around the lead for texture and thickness, rather than a straight ADT double.

## Lane 3 — Chopped and screwed (Outside)

1. **Little AlterBoy → Phaser-Flanger → Cableguys HalfTime** *(unowned — Plugin Wishlist)* — gives a slowed, warped "chopped and screwed" feel.
2. **A shaper-box stage last** *(likely Cableguys ShaperBox — unowned, Plugin Wishlist)* — described as "completely" changing the vocal's sound; treat this as the stage doing the real character transformation, with the pitch/flange/half-time stack before it only setting up the raw material.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | single, present, filtered | nothing, or one low double |
| Hook | doubled, filter opened | harmony thirds + one octave-down layer |
| Bridge / switch | the chopped-and-screwed lane | pitched-down copy of the same line |

**The move — the filter is the section marker.** The "muffled through something" pass is dialed *back* for the hook and pushed harder for the verse, so the same voice reads as arriving without a level change. Cheaper and more on-genre than adding parts.

**Stack count: 1 → 3–4.** Modest. He stays upfront rather than becoming a wall — that's what separates this from a straight lo-fi vocal.

## Notes / variations

- All three lanes share the same **skeleton** — pitch tool → space (reverb/EQ/delay) → a time-or-lo-fi finishing stage — with the finishing stage swapped per song: sample-rate reduction (Lane 1), nothing extra (Lane 2), or half-time + shaper (Lane 3). Pick the finishing stage by how "degraded" the target vocal should read.
- Companion instrumental recipes for the same three songs (guitar sample layers, vintage piano, reversed synth, the Serum from-scratch bass) are on the source video page, not duplicated here — see Source.
- Not yet built against a real UAD/tracking chain (no recording-stage info in the source) — treat this as a **processing-only** style chain, layered on top of whichever track chain ([Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) etc.) captures the performance.
- Sibling in the same trapsoul/2000s-R&B lane: [2000s R&B Piano Sample Chain](#/chain/2000s-r-b-piano-sample-chain) — a full instrumental+vocal sample build (piano/counter-melody/strings/vocal) explicitly aimed at Tory Lanez/Bryson Tiller, with its own 6-stage lead-vocal chain (octave-up → AlterBoy → EQ → Decapitator-if-needed → reverb → light delay).

**Sources:** loner, [the secrets behind bryson tiller's 'trapsoul' sound!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RVJ5fOlLy4w) — video-derived, 2026-08-11.

chains.title: Charli XCX Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Charli XCX / A.G. Cook (360, Von dutch, Vroom Vroom, Track 10, Everything is romantic)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** the voice as plastic — hard Auto-Tune worn as jewelry ("I drink and I smoke and I use Auto-Tune"), distortion for attitude, **formant shifting as an expressive tool** (A.G. Cook shifts formants to make lines read younger/older without pitch change), all presented bone-dry and abrasively upfront over minimalist club production punctuated by abrupt silences.
**Signal source:** Neumann TLM 102 close and confident — delivery is *spoken-bratty* as much as sung; attitude over accuracy (Auto-Tune will handle accuracy anyway).

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — driven a little (the edge starts here)
2. **UAD 1176LN** — 4:1 fast, 3–4 dB
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — bypass

## Chain overview
Hard tune → formant play → crush → distort → dry presentation. Brat-era vocals are *more* processed than Travis but *less* spacious — the effects are on the voice itself, not the room around it.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Auto-Tune Pro — Jewelry-grade tune
- **Retune 0, Humanize 0**, Classic algorithm — the snap is celebrated. Automate key/scale changes for deliberate warble moments.

### 2. Little AlterBoy — Formant character (the A.G. Cook move)
- Formant ±2–4 (pitch untouched): up = brattier/younger, down = darker/detached — **automate it per section or per line** ("Everything is romantic" style). Print bold choices as separate takes/layers.

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Flatten hard
- 6:1, **5–8 dB** — zero dynamics; the voice becomes a synth stab.

### 4. Decapitator — The attitude
- Style E, Drive 4–6, Mix 40–60%, Punish for the shouted lines — audible, unapologetic distortion (this is an *insert*, not a send — the dirt IS the tone).

### 5. Pro-Q 4 — Bright plastic finish
- HPF 100–120 · presence 3–5 kHz forward · air up — hyperpop vocals are bright to the point of glassy (opposite of the Travis hood).

## Step 3 — Effects (dry, then extreme — no middle)
- Default state: **dry, center, loud.** The minimalism (A.G. Cook mutes everything, leaves silences) makes the dry voice enormous.
- The extremes, automated in for single words/bars: pitch-throw an entire line ±12 (Little AlterBoy), [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other) feedback spikes into self-oscillation as transitions, one sudden cavernous [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) word, stutter/retrigger edits (chop the audio itself).
- Stacks: unison clones (same take duplicated with different formant/distortion settings) rather than re-sung doubles — the *clone* aesthetic, deliberately inhuman.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | **spoken or half-sung**, retune 0, bone dry | nothing |
| Pre | same, formant shifted up | one clone |
| Hook | hard-tuned, sung | 4–6 clone stacks, formants split high/low |
| Break | *silence* — the vocal stops mid-phrase | — |

**The move — spoken verse against tuned hook.** That's the dynamic, and it's the whole vocal arrangement. Formant automation does what a key change would do elsewhere: a line reads younger or older with no pitch change.

**The silence is a part.** A.G. Cook's mute is an arrangement event — see Dance Pop (Dua Lipa, Charli XCX) § Arrangement. Write it in deliberately rather than letting a section just end.

**Stack count: 1 → 6, all clones of one take.**

## Notes / variations
- **Pop lane (Track 10 / party 4 u):** keep the hard tune, drop distortion, add wash — hyperpop's soft inverse.
- **Club lane (Vroom Vroom / 360):** distortion forward, sidechain the vocal itself to the kick, spoken-word verses barely tuned against hard-tuned hooks (the contrast is the writing).
- Production context: EDM Subgenres + Modern Pop arrangement discipline — mute more than you add.

**Sources:** [MusicRadar — the theory behind Brat](https://www.musicradar.com/music-tech/recording/i-drink-and-i-smoke-and-i-use-auto-tune-but-whats-the-music-theory-behind-charli-xcxs-brat) · [A.G. Cook vocal processing breakdown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WnQ9Hr_YS2U) · [Noise Chest — 360 remake](https://noisechest.com/articles/charli-xcx-360)

## From videos — Music, Fashion, Film era (Tape Notes) — a deliberate pivot away from the Brat sound above

Charli, A.G. Cook and Finn Keane frame this album explicitly as "the polar opposite" of *Brat*'s hard-tuned, hyperpop-plastic vocal approach — rawer, more "bendy" and live-feeling. Newest-first:

- **Vocal moving in and out of tune within a song, for a raw-vs-classic contrast — the direct inverse of the Brat-era "always hard-tuned" default above.** "Rock Music" alternates a loosely/barely-tuned, live-feeling delivery against sections of classic hard Auto-Tune, rather than committing to one setting throughout. *(general starting point — no specific Retune/Humanize values given)* → Vocal Tuning — Tape Notes, TN 185 Charli XCX, A. G. Cook, Finn Keane - Full Video Episode
- **AlterBoy's Robot/Quantize mode for flat, static backing textures, not the formant-automation move above.** On "Card Declined," nonsense-syllable backing vocals run through AlterBoy's robot mode read as "static one-note things," not real harmonies — a different AlterBoy use case from this chain's usual per-line formant automation. → Little AlterBoy — TN 185 Charli XCX, A. G. Cook, Finn Keane - Full Video Episode
- **Crunched, hard-panned backing vocals (Waves Butch Vig Vocals) promoted to lead at a song's end, artifacts deliberately left in.** On "Rock Music," heavily distorted BVs sit hard-panned for most of the song, then become the loud lead at the very end — extra digital grit from AlterBoy/Butch Vig is kept rather than cleaned up, with only light compression for range. Explicit philosophy: "we're leaning into all of that sort of extra dirt... doesn't really matter [if it's] digital or analog." → **Waves Butch Vig Vocals**, Little AlterBoy — TN 185 Charli XCX, A. G. Cook, Finn Keane - Full Video Episode

## From videos — Ian Kirkpatrick ("Move Me", Crash era)

The documented lead chain from Ian's Move Me breakdown (tracked on the SM7 in-session; Charli "backs off the mic when loud — a real-life compressor"). Order: **Squasher** (light) → **mostly-dry SSL bus comp** (parallel, dry/wet to dodge phase) → **Soothe 2** (~1k–8k thrash; soft-cranked vs hard-subtle react differently) → **FabFilter Pro-C2** (peak-reduction *automated* as dynamics) → **gem Dopamine** (air back post-de-ess) → **Pultec Pro** (cut ~30 Hz, boost 16k). Newest-first:

- **Automate the compressor's peak reduction for a "naked" moment** — pull reduction back on a lyric so the vocal jumps out; lower loud words into the comp so they don't over-trigger. → Compression, Automation — [Move Me Full](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22odAiV5I5w)
- **Mono→stereo-double dynamic** — verse mono/intimate, hook stereo double (spatial contrast, not volume). → Width and Stereo — [Charli Vocal FX](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByPr9CMVnIg)
- **Hide synths from the vocal word (PadShop granular, recorded live not printed)** + octave-up **Little AlterBoy** (drive maxed) as a hook-escalation layer; **double-time individual words** on the looped last chorus. → PadShop, Little AlterBoy, Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — [Charli Vocal FX](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByPr9CMVnIg)
- **Keep the tuning artifact** — a Melodyne squeak became the song's hype "woot." → Melodyne — [Charli Vocal FX](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ByPr9CMVnIg)

chains.title: Dijon Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Dijon (Absolutely — Many Times, Talk Down, Big Mike's; Baby-era rawness)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** cracked, desperate, *performed* — a voice breaking up at the edges with the whole room bleeding in. The character is mostly capture, not plugins: omni mic in an untreated room, monitors blasting, take-one energy kept. What sounds like "processing" on Absolutely is largely **bleed** — the entire song coming back through the vocal mic ("It's literally just his voice… you're hearing the entire song coming through" — Tommy King).
**Signal source:** a raw, committed take. Comp *lightly* — imperfections are the genre.

## Step 1 — Record (this chain lives or dies here)
- **Mic:** Neumann TLM 102 in **omni** if available — otherwise back off the mic 1–3 ft in an untreated room. His album chain was an AKG 414 (omni) → Neve 1073 — yours: **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)**, driven harder than a clean pop vocal (the 1073 pushed = the first distortion stage).
- **Record with the speakers ON** (moderate, or one small speaker) — the bleed is the glue. Or the Shure SM57 handheld with monitors up for the aggressive lane.
- Sing it like a take, not a comp — punch full phrases, keep cracks, breaths, mic handling. No **UAD 1176LN** needed on the way in unless peaks are wild (2 dB max); **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** bypass.

## Chain overview
Level → drive → band-shape → break up → real-room space. Everything pushes toward "performance in a room," away from "vocal on a track."

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. LALA — Leveling
- **3–6 dB GR**, pushed harder than tasteful — the constant opto squeeze keeps the quiet cracked phrases as loud as the shouts (that suffocating closeness).

### 2. Decapitator — The break-up
- Style N or E · Drive 4–6 · **Punish on for the peaks moments** · Mix 50–70% — this is a *lead* effect, not seasoning
- **Why:** The signature — the voice audibly distorting when he pushes. Automate Drive/Mix up on the emotional peaks so the breakup follows the performance.

### 3. Pro-Q 4 — Rough shape
- Gentle HPF ~80 Hz (keep chest — don't clean it) · tame 2.5–4 kHz only if the distortion gets spiky · **no air shelf** — polish is the enemy.

### 4. RC-20 Retro Color — Texture
- Tape/Lo-Fi · wobble 10–20% · noise 10% · Mix ~30% — the take sounds *found*, not produced.

### 5. Soothe2 — Only if needed
- Light, 2–5 kHz — rescue listenability without sanding the grit.

## Step 3 — Effects (sends)
- [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) pushed **hot** (this mix's "space" = one shared room, everything in it) · [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) wobbly · occasional one-word throws ([Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other)) that distort with the voice.
- Stacks: loose, unaligned, different distances from the mic — pile takes like a crowd, not a choir (opposite of the pop rules).

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| All of it | **one take, start to finish** | the room, and the rest of the song bleeding through the mic |

**The move — there is no vocal arrangement.** The performance is the arrangement. Sections differ by how hard he pushes, where the voice cracks, and how much the monitors bleed back in. Stacking would destroy the thing that makes it work.

**What to actually plan:** which section he sings *hardest*, and whether the bleed gets louder with it. That's the only structural decision on the table — and it's made while tracking, not after.

**Stack count: 1. Always.**

## Notes / variations
- **The arrangement is the effect:** vocal LOUD and center (louder than a "correct" mix), band sparse and bleeding — if the vocal feels uncomfortably present, it's right.
- **Screamed lane ("Big Mike's"):** Shure SM57 → UAD Neve 1073 slammed → Decapitator Punish, no cleanup.
- **Soft lane ("Skin"):** drop Decapitator to mix ~20%, keep RC-20 + room — intimate but still textured.

**Sources:** [Reverb — Dijon's omnidirectional process](https://reverb.com/news/dijon-interview) · [MusicRadar — the "secret sauce"](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/people-ask-that-question-so-much-because-he-has-such-an-identifiable-sound-its-literally-just-his-voice-the-secret-sauce-that-creates-dijons-distinctive-vocal-sound-isnt-what-you-thought-it-was)

chains.title: Dua Lipa Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Dua Lipa (Don't Start Now, Levitating, Physical, Houdini)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** the disco-pop powerhouse — a naturally dark, low-mid-rich alto kept punchy and rhythmic over a busy dance floor. The documented chain (Ian Kirkpatrick, "Don't Start Now") is instructive: **many of her vocals are cut on a handheld Shure SM7B** — close cousin of your Shure SM57 — with the character coming from smooth opto compression and *taming her prominent low mids* so the voice cuts without shouting.
**Signal source:** Shure SM57 handheld (yes, really — the movement/energy in the performance beats mic technique here), or TLM for the balladry.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — solid gain (a dynamic needs it), clean
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 2–3 dB smooth (the LA-3A in Kirkpatrick's chain is this family — opto glue)
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — low ATTEN @ 60–100 Hz (handheld rumble), nothing else

## Chain overview
Sweep the subs → smooth opto → soothe the low mids → tune tight-ish → bright rhythmic finish. The dance-pop insight: the vocal is a *rhythm instrument* — consonants land on the grid, dynamics flattened enough to ride the groove.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Clean sweep
- HPF ~30–40 Hz first (the documented first move — the comp shouldn't react to sub junk), then a real HPF ~90 · check 200–400 Hz but *don't* gut it yet (next stage handles it dynamically).

### 2. LALA — The smooth engine
- **3–5 dB GR** constant — the LA-3A-style always-on silk that keeps power without edge.

### 3. Soothe2 — The documented trick
- **Pre-emphasis centered on the LOW MIDS (200–500 Hz)**, soft mode — her body/power lives there and overpowers the track; soothe ducks it only when it blooms. (Most vocal soothe targets 2–6 kHz — this is the opposite move, and it's the Dua-specific one.)

### 4. Auto-Tune Pro — Tight pop
- Retune 20–35, Humanize 50 — locked enough to be rhythmic, not robotic.

### 5. Pro-C 2 — Rhythm flatten
- 4:1, 2–4 dB — dance vocals sit *still* on top of a pumping track.

### 6. Pro-Q 4 — Finish
- Presence +1–2 @ 3–4 kHz · air +1–2 @ 12 kHz · the low mids are already handled — resist cutting them statically.

## Step 3 — Effects (sends)
- **Tight and rhythmic, not washy:** [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other) 1/8 synced, ducked hard (the delay pumps with the track) · [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) short/bright · plate bloom only on pre-chorus/breakdown moments.
- Stacks: chorus doubles hard L/R tuned tight, low octave tucked under hooks (the disco thickener), ad-lib answers drenched while the lead stays dry.
- Send the lead through the mix's **pump** lightly (a touch of Kickstart 2 on the vocal bus in four-on-floor sections glues her to the groove — subtle).

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | single, dry-ish, mono-ish, rhythmic | nothing |
| Pre-chorus | single, widening | one double, stack starting to open |
| Chorus | lead + doubles **hard-panned in fours** | harmonies inside the stack, ad-lib answers wide |
| Post-chorus | out — the instrumental hook takes over | — |

**The move — the stack widens into the chorus.** Verse mono, chorus in fours: that width jump *is* the lift, not a fader. Pair it with the filter opening on the track (see Dance Pop (Dua Lipa, Charli XCX) § Arrangement) and the chorus lands with no level change at all.

**Everything serves the groove grid.** Consonants land on the beat — the vocal is a rhythm instrument first, which is why the stacks can be this dense without turning to mush.

**Stack count: 1 → 4 + harmonies.**

## Notes / variations
- **Future Nostalgia lane:** brighter, more air, funk-guitar-like rhythmic phrasing.
- **Houdini/dance lane:** harder tune, more delay throws, vocal chops as instruments (House - EDM vocal rules).

**Sources:** [SOS — Inside Track: Don't Start Now](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-dua-lipa-dont-start-now)

## From videos — Ian Kirkpatrick streams

The producer's-eye view of her records (New Rules, Don't Start Now, Fever, Pretty Please). Signal front-end: **SM7 → BAE 1084 → (rarely a Distressor) → Burl B2 Bomber** converter/clock. He tracks *in the session* — often her **demo take is the record** (Pretty Please, Fever). Newest-first:

- **Half-speed vocal tracking** — keep a copy at half speed, have her sing to it, then speed up so vibratos come out fast and tight; also the "weird" double-time parts (sing the rhythm at half, Cubase speeds to double). → Pitch and Formant — [New Rules (25 Tips)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHSmH57_wY8) · [Fever](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0cG4_vxe1tY)
- **Auto-Tune on while tracking (speed), then Melodyne everything after** — light AT to keep it usable, real tuning in Melodyne (tune only what needs it, chop notes first, average-line, some notes slammed hard for effect). → Auto-Tune Pro, Melodyne — [New Rules](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHSmH57_wY8) · [SLDMML](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IRQC25nu_s8)
- **Lead chain (chopped-vocal version):** Clean-Sweep EQ (kill 22–25 Hz so the comp acts on audible signal) → **UAD 1176 all-buttons "smash"** → responsible OTT → **Pultec boost 10k *into* the de-esser** → de-ess. Personality = chop + smash. → UAD UA 1176LN, OTT, UAD Pultec EQP-1A, De-essing — [HIT Vocal Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LMjkfMIhXdA)
- **Reverb-width automation 30%→100%** across the song; **print reverbs to envelope/cut them**; print-mono-compress the verb for dense ambience. → Reverb, Width and Stereo — [Vocal Production for Dua Lipa](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0cG4_vxe1tY)
- **Background-vocal group:** ~60% wet, heavy GR (want them far), EQ boost 16k / dip 700 / atten 100, then Avox Sybil de-ess; de-ess BVs hard for center definition; **separate the breaths** to a high-passed track. → [2 Backup Vocals Group](#/chain/backup-vocals-group), De-essing — [New Rules](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHSmH57_wY8) · [Fever](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0cG4_vxe1tY)
- **Hide a synth (PadShop from the vocal word) behind a standout lyric** instead of a reverb throw; chop tiny vocal fragments to a dedicated echo track. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, PadShop — [Hiding Synths](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/9Eza4jngazI)

## From videos — Josh Gudwin (mix engineer, "Electricity")

Mix engineer's-eye view (not the producer/writer above) of a real stem-handoff mix — Josh Gudwin working from a track a producer ("Mark") sent him already sounding good, at 118 BPM. Stated approach throughout: build off the existing mix rather than replace it, keep the producer's engineer's sends/plugins where they already work, and split every vocal onto its own track for individual (not blanket-bus) treatment. Newest-first:

- **Per-track vocal chain, in order: Pro-Q 4 (filtering) → an SSL-style channel EQ (broad, unowned — Plugin Wishlist) → an SSL-style channel comp's "Z" default preset (very light, barely audible, no EQ — owned stand-in Glue Compressor) → Soothe2 (Mix 38%, never run a resonance-suppressor plugin at 100% on vocals) → Pro-Q 4 again (~2–2.5 dB broad) → narrow multiband problem-frequency cuts at 2.5–4.5 kHz → UAD Teletronix LA-2A (Peak Reduction 3–7, Gain to taste) → a subtractive-only multiband EQ + de-esser (McDSP C6, unowned — owned stand-in Pro-MB) for low/high shelving and problem-frequency notches.** Every vocal performance is on its own track and gets its own version of this chain, tailored — "some need a little bit more compression, some need less compression" — never copy-pasted wholesale. The C6-style stage is deliberately all-subtractive (no boosts); the only boost anywhere in the chain is the small SSL EQ move upstream. → Pro-Q 4, Soothe2, UAD Teletronix LA-2A, Pro-MB, Glue Compressor, Compression, Multiband Compression, De-essing, Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **A parallel "girth" aux for a fuller/louder vocal revision without raising the fader: duplicate the vocal's master aux, EQ it with a default filter pass (cut a little low and high), hit it with an 1176-style compressor ("smashing" but not fully), and blend the duplicate back in at roughly −33 dB.** "That's a quick little trick if you need to get a little change in your vocal and you can't figure out what you're doing, just duplicate your aux and put some different plug-ins on there. Filter out frequencies that you don't need, and accentuate those that you do or take out the ones that are bothering you, and hit it with some compression, and turn it up or down to taste." The 1176 stage is captioned as "CLA-76" — mapped to owned UAD UA 1176LN. → Pro-Q 4, UAD UA 1176LN, Parallel Processing — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **A personal default OPTO compressor recipe for background/other vocal parts: mid Attack, mid Release, ~3.5 dB GR, make-up gain set to roughly three-quarters of the GR amount.** Read as Waves R-Comp (unowned — Plugin Wishlist); owned-lane stand-in UAD Teletronix LA-2A. → UAD Teletronix LA-2A, Compression — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **Kick-triggered sidechain compression (a C2-style plugin) on a lead vocal track, kept from the producer's stem even though its origin was unclear** — "not sure if Mark had it... but it's on there now." A separate sidechain move on the a cappella hook section WAS the producer's own choice, kept untouched and called out as one of the mixer's favorite moments in the song. → Sidechaining — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **Kept the producer's original vocal reverb + delay sends rather than rebuilding them: UAD Pure Plate Reverb (demoed, then had to buy after mixing on it) plus a second unidentified reverb, and an H-Delay + ValhallaDelay pair with a ~1.5 kHz EQ cut on the harsh part of the return.** Also sends to a Bricasti hardware reverb (unowned — Plugin Wishlist) and a separate hall reverb. A three-layer "ear candy" delay-throw send (tucked quarter-note + audible filtered reverb + a "half-verb blast," then trimmed further after listening) is dialed for feel, not clarity. → UAD Pure Plate Reverb, H-Delay, ValhallaDelay, Reverb, Delay, Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **Inherited plugins kept without knowing their origin, purely because the sound already worked — RVox on a "screwed hook" vocal, and a "Studio D" stage kept explicitly "not trying to take away the vibe, I'm trying to keep the vibe and build upon that."** The clearest single statement of this mixer's overall philosophy: build off a good producer mix rather than replace it. → RVox, Mix Handoff — Mix with the Masters, Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin

chains.title: Frank Ocean Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Frank Ocean (Blonde — Self Control, Ivy, Nikes, White Ferrari; channel ORANGE ballads)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** bone-dry, dead-center, *breathing* — the anti-Travis. Dynamics kept (whispers stay whispers, belts stay belts), pitch edited by hand not snapped, and the production interest comes from **many differently-treated voice layers placed in 3D** rather than effects on one voice. Garage-recorded intimacy with the confidence to be nearly naked.
**Signal source:** Neumann TLM 102 close (3–5"), a real room but not a dead booth. Performance-first: comp for *emotion*, not accuracy — the best crack wins.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — clean, low gain
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 1–2 dB only (the dynamics ARE the record)
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — bypass or hair of 12 kHz

## Chain overview
Hand-tune → light shape → gentle 2:1 → placement layers. Less chain than any other style note — restraint is the technique.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Manual pitch (Melodyne-style — his documented tool)
- Hand-correct only the notes that *distract*; leave drift that carries feeling. No Auto-Tune Pro on the natural lane. (For the "Nikes" pitched voice: Little AlterBoy pitch +3–5 or formant-shifted, printed as its own track — a *character*, not a correction.)

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Light shape
- HPF 70–90 · small mud cut ~300 · presence untouched (closeness comes from the mic distance, not 4 kHz).

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Preserve
- **2:1, slow attack, 1–3 dB** on peaks only — the documented "let it breathe" setting. Automate clip-gain per phrase instead of compressing deeper.

### 4. Saturn 2 — Barely
- Tape, mix ~15% — analog rounding, nothing audible.

## Step 3 — Effects (placement, not wash)
- **Dry lead, dead center** — often literally no reverb send. Space comes from *other layers*:
  - Harmony layers panned wide with **different treatments each** (one dark + roomy, one pitched-up + dry, one whispered + close) — the Blonde signature 3D stack
  - A distant double: same line re-sung soft, 2–3 ft off mic, tucked −12 dB (real depth beats reverb)
- [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) mono, low, for select phrases · [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) only as an *event* on a single line, automated in and out.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | one voice, dry, dead center, dynamics intact | often literally nothing |
| Lift | same take | a pitched-down "alter ego" layer, or a telephone-EQ'd one |
| Hook | the fullest 3D placement — 3–5 layers | each layer treated *differently* and placed at a different depth |
| Outro | strips back to one, or to none | — |

**The move — layers differ by treatment, not by note.** This is the whole method and it's the opposite of a pop stack. Where Dua stacks four identical takes for width, Frank stacks four *differently-processed* voices — one clean, one pitched, one filtered, one drenched — and places them at different depths. The interest is spatial, not harmonic.

**Dynamics are kept.** Whispers stay whispers and belts stay belts, which means the arrangement can be sparse and still move. Don't compress the sections into one another.

**Stack count: 1 → 5, every one a different chain.**

## Notes / variations
- **The arrangement move:** strip everything under the best vocal moment (Self Control's ending) — the layers enter one at a time, each with its own space.
- **channel ORANGE lane:** more polish — normal pop chain ([Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track)) but keep the 2:1 dynamics philosophy.
- **Pitched-character lane ("Nikes"):** AlterBoy shifted voice AS the lead for a verse — commit, don't blend.

**Sources:** [SOS — Jeff Ellis: Engineering Frank Ocean](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/jeff-ellis-engineering-frank-ocean) · [TuneDrip — Frank Ocean vocal production](https://tunedrip.com/blogs/news/how-to-sound-like-frank-ocean-vocal-production-techniques-you-can-actually-use)

chains.title: Gorillaz Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Gorillaz (2D lead vocal — Feel Good Inc, Clint Eastwood, DARE, On Melancholy Hill)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** 2D's lead vocal — lo-fi, band-limited, tape-warped, slightly detached and unpolished on purpose. The character comes from narrowing the vocal's frequency window and degrading it, not from cleaning it up.
**Signal source:** Dry lead vocal, already comped/edited, no processing yet.

## Chain overview
Tune → band-limit → level → degrade (the core ingredient) → tame new harshness → subtle wobble/width → dub-style delay → boxed reverb. The whole chain works against "clean" — every stage after compression is there to remove fidelity, not add polish.

## Signal chain

### 1. Auto-Tune Pro — Pitch character
**Starting point:**
- Mode: Classic
- Retune Speed: 35–50
- Key/Scale: match song key
- Humanize: on, ~50%
- Natural Vibrato: default

**Why:** Keeps the vocal glued to key without the hard-tune snap — 2D's delivery is laid-back and occasionally loose, not robotic. Faster retune speed (20–25) is a valid variation for the more processed/detached lines.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Band-limiting EQ
**Starting point:**
- HPF: 24 dB/oct @ 120–150 Hz
- LPF: 24 dB/oct @ 5–6 kHz
- Broad cut: −2 to −3 dB bell @ 350–500 Hz
- Small shelf boost: +1.5 dB @ 2.5 kHz

**Why:** This is the single most defining move in the chain. Cutting both extremes narrows the vocal into a boxed, "small speaker" window before anything else touches it — everything downstream degrades that narrowed signal.

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Leveling compression
**Starting point:**
- Style: Vocal
- Ratio: 3:1
- Attack: 10 ms
- Release: Auto
- Gain reduction: 4–6 dB
- Knee: soft

**Why:** Evens out the performance without squashing it pop-vocal tight — keep enough dynamic looseness that the lo-fi stage has real transients to chew on.

### 4. RC-20 Retro Color — Lo-fi degrade (core ingredient)
**Starting point:**
- Mode: Lo-Fi or Tape
- Wow & Flutter: 15–25%
- Noise (vinyl/tape): 10–15%
- Bit Crush: 20–30%
- Mix: 40–60% (blend, don't commit fully dry/wet)

**Why:** Does the heavy lifting for the "Gorillaz" texture in one plugin — unstable pitch wobble, crushed bit depth, and print noise. Keep it as a blend so words stay intelligible; push higher for hookier/more processed lines, pull back for verses that need to sit under a busy arrangement.

### 5. Pro-DS — De-ess
**Starting point:**
- Range: 6–8 dB
- Frequency: 4–6 kHz (lower than a normal de-ess band since the top end is already rolled off by Pro-Q 3)
- Mode: Split-band

**Why:** Bit-crushing and tape saturation both add digital/harmonic harshness in the sibilance range — this reins it in without smoothing away the grit from step 4.

### 6. kHs Chorus — Subtle wobble/width
**Starting point:**
- Rate: 0.3–0.6 Hz (slow)
- Depth: 15–25%
- Mix: 15–20% (parallel)

**Why:** A touch of instability and width reminiscent of the slightly-detuned doubling in Gorillaz vocal stacks — not a lush pop chorus, just enough to feel unstable.

### 7. Echo — Dub slap delay (send/return)
**Starting point:**
- Sync: dotted 1/8 or 1/4 note
- Feedback: 15–25%
- Filter repeats: band/low-pass around 1.5–3 kHz
- Return level: 10–15%

**Why:** Filtered, degraded slap-back repeats sitting behind the dry vocal are a recurring Gorillaz production signature — the repeats should sound more boxed than the source, not less.

### 8. ValhallaRoom — Boxed reverb (send/return)
**Starting point:**
- Size: small–medium
- Decay: 0.6–1.0 s
- Pre-delay: 15–25 ms
- Damping/filter: roll off both highs and lows on the return
- Return level: 15–20%

**Why:** Gives space without restoring fidelity — filter the return to match the vocal's narrowed band so the reverb doesn't sound cleaner/wider than the dry signal it's tailing.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | 2D — band-limited, tape-warped, detached | nothing |
| Chorus | 2D doubled, still narrow | a loose octave-up or a woolly harmony |
| Feature | **a different character entirely** — different voice, different degradation | — |

**The move — the guest verse is a different treatment, not just a different person.** The band's structural signature is that each character gets their own frequency window and their own damage. A section changes because the *processing* changes hands.

**Narrow it, don't clean it.** The character comes from the shrunken frequency window (see the chain above), so a "bigger" chorus means more of the same narrow voice, never a wider one.

**Stack count: 1 → 2–3.**

## Notes / variations
- For a more extreme/robotic 2D moment (bridge ad-libs, "Murdoc"-style lines), push Auto-Tune retune speed down to ~10–15 and RC-20 bit crush past 40%.
- If the track is dense, drop the Echo/ValhallaRoom return levels first — the band-limiting + RC-20 stages carry the vibe even dry.
- kHs Bitcrush or Decimort 2 are viable swaps for RC-20 Retro Color if you want to dial bit-crush and wow/flutter independently instead of RC-20's bundled character.

chains.title: Jack Antonoff Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Bleachers — Everyone for 10 Minutes (I'm Not Joking, We Should Talk, Dancing)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** not one fixed signal chain but a philosophy of matching mic + processing to the emotional read a specific song needs, then deliberately breaking his own rules when it serves the song. Three distinct approaches across three songs on the same album: a bone-dry room-mic'd band take, a deliberately mistuned/broken vocoder hook, and a fully tuned lead vocal (the only one on the record) used specifically because the artifact reads as "a soul stuck in a machine."

**Signal source:** Shure 50-series dynamic ("singing on a 50") on *I'm Not Joking* for maximum transient/proximity feel; Shure SM58 on *We Should Talk*; unspecified on *Dancing* (recorded twice as two separate full takes).

## Chain overview — three songs, three deliberately different vocal treatments

### 1. "I'm Not Joking" — dry, room-mic'd, zero-plugin band take

- **Mic:** a Shure 50-series dynamic, chosen specifically over a condenser (47) or an SM58 for how close/live it feels — "I want to feel like it is live... you lose that transient with [a booth mic]." Deliberately not isolated in a booth; recorded live with the band.
- **Processing:** none. Antonoff turns off every plugin in the session mid-demo to prove the vocal (and the whole band take) sounds no different — the point of the song is that almost nothing is processed.
- **Backup layer:** a hard-panned "choir of a man talking to himself in the mirror" — multiple takes of himself doing different character voices/registers, layered as a gang-vocal texture rather than a normal harmony stack. → Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs
- **Contrast technique (described, NOT used on this song — a "what not to do" demo):** his normal horn-doubling move — double the horn track, offset it (ideally on tape), pan hard, add a chorus/doubler on one side, ride automation into the bus. Real technique, just deliberately withheld here to keep the take pure. → Layering and Stacking

### 2. "We Should Talk" — tight machine grid + loose human "shitstorm," mistuned vocoder hook

- **Foundation:** the **Korg M1**'s (unowned — see Vintage Gear Worklist) built-in drum sounds with their stock early-90s reverb kept as-is (unashamedly, for the "Shania Twain"-era character) as the rhythmic grid, plus a static/unmoving ARP synth note held for tension underneath.
- **Mic:** Shure SM58, tracked live in the room over the grid.
- **Hook processing — TC Helicon, deliberately mistuned:** the "We should talk" hook vocal is doubled through a TC Helicon **left on the wrong pitch/tuning setting on purpose** — "wasn't even set to the right tuning but it's cool." A broken-preset-as-texture move, not a mistake he fixed.
- **Loose instrumental layer ("personality bits"):** a trace (3-string Cuban instrument, "12-string mandolin world"), doubled with a baritone 6-string played high plus a second baritone doing a rhythmic pattern, a direct-DI'd Ovation acoustic-electric (praised for a Lindsey Buckingham-style tone), banjo, and Moog Model D noise — all played slightly loose/"sloppy," explicitly to remind the listener "we're not living on this grid" against the tight M1/ARP foundation. → Layering and Stacking, Rhythm and Groove
