- **Space Echo played as a pitched instrument:** turn the unit's echo return up loud enough to self-oscillate/feed back, then manually ride the delay-time knob live to tune the resulting drone to a note that's "not really in key but hovering around it" — a real, repeatable technique (self-oscillating tape-echo feedback, pitch-tracked by ear) distinct from using the unit as a normal echo. → **Roland Space Echo RE-201** (unowned — see Vintage Gear Worklist)
- **The one tuned vocal on the whole album:** normally records a tuned scratch vocal then re-tracks it untuned for the final — on this song he kept the Auto-Tune specifically because the correction artifact read as "a soul stuck in a machine," matching the lyric's theme of being trapped in forward motion. → Vocal Tuning
- **General vocal-processing philosophy stated here:** TC Helicon / Korg VC-10 vocoder / Auto-Tune are treated as three different flavors of the same idea — a voice audibly processed/"digital and cold," used as an emotional device (someone "stuck" or "trapped") rather than for correction or polish.

### 3. "Dancing" — two full takes layered on top of each other

- **The core trick:** recorded the ENTIRE song twice as two independent, complete performances, then played both simultaneously as the final mix — not doubling one take, but layering two different full recordings. Credits Elliott Smith's habit of re-performing (not just doubling) guitar and vocal as the direct inspiration, taken one step further.
  - **V1** — minimal: one detuned acoustic guitar + one doubled vocal take, recorded at Church Studios, London.
  - **V2** — ornate: harpsichord, clavichord, an E-mu sampler and an unidentified Korg synth both holding sustained "stagnant" pad notes, and heavily tremolo'd electric guitars — a dense wash described as "a kaleidoscope of memory."
- **Manual fader-style automation:** rides V1 and V2 in and out of each other by hand in Pro Tools, explicitly likening it to riding a physical console fader rather than drawing automation curves — "manual automation isn't super common on Pro Tools."
- **Session color convention (his own, non-standard):** bass = red, main lead vocal = blue (other vocal/double takes = other shades of blue), guitars = green, ear-candy/texture tracks = yellow, older/alternate vocal takes = orange-brown — a personal navigation system for high-track-count sessions.
- **String part as a single unprocessed take:** wrote a "stagnant" string-style part (cello + plucked-violin idea) and played/recorded it himself in one take rather than sending it out for real strings, then drowned it in reverb — the pitchiness and imperfection of the single take is treated as a feature ("blips of memory"), not corrected. → Reverb

## Recurring, album-wide device (not song-specific)

**Harpsichord + clavichord as a deliberate "forgotten instrument" character**, used three ways across the record: straight (as a harpsichord), as a big stacked reverb-drenched dreamscape texture, and as a direct substitute wherever he'd normally reach for celeste/glockenspiel/tubular bells — chosen specifically because the sound has fallen out of use and reads as fresh again. The clavichord's pitch bends under harder playing, giving it a percussive, slightly "wild"/out-of-tune quality he leans into rather than avoids. Named (alongside the baritone guitar) as one of the two defining textural "heroes" of the whole album. → Sound Selection Guide

## Mixing/production philosophy (applies across the whole record, not one song)

- **Judge a mix outside the room.** Always leaves the studio and listens walking/driving before calling a mix done — the test is whether it reads as "just a song, in its best outfit" rather than "a bunch of interviewed parts."
- **Vocals can be deliberately UN-glued from the track.** Rather than always matching reverb/frequency content to blend the vocal into the instrumental (his usual approach), sometimes leaves the vocal sonically separate on purpose for a "hear the overdubness" aesthetic, citing later Lou Reed/Beatles records as reference. → Vocal Mic Technique
- **When a big vocal stack hits a wall, mute — don't add.** When five-to-ten-track harmony/double stacks stop cutting through, muting roughly half the tracks (rather than EQ'ing or compressing harder) makes the remainder read as bigger, because each surviving part gets more space. → Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs
- **Seek out unfamiliar gear on purpose.** States his best takes come from playing synths/instruments he doesn't know well — deliberately avoids "tasteful" playing on gear he's mastered, because familiarity produces safer, more generic results ("golden age" synth recordings existed because nobody knew the "right" way to play them yet).
- **Happy accidents are real but not the whole story.** Distrusts studio lore that reduces every good idea to a single lucky accident, but agrees the actual mechanism is putting yourself in a position (live band, unfamiliar gear, deliberate imperfection) where accidents can happen — not a passive "it just happened."

**Source:** Tape Notes, TN 182 Bleachers (Jack Antonoff) - Full Video Episode (Everyone for 10 Minutes — I'm Not Joking, We Should Talk, Dancing) — real subtitles, high confidence.

chains.title: James Blake Vocal Chain
chains.reference: James Blake — vocal delivered pre-reverbed/"wet" from the artist, mixed against a second co-lead vocalist (Slowthai — song unconfirmed, likely the slowthai *TYRON* era, Dec 2021)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a two-co-lead-vocalist mix where James's vocal arrived **already printed through the artist's own reverb** — the engineer's whole approach pivots on *not* touching that space, then building a fairly dense correction/taming chain underneath it, and finally solving the two-vocalist collision with a surgical, frequency-selective sidechain duck rather than manual automation. The interesting engineering here is less "how to make James Blake sound like James Blake" and more "how to mix a vocal you didn't record, without breaking what the artist already committed to."

**Signal source:** none — this is a mix-only breakdown of delivered stems (wet/printed lead + printed reverb channel + ad-libs with reverb baked in). No tracking chain to document.

## Chain overview

Per-track taming (de-ess → drive/character → EQ → resonance suppression → proximity fix → parallel comp → de-ess) → per-group bus shaping (group de-ess + darkening EQ, split lead vs. BV groups) → combined-group cross-vocalist sidechain duck (the headline move) → final air restoration. Two governing constraints run through every stage: (1) the printed reverb must never get touched by anything downstream, and (2) James's dynamics must survive intact since the take is already mixed-feeling on delivery.

## Step 1 — Per-track chain (lead vocal, repeated per lead + adjusted for BVs)

1. **Pro-DS — De-ess (first pass)** — FabFilter de-esser, tame the raw take before anything else touches it. *(no exact threshold/range given)*
2. **"Drive" — character/distortion** — plugin identity unconfirmed from audio alone; light saturation stage. See Saturation and Distortion.
3. **Pro-Q 4 — Basic EQ** — HPF the low end (general starting point ~80–120 Hz), one narrow-Q cut pulling out a single ugly resonance found by ear. Owned stand-in for the source's "basic SSL EQ." See EQ.
4. **Soothe2 — Resonance suppression** — "softening the aggression," a second-pass catch for whatever the EQ notch above didn't fully deal with.
5. **Pro-Q 4 — Proximity-effect correction (AudioSuite/offline)** — a batch, non-realtime dynamic-EQ pass targeting inconsistent low-mid buildup from mic-distance changes between phrases, applied surgically to specific bothersome words rather than the whole take. See Vocal Mic Technique. 🎬 *From video:* this whole stage only exists because the vocal is wet/printed — a dry take would get a normal compressor here instead.
6. **Pro-C 2 — Parallel compression (the only compression on the lead)** — deliberately parallel, not serial, specifically to preserve the artist's original dynamic performance while still "tucking in" a slightly denser version. See Parallel Processing.
7. **Pro-DS — De-ess (second pass)** — catches sibilance any of the above stages (esp. the drive/saturation stage) reintroduced or exaggerated.

## Step 2 — Group/bus stage (lead Group vs. BV Group, kept separate)

- **Lead Group:** bus de-esser targeting the 'ch'/'esses' consonant cluster, one named parameter value **set to 3.7** *(unit unconfirmed — likely a threshold or range)* → gentle low-pass around **10 kHz** on everything above → a broad **mid-frequency cut**. A deliberate darkening/thinning move on the lead bus, not the usual "add air" instinct — see Masking and Carving, MIDS Slot.
- **BV Group:** same chain shape, but its own named de-esser — **"Weiss Deess"** (unowned, see Plugin Wishlist) — rather than a copy of the lead group's de-esser.

## Step 3 — Combined Group: the cross-vocalist sidechain duck (headline move)

Both the lead Group and BV Group feed a single combined vocal Group. On that combined Group:

- **"Trackspacer" — 32-band dynamic EQ, external-sidechained to the OTHER vocalist (Slowthai)**, set to **M/S mode, Mid-channel only**, ducking the **1–6 kHz** zone specifically at the moments the two vocalists overlap.
- **Why Mid-only:** the Group also carries the printed reverb tails from Step 0 (James's delivered wet vocal) — running the duck broadband/stereo would pull the reverb down with it. Restricting the trigger to the dead-center Mid image ducks only the dry vocal content and leaves the (wider) reverb tail alone.
- **Why 1–6 kHz specifically:** that's where both vocalists' presence/intelligibility content collides — ducking James there "allows Slowthai to cut through the most" exactly when he enters.
- **Stated payoff:** without this, overlapping sections read as "mess in the middle" — a specific example called out is the word "champagne."
- **Owned equivalent:** Pro-Q 4 per-band **Dynamic EQ + External Sidechain + Stereo Placement (Mid/Side per band)** — build several dynamic bands spanning 1–6 kHz on James's group, point each band's sidechain input at Slowthai's vocal, and set Stereo Placement to Mid only. Soothe2's **external sidechain** mode is a rougher, broadband-only fallback for the same masking-avoidance job. See Sidechaining, Masking and Carving, Width and Stereo.

## Step 4 — Finishing

- **Clariphonic DSP MKII** — run last, explicitly framed as restoring "shimmer" the chain above may have cost rather than a first-pass brightening move. See AIR Slot.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | one voice, printed reverb intact | nothing, or a low pad-like held layer |
| Lift | same | **chopped / vocoded stacks used as an instrument**, not as harmony |
| Two-lead sections | both vocalists at once | resolved by frequency-selective ducking, not by automation |

**The move — the second vocal is a synth.** Chopped, pitched, vocoded stacks occupy the BED/MIDS slots the way a pad would. Treat them as instrumentation when you're deciding what else can play, or you'll double-book the slot.

**The real arrangement problem here is collision.** Two co-lead vocals in one section is a masking hierarchy question, not a mixing one — see Masking and Carving. The chain above solves it with a surgical duck; the cheaper fix is arranging them so they trade rather than overlap.

**Stack count: 1 → many, but as texture.**

## Notes / variations

- **Respect the delivered space rule:** when a vocal arrives pre-reverbed/printed, the whole downstream chain has to actively route around disturbing that reverb (see the Mid-only sidechain restriction above) — a constraint that doesn't exist on a dry delivery.
- **Two-lead-vocalist masking is a sidechain problem, not an automation problem** here — rather than riding faders by hand at the overlap points, the fix is a standing, always-on frequency-selective duck triggered automatically by the other voice's presence. Generalizes to any feature/duet arrangement with two vocalists sharing register.
- Not a full genre/artist "sound" template like the other Artist Chains notes — this is a single mix-session's problem-solving order, video-derived from one short breakdown clip. Treat Steps 1–2 as reasonable defaults for "taming a wet, already-processed vocal delivery"; Step 3 is the reusable, most-valuable idea.

**Source:** Mix with the Masters, MSM Mixing James Blake's Vocals ([watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7QJYsvr1Cuk)) — captions transcript, high confidence.

chains.title: Kenny Beats Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Kenny Beats vocal template (Alex Tumay lineage, 2020 → 2022 versions; ~150 released songs)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** the modern rap/melodic-rap *engineer's* chain — not an artist tone but the template that recorded ~150 songs (Vince Staples, 03 Greedo, Dominic Fike lane). Clean, fast, identical on every punch-in: lean tracking chain, **the chain lives on the group**, all space on shared sends, and the tune amount calibrated to the artist's identity. Built by copying Alex Tumay's (Young Thug's engineer) Pro Tools template into Ableton; updated 2022.
**Signal source:** condenser through a clean pre — Neumann TLM 102. Delivery: anything from dry rap verse to fully tuned hooks; the chain doesn't change, the Auto-Tune settings do.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — clean gain, barely driven; Kenny's chain colors later, not at the pre
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — his 2A stage, as **peak reduction not tone**: loudest word toward the quietest, "needle never past 7, 10 is really pushing it" on screams
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — low ATTEN only; no air boost printed (the raise happens in the box, adjustable)

**Track every take on TWO tracks** — monitored FX track + ghost latency track (no plugins, monitor off, out to a spare hardware pair); keepers come off the ghost track → Latency-Free Tracking. Record against a **2-track beat bounce** in a separate session — no limiter on the beat, ever. Lock tempo + key *before* anyone sings.

## Chain overview

Gate the room → tune per-lane → lean corrective chain **on the group, tracks empty** → everything spatial on shared sends (one EchoBoy family, three reverb tiers) → the "sound-good-izer" lift stays OFF until the song is done. Punch-ins 30 minutes apart sound identical because there is exactly one chain.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton, on [Main Vocal Group](#/chain/main-vocal-group))

### 0. Gate — room killer
- Low threshold (−40 dB zone) — chip bags, chair creaks, HVAC between phrases die here even in an imperfect booth.

### 1. Auto-Tune Pro — per-lane, the ONE plugin allowed on individual tracks
- **Five settings, done:** input voice type → key → scale → retune speed → style. Voice type is the forgotten one (Low Male/Alto/Soprano = range switch) — wrong = everything misreads
- **Retune map:** ~30–40 invisible support · **~7 = audible Travis/Greedo bite** · >10–12 full T-Pain chip
- **Humanize 0, always** — naturalness comes from low retune + **Legato** style instead (opposite knob-philosophy from Nate's Humanize-100 default — pick ONE per song)
- Mains vs ad-libs get *different* tune (ad-libs more, or Legato-vs-Soft-EFX split); goes on tracks when takes need different keys/settings.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — channel EQ
- Low cut + a small high raise ("people's voices just don't punch enough"), adjusted per voice · **Zero Latency while tracking → Natural Phase when mixing**.

### 3. Pro-DS — de-ess (2022 order: BEFORE the comp)
- Male Wide Band preset, threshold to taste — tames S's on the way *into* the compressor so the comp doesn't pump on sibilance. (His 2020 chain had it last; 2022 moved it up.)

### 4. Pro-C 2 or LALA — R-Compressor slot
- Gentle leveling, 2–4 dB GR — stage two after the tracking 2A (Compression Staging).

### 5. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — "fake Pultec" sweetening
- Light low boost + broad air lift, last in the chain — the polish stage.

### 6. — the "sound-good-izer" (OFF until the song is done)
- CLA Vocals-style last-mile lift: owned lane = Oxford Inflator or Saturn 2 light. It adds latency + character artists get used to while tracking; toggle on when the record is finished, then re-trim. → [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus)
- **Playback psychology:** the group chain runs slightly nicer than the headphone chain — drag-down playback sounds *better* than the take felt and artists push harder. "Psychological warfare, but healthy."

## Step 3 — Effects (sends — shared by ALL vocal tracks)

- **Delays: ALL EchoBoy** — 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, slap, 1/2 returns share one EchoBoy setting varied only by subdivision; **band-limit with EchoBoy's internal high/low cut**, no EQ after (one plugin per return, one tone family). → [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap), [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other)
- **Delays sidechain-duck to the lead** — compressor on the returns keyed from the vocal: tails tuck under words, bloom in gaps. → Sidechaining
- **Reverb tiers:** short = Pro-R 2 "Vocal Backings Bright" (tweaked; Kenny used the original Pro-R in 2022) — body only, "you don't really hear it" · long + super-long = ValhallaVintageVerb ("just sounds right on vocals"). 2020 alt-recipe: ValhallaRoom 3.0 s, 100% wet, ~90% depth, EQ on the return. → [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room), [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long)
- **Doubler:** dropped from the 2022 chain. 2020 mode: Doubler2 at ~20% on everybody — "a little bigger," never audibly doubled.
- **Ad-lib group = pan-L + pan-R + phone-filter center track** — the band-limited phone track cuts through *between* the mains; optional PanMan drifting center ad-lib. Harmony stacks: copy-pairs at stepped pans (25L/25R, then 15L/15R in Live terms) — width with no widener plugin. → [Backup Vocal Track](#/chain/backup-vocal-track), [Double Vocal Track](#/chain/double-vocal-track)
- **The "effects track"** — drag a line-end word to a dedicated track: loud EchoBoy **insert** (not send), high end cut, subdivision changed per throw, + long-verb send ducked under the ad-libs. Throws as arrangement events. → Automation

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lane | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | main vocal, punched in | doubles only on emphasis words |
| Hook | main + a tight double | harmonies + a low octave |
| Ad-libs | **own track, own group**, panned wide | delay throws on line-ends |

**The move — the arrangement is a template, not a decision.** The chain lives on the group and is identical on every punch-in, so an artist can build a stack in real time without anyone stopping to dial anything. That's what makes ~150 songs possible: the vocal arrangement is *fast* rather than clever.

**Doubles on emphasis words only** — not whole verses. Full-verse doubling flattens the delivery, which is the one thing this lane can't afford.

**Stack count: 1 → 4, built live.**

## Notes / variations

- **Sends are shared by mains AND ad-libs** — one space for the whole stack; that's why it glues.
- **Dry-verse / tuned-hook split (Greedo mode):** same chain, Auto-Tune bypassed on verse takes, ~7 retune on hooks — tune amount is the artist's identity, ask them.
- **vs [Travis Scott Vocal Chain](#/chain/travis-scott-vocal-chain):** Travis = the *drowned* version of this architecture (same tune + sends skeleton, wet/dark pushed to the aesthetic); Kenny's default stays clean and upfront.
- This is the lineage [Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) / [Main Vocal Group](#/chain/main-vocal-group) / [Vocal Bus](#/chain/vocal-bus) were built from — use those for the house default; use this note when you want the *all-Kenny* setup verbatim.

**Sources:** [Vocal Template (2020)](https://youtu.be/X_iDENABLmk) · [New Vocal Chain 2022](https://youtu.be/-SvBNOBWJ_8) · [Auto-Tune Process](https://youtu.be/dyr6F9DLG7c) — full notes: Kenny Beats - Recording and Voice Mix Process (Vocal Template) · Kenny Beats - New Vocal Chain 2022 · Kenny Beats - Auto-Tune Process

chains.title: Mac DeMarco Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Mac DeMarco (Chamber of Reflection, My Kind of Woman, Freaking Out the Neighborhood, Heart to Heart)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** the slacker croon — lazy, warm, slightly seasick. One voice, barely tuned, wrapped in **tape slap and pitch wobble** instead of reverb. The whole aesthetic is "expensive tape machine in a cheap bedroom": his records are tracked to actual tape with the vari-speed drifting.
**Signal source:** Shure SM57 — a cheap dynamic suits the croon (his classic era was cheap dynamics anyway — an SM57 is *more* period-correct than an SM7B). Relaxed, low-effort delivery *is* the instrument.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD UA 610-B (Unison)** — tube, pushed a little (soft round drive)
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 2–3 dB lazy
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — bypass

## Chain overview
Level → warm → wobble → slap. Four moves; stopping early is the style.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. LALA — Croon leveler
- 3–4 dB, constant gentle squeeze — flatters the lazy delivery into evenness.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Round it
- HPF 80 · LPF or high-shelf down above ~10 kHz (no modern air — this voice is AM-radio warm) · small 3 kHz lift if the words blur.

### 3. Kramer Tape — The machine
- 7.5 ips (darker) · flux medium · **wow/flutter ON and audible** (10–20%) · noise a touch
- **Why:** this stage is the genre — the pitch instability reads as nostalgia/unease. His actual method is vari-speed tape; Kramer's wow/flutter is the plugin path. (RC-20 Retro Color wobble is the alternative flavor.)

### 4. Chorus-Ensemble — Seasick (optional, for the synthy cuts)
- Slow vibrato-leaning setting, shallow, ~20% — the Chamber of Reflection queasiness (on that song the *whole track* wobbles, not just the vocal).

## Step 3 — Effects (sends)
- **[Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) is the reverb:** 100–140 ms, wobbly EchoBoy tape mode, feedback ~10%, send generous — the doo-wop slapback croon. Real reverb barely used ([Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) whisper at most).
- Doubles: loose unison on hooks only, drift kept.

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | one voice, barely tuned, tape slap | nothing |
| Chorus | same voice, slap send pushed | maybe one loose harmony, drifting |
| Outro | talking, laughing, or the tape running on | — |

**The move — the wobble is the width.** No stacks, no widening. Vari-speed drift and tape slap do the job doubles would do elsewhere, which is why one voice never sounds thin here.

**Don't tighten the double if you add one.** Drift is the point — the alignment rules that apply to a pop stack are exactly backwards for this lane.

**Stack count: 1, occasionally 2.**

## Notes / variations
- **Full-track move:** print gentle wow/flutter on the *mix bus* for a section (or whole song) — vocal wobble alone reads as an effect; everything wobbling reads as a world.
- **Another One / synth-ballad lane:** more chorus, softer slap, LALA deeper.
- **Rock lane (Freaking Out the Neighborhood):** drop the chorus, slap shorter (80 ms), let the 610-B drive harder.
- Pairs with Bedroom Pop - Indie and the Neo-Soul - Lo-fi texture rules.

chains.title: Myles Smith Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Myles Smith / Peter Fenn — *My Mess, My Heart, My Life* (Stargazing, My Mess, Dying Day)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** an emotionally raw, deliberately imperfect pop-vocal system built around a fixed stacking rule (lead + doubles + hard-panned doubles as the floor, on every hook, no exceptions) with two swappable extra layers on top depending on how big the song needs to feel — a named, physically-performed ad-lib layer ("Milesauce") for anthems, and nothing extra at all for intimate songs. Mic choice is treated as a raw-vs-clean performance decision, not a fidelity one, and can change mid-album for a single song when it serves the take.

**Signal source:** Neumann U87 (not owned) is the default tracking mic on their mobile rig; Shure SM7 (not owned, Shure SM7) swapped in specifically for texture/relaxation, sometimes for a whole lead vocal.

## Chain overview

Track (mic choice by feel) → lead + doubles + hard-panned doubles (fixed floor, every hook) → optional "Milesauce" ad-lib layer (Decapitator → 1176 → Capitol Chambers reverb) → vocal bus (DynOne multiband + Soothe2, both standing) → master bus (bleeds in from a continuously-running mix-bus chain, not a separate stage).

## Step 1 — Tracking: mic choice as a performance decision

- **Default:** Neumann U87 (not owned) on Miles' lead vocal, through a small Apollo on their mobile rig (Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII).
- **Swap to Shure SM7 when raw texture matters more than clean tone.** Most ad-libs/BVs go through the SM7 "just because it sounds raw"; one full song ("Solo") was tracked on an iPhone for the identical reason. On *Dying Day* the ENTIRE lead vocal moved to the SM7 instead of the usual U87 purely because it let Miles sit back and relax into the take — a performability-over-fidelity call, not a tonal endorsement of the mic itself. → Vocal Mic Technique.
- No heavy vocal tuning/processing mentioned at the tracking stage — the raw-texture philosophy starts at mic choice, not in post.

## Step 2 — The fixed stack floor (every hook, every song)

1. **Lead** — the main take.
2. **Doubles** — at minimum one double on every hook across the whole album, "I don't think there's a single hook I've done that's not at least a double" — even on the most stripped-back acoustic tracks (named example: "Grandma's Place").
3. **Hard-panned doubles (left/right)** — doubles panned hard to widen the hook further.

This three-layer floor is non-negotiable per their own description; everything below is additive on top of it, scaled to how big the song needs to read.

## Step 3 — "Milesauce": the named ad-lib layer (big songs only)

- **What it is:** Miles physically steps back from the mic and shouts/moves around it for a fourth, more aggressive texture layer — treated as its own instrument, not a normal double.
- **Chain (a saved preset, reused across songs):** Decapitator (driven hard, audibly distorting on purpose) → UAD UA 1176LN → UAD Capitol Chambers reverb (unowned — see Plugin Wishlist). Demoed dry vs. wet on *Stargazing*: dry is essentially room tone with no vocal-track plugins, wet pushes the Decapitator drive hard enough to make an already-deep voice sound "thick."
- **When to skip it:** deliberately left off *My Mess*, their most intimate/vulnerable song — "on an intimate song like this, you just gotta do what it calls for." The fixed stack floor (Step 2) still applies even when Milesauce doesn't.

## Step 4 — Vocal bus (standing, applies across songs)

- **Leapwing DynOne (unowned, multiband) run across the ENTIRE vocal bus** — every vocal element together, not per-track. On *Stargazing*: subtle, "brings out the transients." On *My Mess*: paired with the next stage for de-essing.
- **Soothe2 on a saved preset called "DS"**, paired with DynOne specifically on *My Mess* for harshness/sibilance control without a dedicated de-esser.

## Step 5 — Master bus (bleeds in continuously, not a separate mastering stage)

A standing master-bus chain (UAD Hitsville EQ "Mix" preset + God Particle with the limiter backed off — see [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)) runs throughout production, so the vocal bus above is always being heard against a near-final master rather than in isolation. See Creative Process and Idea Capture for the full mixing-as-you-go workflow this depends on.

## Notes / variations

- **The stack floor scales UP (Milesauce) or holds flat (My Mess) — it never scales down below lead+double+pan.** Treat the three-layer floor as the non-negotiable baseline for any hook, and decide the ad-lib layer per song based on how anthemic it needs to read.
- **Mic choice is a repeatable lever, not a fixed setup.** If a take feels stiff on the "good" mic, trying a rougher one (SM7, even a phone) is a documented fix here, not a downgrade.
- **This chain shares its reverb (Capitol Chambers) and its 1176 with the rest of the session's instrument busses** (shaker/tambourine, mandolin) — see Reverb — rather than using a vocal-only reverb, which is part of why the whole record reads as one cohesive room.

**Source:** Tape Notes, TN 184 Myles Smith & Peter Fenn - Full Video Episode ([watch](https://www.patreon.com/posts/161939546)) — real subtitles, high confidence.

chains.title: Tame Impala Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Tame Impala / Kevin Parker (The Less I Know the Better, Borderline, Eventually, Feels Like We Only Go Backwards)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** soft, dreamy, dissolved into the track — a falsetto-leaning voice **layered until Parker "can't recognize the sound of his own voice,"** phased and echoed, sitting 2–4 dB lower than a pop vocal ("the instruments are brutal, the voice is really soft"). Another instrument, not the focus.
**Signal source:** relaxed, breathy delivery — simple melodies, no runs. Parker tracks on a dynamic (MD-421); your Shure SM57 is the closer match, Neumann TLM 102 for the airier lane.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD UA 610-B (Unison)** — soft tube, gentle level (the round choice over the 1073 here)
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 2–3 dB smooth
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — bypass
- **The real step 1 is takes:** 4–8 unison layers of the same line, soft delivery — the blur between them IS the sound. Pitch-shifted doubles (octave/5th at low level) for thickness without "chipmunk."

## Chain overview
Thin it → level it → color it → smear it. His voice reads *thin on purpose* — don't fatten it; the lushness comes from layers + effects, not body.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Thin and seat
- **HPF up to ~150 Hz** (yes, that high) · scoop low mids −2 to −3 dB @ ~350 Hz · gentle presence, no aggressive air
- **Why:** the vocal cuts by being *narrow*, floating above the brutal instruments rather than competing.

### 2. Pro-C 2 — Subtle level
- 3:1 · 2–4 dB — even, unremarkable, invisible.

### 3. Saturn 2 — Warm blur
- Tape, low drive, mix ~25% — softens consonants into the wash.

### 4. PhaserFlanger or ValhallaSpaceModulator — The psych movement
- Slow phaser, low depth, ~20–30% mix — constant gentle sweep. Automate deeper per section/line ("Mind Mischief" moments).

## Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is most of the sound)
- **Tape echo:** EchoBoy Space Echo/Tape mode, 1/8 or dotted-1/8, feedback 25–40%, wobble/saturation ON, send generous — echoes louder relative to the dry than pop would allow.
- **Long modulated verb:** ValhallaVintageVerb (70s mode, 2.5–4 s, modulation high) — the dissolve. Send hot; duck it under the dry only if lyrics vanish entirely.
- [Width Send](#/chain/width-send) on the layered stack; slap for the drier RnB-leaning cuts ("The Less I Know the Better" verses).
- **Automate the delay time knob** for detune-warble transitions (the hardware move).

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | **no lead** — 4–8 unison layers blended equal | the layers are the vocal |
| Chorus | the same stack, phaser deepened | pitched-shifted octave/5th layers at low level |
| Transition | delay-time automation, detune-warble | — |

**The move — there is no lead take.** Parker layers until he can't recognize his own voice, blended so no single take is "the one." That's a structural choice, not a mixing one: it's why the vocal can sit 2–4 dB under a pop vocal and still read.

**Automate the effects per line, not per section.** Phaser depth and delay feedback move on individual words ("Mind Mischief"), which gives sectional contrast without touching the arrangement — the same timbre-over-density habit that runs through Psych-Pop (Tame Impala) § Arrangement.

**Stack count: 4–8, flat across the song.**

## Notes / variations
- **Mix placement is the trick most people miss:** tuck the vocal down until it *just* reads, glue it to the band with the shared verb — resist the pop instinct to feature it.
- **Currents/Slow Rush (cleaner):** less phaser, more chorus width, verb slightly shorter.
- **Lonerism (rawer):** more Saturn drive, echo feedback higher, everything wetter.
- **Deadbeat (2025) — Parker's own account, first-party, contrasts with the default recipe above.** Tracking: Shure SM7, held in hand while performing (chose it over a U47 clone specifically because he could hold and move with it while singing); tracked through a **dbx 165** compressor live. Post: "just compression and EQ… quite stock standard" — the character lives in the effects bus, not the tracking chain. **Doubling is a per-song call, not the 4–8-layer default:** on "My Old Ways" the main hook is deliberately left **single/undoubled** (to read as a sampled vocal), verses are the usual double-track. **Hard-panned whisper layer:** an extra whispery pass, panned hard L/R, heavily filtered (little bass or treble, midrange only) and heavily compressed — a near-inaudible "ASMR-y" width element distinct from the doubles (4 vocal elements total: 2 center doubles + 2 hard-panned whispers). Effects: EchoBoy (switched to from stock Ableton delay specifically for its stereo image, replacing *Currents*/*Slow Rush*-era stock echo), ValhallaRoom + Ableton's stock convolution Spring reverb on most tracks, Decapitator for light grit on some songs (e.g. "Dracula"). → TN 188 Tame Impala - Full Video Episode (Part 1) (Tape Notes)
- **Justice collab (Neverender, Hyperdrama, 2024) — the opposite of this chain's default: simple, live, single-take, minimally processed.** "The vocals are very simple. We recorded them in Conway in Los Angeles. And as soon as we were all together back in the room, and he was in the couch holding the mic like this, he sounded like an angel — he was singing everything perfectly." No 4–8 unison layers, no described phaser/echo/verb wash — Justice frame the whole session around being in one room and "rebounding on each other's musical proposition," not around the usual dissolve-into-the-track treatment. *(No mic, chain, or effects details given — logged as a contrasting reference point, not a settings recipe.)* → Vocal Mic Technique — Justice x Kevin Parker (Mix with the Masters), [Behind the Track｜'Neverender' by Justice & Tame Impala](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=emP9EWcqss4)
- Full genre context: Psych-Pop (Tame Impala).

**Sources:** [MusicTech — Tame Impala vocal effects guide](https://musictech.com/guides/essential-guide/learn-how-to-create-vocal-effects-like-tame-impala/) · [Reverb Machine — production tricks](https://reverbmachine.com/blog/tame-impala-production-tricks/) · [AudioTechnology — Currents live](https://www.audiotechnology.com/features/wild-things-how-tame-impala-plays-currents-live) · Justice x Kevin Parker (Mix with the Masters) — [Behind the Track｜'Neverender' by Justice & Tame Impala](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=emP9EWcqss4)

chains.title: The Weeknd Vocal Chain
chains.reference: The Weeknd (Blinding Lights, Die For You, Call Out My Name, Is There Someone Else?)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** the modern pop-R&B gold standard — silky, breathy intimacy that can open into a huge 80s belt without ever getting harsh. Warmth at 200–300 Hz + extended air above 10 kHz + *controlled* mids (slight 1–2 kHz dip) — expensive-sounding restraint, tuned invisibly, stacked wide on hooks.
**Signal source:** U87-class condenser in the references — your Neumann TLM 102 is the right family. Breath control IS the instrument; record close (3–6") for the intimacy proximity warmth.

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — clean-rich, minimal drive
2. **UAD Teletronix LA-2A** — 2–3 dB smooth optical (the CL-1B-style silk in his documented chains; LA-2A is your equivalent)
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — +1–2 @ 12 kHz air, low ATTEN @ 60 Hz

## Chain overview
Tune (subtle) → clean → two-stage comp → dynamic mids → color → de-ess → air. His documented mix chains run deep (Auto-Tune EFX → Pro-Q → Pro-MB → 1176 → doubler → MicroShift → plate) — the theme is *many light touches*.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Auto-Tune Pro — Invisible tune
- Retune 30–45, Humanize 100 — locked but human (the EFX-era pull is slightly rubbery; a touch faster than you'd expect for how natural it reads).

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Sculpt
- HPF 70–90 Hz · **keep 200–300 Hz** (his warmth — don't scoop it like a rap vocal) · dip 1–2 kHz −1 to −2 dB (the anti-harshness move) · air shelf +2 @ 10 kHz+.

### 3. Pro-C 2 → LALA — Two-stage
- Pro-C 2 Vocal style 3–4 dB, then LALA 1–2 dB ride — glassy evenness for long sustained notes.

### 4. Pro-Q 4 (dynamic) or Soothe2 — Mid control
- Dynamic dip 2–4 kHz on the belts only — how he gets loud without ever biting.

### 5. Little Radiator — Tube silk
- Low drive (it's in his documented chain) — warmth that reads as "expensive," not "dirty."

### 6. Pro-DS — De-ess
- Split-band, slightly firm — all that air makes S's expensive too.

## Step 3 — Effects (sends)
- **[Width Send](#/chain/width-send) (MicroShift — literally his documented plugin):** hooks and stacked choruses wide, verses nearly dry-center.
- **Plate:** ValhallaPlate 1.5–2.5 s, pre-delay 30 ms, ducked — the 80s bloom on "Blinding Lights"-style choruses.
- [Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap) subtle + 1/4 throws on phrase-ends · Doubler4 barely-on for the chorus thickener.
- Stacks: octave-down whisper layer under big hooks (tucked), harmonies bright and wide per the pop rules ([Harmony Vocal Track](#/chain/harmony-vocal-track)).

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | single, breathy, intimate, close | nothing, or one low double |
| Pre | single, opening up | doubles enter, width starts |
| Chorus | the 80s belt | doubles hard-panned, harmonies inside, long verb ducked under the dry |
| Bridge | back to one breath-close voice | — |

**The move — intimacy to enormity, on the same voice.** The verse and the chorus are the same singer and the same chain; what changes is the layer count and the width. Restraint in the verse is what buys the chorus its size.

**Tuned invisibly, always.** Unlike the Travis lane, the tune is never the effect here — so the arrangement carries all the contrast.

**Stack count: 1 → 4 + harmonies.**

## Notes / variations
- **After Hours synthwave lane:** more plate, wider stacks, chorus on the doubles.
- **Trilogy dark-R&B lane:** slower tune, more room than plate, RC-20 light for haze, falsetto layers drenched.
- The discipline: every stage does 1–3 dB of work. If any single plugin is obvious, it's overdone.

## Step 4 — Illangelo's own lead-vocal chain (primary source, product-and-setting-level)

Everything above this section was reconstructed from press/blog sources. This section is the real thing, straight from Illangelo (Abel's longtime co-producer/engineer across *Trilogy* through *After Hours*), screen-sharing his actual Ableton session — product names and numbers, not inference. Where it diverges from Step 1–3 above, **trust this section**; where it's silent, the earlier steps still hold as a general Weeknd-family starting point.

**Tracking (before Ableton):** everything goes direct into a **UAD audio interface**, monitored live so Abel hears Auto-Tune + compression/limiting in real time while singing — controlled playback without printing anything heavy. Preamp of choice among the UAD Unison roster: **Manley VOXBOX** (unowned — see Plugin Wishlist; owned equivalent UAD Neve 1073 or UAD UA 610-B for tube warmth). Tracking compressor recipe (maps directly to owned UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII): **on**, Release Medium/Medium-fast, Attack Medium/Medium-slow (song-dependent), **Threshold left alone — level controlled via Input drive only**, targeting only slight needle movement (bumps to ~−1 dB, peaks −3 to −7 dB at most — nowhere near −10/−20). Reverb monitored live + a delay on a secondary Aux while tracking, so the performance is sung against real space/repeats from take one. Stated reason for staying interface-direct over vintage mics/hardware chains (which he rates highly but doesn't reach for): a full year of Abel sessions jumping between studios makes a portable, consistent signal path matter more than hardware character that can't travel.

**In Ableton, in signal order:**
1. **Utility** — manually removes one specific breath, right at the top (not a dedicated breath plugin) — a habit carried over from Cubase's hotkey breath-editing, which he still prefers but had to partly adapt away from.
2. **Pro-Q 4** ("Q3" in his own terms) — steep low roll-off, a boost around **1500 Hz, ~+4 dB**, gentle top-end smoothing filter. **Linear Phase / Medium** only at the very end of finishing a record; **Natural Phase** the other 99% of the time.
3. **Vocal Rider (Waves, unowned — Plugin Wishlist)** — Range maxed **12 dB up/12 dB down**, Center 0, Sensitivity maxed, Speed Fast. Real-time gain-riding BEFORE any compression, specifically because tracking stays clean/uncompressed — likened to the singer physically moving toward/away from the mic (pushed back when loud, pulled in when soft). His words: "we're just trying to get the strongest base possible for the lead vocal... little bit by little bit, chipping away at it." Owned lane doing a related job: RVox (see §5 below for why he splits this out instead).
4. **Pro-G** — gate/expander creating contrast between the eventual hyper-compressed vocal and audible space between phrases: opens above threshold, tucks ~**12 dB** below it.
5. **DeBreath (Waves, unowned — Plugin Wishlist)** — dialed to **−9**, a touch-up pass on breaths the top-of-chain Utility move didn't catch. Adds serious latency with no workaround found — kept anyway for the hours it saves over manual breath-cutting.
6. **Eiosis E2 Deesser (unowned — Plugin Wishlist)** — his strongest endorsement in the whole video: "nothing does what this de-esser does... this should be almost your first choice in de-essing. It's my first choice." → De-essing
7. **Pro-L 2** — run on the LEAD VOCAL TRACK ITSELF, not the master. **Attack deliberately slow** so each phrase's initial transient energy pokes through before clamping — peaks visibly land at phrase starts as a result. Philosophy: many gentle stages in series so the vocal never arrives "already clamped down."
8. **Pro-MB** — most gain reduction on the low end; the top end is mostly let through except when specific moments trigger it (wanted). His framing: a standard static EQ "is not going to sound as alive as when you're doing it with something that reacts instantly in the moment as needed."
9. **A second, unnamed de-esser** — light cleanup catching a couple of remaining peaks the Eiosis stage left; explicitly not the heavy lifter. Confirms a **two-de-esser layering pattern**: one primary (Eiosis), one late touch-up.
10. **Utility → a favorite EQ with a dedicated "Air band"** (plugin name not confirmed — the source video's captions cut off before he names it) — a gentle boost around **20 kHz** (~0.5 in this session, sometimes cranked to 4–6). Compared directly to owned **Fresh Air**: "I think Slate Digital might have just released something called Fresh Air... it's fire. This one also does a similar thing." Called his favorite plugin overall.

**Why this differs from Step 2 above:** the press-sourced chain (Auto-Tune EFX → Pro-Q → Pro-MB → 1176 → doubler → MicroShift → plate) is directionally right but compresses a much longer real chain into a few named stages. The real chain runs Vocal Rider *ahead* of any hard compression (not after), splits gating and de-essing into multiple dedicated single-purpose plugins rather than one or two multi-tools, and puts Pro-L 2 on the *track*, not the bus — reinforcing this chain's overall "many light touches, nothing obvious" discipline rather than contradicting it.

## Step 5 — The "backgrounds" reverse-reverb texture (opens the record)

The swelling reverse-reverb intro heard on Weeknd records comes from a group Illangelo calls **"backgrounds"** — a genuinely different animal from the lead vocal chain above, built for atmosphere rather than intelligibility. Three parallel vocal layers feed it: one pitched an **octave up**, one **dry**, one through **OTT** (pushing mids/highs, controlling lows). From there: an unidentified plugin/nickname ("Denise, The Sweeper") + a second EQ pass doing low-end notching, with a companion low band that fades back in as the sound decays → **Utility** automation accenting the swell's rise → **ShaperBox** (Cableguys, unowned) Mix 22%, pumping at half-beat → **Sinevibes Blend** multi-chorus (unowned), deliberately locked to **2 voices** ("there's something about keeping it to the simplistic nature of just two") → **MondoMod** (SoundToys, unowned), Blend ~60–80% — his own words: "I used this on all backgrounds, I used this on anything that was stereo information... I just want to hear it moving" → an Audio Effect Rack with an unidentified "whirl" device → **Valhalla Delay** → a very long reverb closing the chain (**~19-second decay** — "long decay, 19 seconds... that's beautiful") → a final Pro-Q 4 top-end roll-off.

Not (yet) worth its own dedicated chain note — genuinely reusable for anyone chasing this specific reverse-reverb-swell texture, but built from three unowned modulation plugins (ShaperBox, Sinevibes Blend, MondoMod) with no settled owned-lane substitution yet. Revisit as a standalone Production/Chains entry once those gaps close or a clear owned-plugin stand-in emerges (candidates: Chorus-Ensemble for the 2-voice chorus role, a Max for Live LFO rack for MondoMod's constant stereo-movement role).

**Sources:** [Sound On Sound — Inside Track: The Weeknd](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-weeknd) · [Rys Up Audio — Weeknd vocal chain breakdown](https://rysupaudio.com/blogs/news/how-to-sound-like-the-weeknd) · Mix with the Masters (Illangelo), Producing The Weeknd's vocals with Illangelo

chains.title: Tony Maserati Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Tony Maserati — near-finished multi-vocal mix session (parallel vocal, BVs, lead-in-choruses, "answer" vocal); song unconfirmed
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** not a single-voice "sound" template like the artist-tone chains elsewhere in this folder — this is an **engineer's role-based restraint discipline**, caught mid-session on a track with a lead, background vocals, a lead-in-the-choruses (background role), and an "answer" vocal. The governing idea across every stage: decide what a vocal's *job* is in a given section before deciding how much to process it. A background part gets almost nothing on purpose; the intelligibility device (parallel) gets boosted specifically where effects density threatens to bury it; a compressor gets auditioned and dropped when it isn't earning its slot; and a subtle edit problem gets solved by literally naming the missing consonant rather than re-editing blind.

**Signal source:** none documented — this is a mix-only breakdown of a session already tracked; no recording chain shown.

## Chain overview

Parallel vocal (intelligibility, automated up in dense sections) → BV chain (channel-strip compressor, auditioned against an alternative, mostly untouched) → lead-in-background-sections chain (tape-based de-ess/thin → dynamic EQ dipping attacks → light compression → parallel, unresolved) → answer-vocal punch send (saturation) → editing pass (missing-consonant diagnosis + donor-take paste, run on both BVs and lead) → a non-vocal aside (guitar synth attack reduction to blend against strings).

## Step 1 — Parallel vocal (intelligibility)

- **Purpose-check by mute test:** muting the parallel path measurably drops word intelligibility — confirms the parallel path's job is clarity, not density/aggression (contrast with the usual "add density" parallel-comp framing — see Parallel Processing).
- **EQ'd and automated UP in the bridge**, specifically because other effects are being layered on that section — the intelligibility device gets boosted *ahead of* the effects that would otherwise bury it, not after.
- Owned lane: any of the house parallel returns ([Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send)) or a plugin's own dry/wet blend (Pro-C 2 dry knob).

## Step 2 — Background vocals

- **Tube-Tech-style channel strip** chosen "for a little bit more flexibility" over a plain compressor insert.
- **Compressor audition:** CL 1B vs. an "R Compressor" (Waves Renaissance Compressor — owned best-match Pro-C 2 / LALA). The CL 1B alone did nearly the whole job — "I'm not doing anything really, it ends up all I'm doing is using the CL 1B." → Compression, Compression Staging
- Flagged issue (unresolved on camera): the BVs' *entrance* pops out a bit too much in the ear — leads directly into Step 5's edit fix.

## Step 3 — Lead vocal, background-role sections (choruses)

Deliberately minimal — "he's meant to be part of the overall background sound, so I am doing very little":

1. **Tape-based de-ess/thinning** — Studer A800 tape machine (unowned — see Plugin Wishlist), **"Pop" preset/formula**, chosen specifically to make the voice thinner while adding analog character; the de-essing is a side effect of the tape stage, not a dedicated de-esser. Owned best-match: Kramer Tape, dialed toward thin/bright rather than warm/full.
2. **Dynamic EQ dipping the ATTACKS** — Pro-Q 3, a dynamic band tuned to the transient/attack energy of the voice rather than a static frequency or sibilance. Owned equivalent: Pro-Q 4.
3. **Light compression** ("R Compressor" again) — framed here as a keep-him-high-in-the-mix move. Owned best-match: Pro-C 2.
4. **Parallel** — routed but **not confirmed as earning its place**: "I'm not sure that's quite working at the moment, maybe we'll get rid of that." A live audit, not a settled recipe.

## Step 4 — "Answer" vocal (punch send)

- Sent to Decapitator specifically for punch, judged by direct without/with A-B, then pushed further by raising both the send level and the Decapitator's own mix.
- A send (not an insert) purely for saturation-driven punch on a secondary/call-and-response vocal line.

## Step 5 — Editing pass: missing-consonant diagnosis

- **Name the specific missing/wrong phoneme**, not just "the edit sounds off": tried "b" of *baby*, then "m" of *maybe*, landed on the actual answer — a missing **"h"** on *"hey there."*
- **Fix by donor-take paste**, run as two separate passes: copy the "h" from elsewhere in the session, paste onto the affected BV tracks (checked against the beat grid), then repeat the same fix on the lead vocal separately — fixing one part never assumed to fix the other.
- → Vocal Comping and Takes for the general technique.

## Step 6 — Non-vocal aside: blending a guitar synth against strings

- A guitar synth's attack was already "left-heavy" and fighting a late-arriving string/cello part.
- **Transient Designer-style attack reduction** (owned: Transient Master / Transient Shaper) pulled the guitar synth's attack down — the blend goal wasn't matching the parts' transients, it was decreasing one so all three (string, cello/viola, guitar synth) read as one texture instead of competing.

## Vocal arrangement

| Role | Job in the section | Processing budget |
|---|---|---|
| **Lead** | carries the lyric | the full chain |
| **Background** | fills, no attention | almost nothing, on purpose |
| **Lead-as-background** (in choruses) | supports its own lead | treated as a background part, not a lead |
| **Answer** | responds in the gaps | boosted for intelligibility where effects density would bury it |

**The move — decide the job before the processing.** The same singer's take gets a different chain depending on what it's *doing* in that section. A lead vocal demoted to a background role in the chorus gets background treatment, even though it's the same voice and the same performance.

**This is a role map, not a stack count.** It's the discipline that makes dense vocal arrangements survive: every layer knows whether it's speaking or listening. Pairs directly with the masking hierarchy in Masking and Carving.

**Test:** if you can't name a layer's job in one word, it doesn't belong in that section.

## Notes / variations

- **Role before processing amount.** The single reusable idea across this whole session: ask what a vocal is *doing* in this section (lead, background, answer, intelligibility layer) before reaching for a chain — the same voice gets radically different treatment section to section.
- **A compressor audition can end in "barely anything."** Trying two options and landing on whichever one does *less* audible work is a legitimate outcome, not a wasted step.
- Not a full genre/artist "sound" template like [Kenny Beats Vocal Chain](#/chain/kenny-beats-vocal-chain) or [James Blake Vocal Chain](#/chain/james-blake-vocal-chain) — like the James Blake note, this is a single mix-session's problem-solving order, video-derived from one short clip with almost no numeric settings given.

**Source:** Mix with the Masters, Vocal chain with Tony Maserati ([watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7R0nD4nCYVU)) — captions transcript, high confidence on wording, low confidence on exact numeric settings (mostly qualitative on screen).

chains.title: Travis Scott Vocal Chain
chains.reference: Travis Scott (SICKO MODE, HIGHEST IN THE ROOM, goosebumps, MY EYES)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** hard-tuned voice as a *synthesizer*, drowned in space — the tune locked to zero, the voice dark and hooded, huge hall/plate behind it, delay throws and pitched ad-lib layers everywhere. Psychedelic rap: the effects are the arrangement.
**Signal source:** U87-class condenser in his sessions — Neumann TLM 102. Delivery: melodic mumble, ad-libs performed with full commitment (they're half the record).

## Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)
1. **UAD Neve 1073 (Unison)** — a little drive; his vocal reads warm-dark, not crisp
2. **UAD 1176LN** — 4:1 fast, 3–4 dB (rap phrasing spikes hard)
3. **UAD Pultec EQP-1A** — low ATTEN @ 100 Hz, no air boost (dark on purpose)

## Chain overview
Hard tune → dark EQ → heavy comp → saturate → the space. The intelligibility rules get inverted: the *blur* is the aesthetic; the dry/wet balance and the throws carry the drama.

## Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

### 1. Auto-Tune Pro — THE effect
- **Retune 0–10, Humanize 0**, key set carefully (a wrong key note = full robot warble) · Classic mode algorithm for the harder snap
- Flip Formant/Throat on ad-lib layers for character spread.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Dark shape
- HPF 90–110 Hz · **shelf DOWN the top slightly (−1–2 dB above 8–10 kHz)** — the hooded quality; presence lives 2–4 kHz, not in air · cut 400–600 boxiness.

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Flatten
- 4:1–6:1 · **4–6 dB GR** — modern rap density; dynamics come from arrangement, not the voice.

### 4. Saturn 2 or Decapitator — Density
- Tube, medium drive, mix ~30–40% — thickens the tuned tone into that synthy sustain.

### 5. Pro-DS — De-ess firm.

## Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is the Travis part)
- **The big verb:** ValhallaVintageVerb or ValhallaPlate — **decay 2.5–4.5 s, pre-delay 20–40 ms**, send/return (never insert), HPF'd return, **ducked hard from the dry vocal** — huge behind him, clear when he speaks.
- **Throws:** [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other) 1/4 (and 1/4T) ping-pong, automated onto line-end words, feedback 30–50% — throws answer *in the reverb*, so they smear into the hall.
- **Ad-lib layers:** Little AlterBoy pitch/formant shifted (±3–5 semis, or octave), panned wide, drenched wetter than the lead — the crowd of hims ("it's lit!" energy).
- [Width Send](#/chain/width-send) on hook stacks · [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) barely used — this aesthetic skips "natural."

## Vocal arrangement

| Section | Lead | Behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Verse | hard-tuned, dark, hooded | ad-libs answering **every** line, panned wide |
| Hook | tuned lead + pitched doubles (octave down, octave up) | ad-lib bed running underneath continuously |
| Throw | a line thrown into delay, dry vocal drops out | the throw *is* the transition |

**The move — the effects are the arrangement.** Stated in the vibe line above and worth taking literally: sections change because the space changes. A hall opens, a delay throw carries a line across a bar-line, a pitched layer arrives. Almost nothing changes in the parts.

**Ad-libs are structural, not decoration.** They run continuously and they're the second most important vocal lane — panned hard, pitched, degraded. Budget real time for them.

**Stack count: 2 → 6+, plus a permanent ad-lib bed.**

## Notes / variations
- **Verse vs hook:** verses = tune + slap + light verb (closer); hooks = everything opens (long verb send up, throws, octave stacks). The wet/dry automation IS the songwriting dynamic.
- **MY EYES / ambient lane:** slower retune (10–20), more formant layers, verb decay toward 5 s, tempo-synced throbbing delay.
- **Rage lane (UTOPIA):** distortion forward (Decapitator Punish on a parallel), verb shorter but darker, tune unchanged.
- 🎬 *From video (God's Country, UTOPIA):* clone the vocal into TWO differently-processed layers rather than one chain doing two jobs. Layer 1 = this chain's default (Auto-Tune → reverb → EQ). Layer 2 = a guitar amp (Morgan Amps Suite) + EQ, run specifically to cut through the mix — an amp-sim used as a presence stage on a voice, not a guitar tone.

## From videos

- **Clone-into-two-layers with distinct JOBS, not just doubled processing.** God's Country's vocal is recorded once, cloned, and each clone gets a *different* chain: the "any vocal" default (Auto-Tune → reverb → EQ) on Layer 1, and a guitar amp + EQ specifically for cut-through on Layer 2 — two layers solving two different problems (tone vs. presence) rather than a stack of the same processing twice. → Auto-Tune Pro, Morgan Amps Suite, Saturation and Distortion, Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs — loner, [the secrets behind Travis Scott's 'UTOPIA' production!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9vHZnAAegfw)

**Sources:** [VocalPresets — Travis Scott chain breakdown](https://vocalpresets.com/blog/travis-scott-vocal-chain) · [MassiveFM — the space around the voice](https://massivefm.com/inside-travis-scotts-vocal-chain-autotune-reverb-delay-and-the-space-around-the-voice/) · [Rys Up Audio — full chain](https://rysupaudio.com/blogs/news/how-to-sound-like-travis-scott)

chains.title: Drums Hat Track
chains.routing: Drums Hat → Drums Hats Group → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Hi-hats — the groove's timekeeper and (in trap) a lead instrument in their own right.

**Chain philosophy:** clean → de-pierce → define. The HPF is the big one; everything else is fatigue control.

## 1 — Sound Selection

- **Selection IS the recording step** — audition in XO. Hats carry more genre signal than any other drum: 909s = house, crisp digital ticks = trap, dusty loops = boom bap.
- 🎬 **Every note a different length, played AND drawn, overlapping across the bar** — the Disclosure 909-hats rule: "not a single loop in this tune" — [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag).

## 2 — Programming Best Practice

- 🎬 **Shorten the tail, pitch down, THEN nudge off the kick with a specific named keyboard workflow — third confirmed sighting of this exact hi-hat recipe on this channel, this time the repeatable shortcut is spelled out.** On an 80s synthwave/pop beat, a light hi-hat gets its decay/tail shortened, pitched down, then timing-shifted off the kick via **Select None → Ctrl+A (select all) → Shift-right arrow twice** — "so it's separated from the kick, it's not hitting straight away." Same three-move recipe (shorten/pitch-down/off-grid) already logged on Pocket and Microtiming from two earlier loner builds; this video is the first to name the exact repeatable shortcut rather than describing the nudge only qualitatively. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns, Synthwave — loner, [how to make an 80's synthwave/pop beat for the weeknd.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dWhh27UFWhY)
- 🎬 **Two-hat garage bounce split: a click-like first hat for subtle bounce, a second hat shifted off-grid AND tightened via its Out knob for "where the bounce really comes in."** Hi-hat 1 sits almost like a click rather than a real hat — quiet, textural, adds a little bounce without a real pattern. Hi-hat 2 is shifted back off the timing grid and has its tail shortened (the Out knob) before placement — named explicitly as the element that actually delivers the garage bounce. Kick stays deliberately minimal/spaced-out underneath since the percussion above is already doing the rhythmic work. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns — loner, [i combined r&b melodies with uk garage drums to make an insane beat (crazy bounce!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I4-jcoCVdC0)
- **Velocity + pitch variation programmed on the instrument beats any plugin** — velocity = volume, vary lengths, triplets scattered.
- **Roll grammar (trap):** base pattern = two-step; rolls before snares and at 8-bar ends; vary density (1/16 → 1/32); triplet-grid switches for bounce; ride roll velocities evenly for shape.
- **Pitch slides:** drop a hat an octave-ish and slide into the next (slide length = zip speed) — the modern "zap" perc; pitch rolls down as they build.
- **Silence is a move:** a beat of dropped hats before a section change hits harder than any fill.
- **Pan the ornaments** — extra rolls/open hats off-center (core hat can stay center); swing/off-grid the extras — Kenny Beats, [Trap Drums More Interesting](https://youtu.be/fo-E8dY81Nw) → [Drums Hats Group](#/chain/drums-hats-group).
- 🎬 **Velocity→pitch in the sampler mod matrix** (small range) — each hit lands slightly detuned; instant humanization — Disclosure, [Remix Stems Stream](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8).
- 🎬 **Vary placement past the default every-4th pattern, and enforce velocity variation** — off-beat hits drive the groove forward past a plain "every fourth beat" pattern; uniform-strength hits read as harsh/mechanical, so vary hit-to-hit velocity like a real player would. Swap the hat for a ride (or combine) to change a section's color without touching the rest of the pattern. Choose tail length per hit on purpose — semi-open for a back-beat hat, short for a dense roll — and enable "cut itself"/choke on the sampler channel so an open-hat tail can't ring through the next closed-hat hit (a real kit physically can't do that). FL's note-repeat function generates fast/triplet/trap rolls without hand-drawing every hit. → Rhythm and Groove — Synthet, [the inarguably best drum sound..](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nJwgwn_jYQ0) · [it hits hard on the feel of your music](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IyVWtRToKsY)

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

Optional analog pass when a sample feels sterile — printed to audio:

### 1. UAD Neve 1073 — Preamp plugin — light, ~0 VU
### 2. UAD UA 1176LN — skip on one-shots
### 3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — high-band sweetening only

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Clean + crisp
- **HPF 300–500 Hz** (hats need *nothing* below — every hat sample carries junk lows that eat headroom; summed across a busy pattern it measurably muddies the drum bus)
- Crisp +1–2 dB @ 8–12 kHz if dull · cut 2–4 kHz if clanky
- 📖 *From book:* the gentler floor for the same HPF is **200–300 Hz "or more, use ears"** — 300–500 Hz stays the default here, but drop toward 200 Hz on a hat whose character genuinely lives low (a soft closed hat, a live loop). Sizzle = high **shelf** 7–10 kHz+ rather than a peak — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

### 2. Soothe2 — De-pierce
- Light depth, focus 5–12 kHz
- **Why:** Hats are the #1 listening-fatigue source; dynamic resonance control keeps sparkle while killing ice-pick hits — better than a static cut that dulls the pattern.

### 3. Transient Master — Definition
- Attack + for tick definition, or sustain − to shorten washy open hats.

## 5 — Track FX (optional)

- 🎬 **Overdrive the shakers — ALWAYS** (Guy's rule): distortion "reminds me of how a shaker sounds on a 7-inch record — it just breaks up" — Disclosure, [Prince Edit stream](https://youtu.be/hOvLf9nX500). Applies to shaker/cabasa lanes on this track too.
- **RC-20 Retro Color** light for vintage texture on live/loop hats.

## 6 — Bus / Send FX (optional)

Routing: **Drums Hat → [Drums Hats Group](#/chain/drums-hats-group) → [Drums Bus](#/chain/drums-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)**.

- **NO reverb on trap hats** — dry = modern. Live/loop lanes: a touch of [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room).
- Haas-delay a stereo aux perc layer (one channel ~680 samples) for super-wide separation — keep it off anything mono-critical (Width and Stereo).

## Variations

- **Trap:** the roll grammar + pitch slides from §2, bone dry.
- **House 909s:** the Disclosure no-loops rule from §1, ride the open-hat lengths.

## From books

- **Hat EQ starting points, agreeing with this chain but from the gentler end.** Low cut **200–300 Hz "or more, use ears"** (this chain's 300–500 Hz sits at the aggressive end of that same instruction) · sizzle via a high **shelf 7–10 kHz+** rather than a peak (vs. this chain's "crisp +1–2 dB @ 8–12 kHz") · high cut **18–20 kHz** for "harsh freq" — headroom hygiene at best; actual hat harshness is the 5–12 kHz band Soothe2 already covers in §4. See the inline 📖 line in §4 above. → EQ, Masking and Carving, AIR Slot — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

## From videos

- **Hi-hat mic proximity-effect fix, solved by moving the mic rather than EQ-ing it out.** Tracking live drums, CLA diagnosed a hi-hat mic's excess low end as proximity effect (a directional mic's bass response rising as it gets closer to the source) and fixed it by having the mic physically pulled back a foot rather than reaching for a high-pass filter afterward — "I really hear... the low end, like, just really killing... pull the hi-hat back a foot." The general discipline: a mic-position problem gets a mic-position fix, not an EQ patch after the take is committed. Full context on Drum Mic Technique (same mechanism already documented for vocals on Vocal Mic Technique). → Drum Mic Technique, Vocal Mic Technique — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Tracking live drums with Chris Lord-Alge
- **Garage two-hat bounce split: click-like hat 1 + off-grid, tail-tightened hat 2** — see the inline 🎬 note in §2 above. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns — loner, [i combined r&b melodies with uk garage drums to make an insane beat (crazy bounce!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I4-jcoCVdC0)
- **Shorten/pitch-down/off-grid hi-hat recipe, third sighting — this time with the exact repeatable keyboard shortcut named** — see the inline 🎬 note in §2 above. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns, Synthwave — loner, [how to make an 80's synthwave/pop beat for the weeknd.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dWhh27UFWhY)
- **Raise the global swing amount as the LAST step of the hat/kick programming pass, after every layer is already placed — a finishing humanization move, not a starting parameter.** Layered hats (a simple bounce pattern + a second copy-pasted layer + a third 4-step hat offset behind the kick's own 4-step fill) were all placed first; swing went up only once every layer existed, explicitly "to create a very natural feel." → Rhythm and Groove, Pocket and Microtiming — loner, [making a billboard number 1 pop beat for post malone's next album from scratch!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WX_IB6K-xIo)
- **Placement/velocity/tail-choice checklist + choke groups** — see §2 above for the full breakdown → Rhythm and Groove — Synthet, [the inarguably best drum sound..](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nJwgwn_jYQ0) · [it hits hard on the feel of your music](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IyVWtRToKsY)
- **LFOTool half-note duck on shaker/perc loops** — gentle volume shape to make static loops groove (also lands as a fake snare-duck); prefer fixed note values over random. And park the shaker where the hat isn't: his lo-fi hat left the high-highs empty, so the shaker got boosted exactly there — Lophiile, [All About Basslines stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tnruvmw_OWc)
## Sources

Disclosure — [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag) · [Remix Stems](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8) · [Prince Edit](https://youtu.be/hOvLf9nX500) · Kenny Beats — [Trap Drums More Interesting](https://youtu.be/fo-E8dY81Nw)

chains.title: Drums Kick Track
chains.routing: Drums Kick → Drums Group → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** The kick — anchor of the groove. Sample selection is 80% of the job; the chain sharpens what the sample already is.

**Chain philosophy:** EQ → transient → comp → clip. Transient shaping before compression (shape the hit, then level it); clipper last to shave the peak for loudness.

## 1 — Sound Selection

- **Selection IS the recording step** — audition in XO until it knocks raw. If the kick needs heavy processing to hit, swap the sample: pick crunchy, don't manufacture crunch.
- 🎬 **Or synthesize it** — Disclosure build kicks from a kick-synth (Ultrabeat / BigKick / Kick 2) and **tune the fundamental to the song key** — full method in Kick Design — [Latch](https://youtu.be/u-0Q41XB7U4) / [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ).
- 🎬 **The "all-knock" kick** — energy ~100 Hz, "nothing at 50 Hz" (old UK garage) — for when a bendy sub or 808 already owns the SUB Slot and the kick only needs to knock through the BASS Slot — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).
- 🎬 **LinnDrum click layered low on a dead kick** — "use it for the click, not very loud" — attack layer only — Disclosure, [Making Beats + Talk](https://youtu.be/1GhqAf9lc3A).
- 🎬 **Or skip the kick entirely** — modern trap often runs an 808 with enough front-end attack alone; audition a harder 808 before adding kick + duck — Kenny Beats, [808 & Kick](https://youtu.be/4iAKvWWlCvY).
- 🎬 **A live-tracking-stage version of "layer two":** a physically distinct 28" marching band bass drum set up in front of the main kit kick and damped with blankets over the top, for character — mic'd with an NS10 monitor driver (reversed as a mic) + D12 on the front head for the tonal split, then a subtle sample layer blended in on top via a Logic drum-replacement plugin ("Trigger" per the transcript, name uncertain — Plugin Wishlist). Full mic/damping detail on Drum Mic Technique. → Drum Mic Technique, Kick Design, Layering and Stacking — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"

## 2 — Programming Best Practice

- **Layer two:** a punchy sub kick + a kick with a hat/click baked in, and **nudge the punchy one a hair ahead** so its transient leads — the "fake compression" move (see [Drums Bus](#/chain/drums-bus)) — Disclosure.
- **Trap (kick + 808 both present):** don't put a kick on *every* 808 note — copy the 808 pattern to the kick, then delete most of them, keeping kicks only on hits that deserve emphasis.
- **Kick + 808 CAN hit together — sidechain is a choice, not a requirement** — when they fight, fix sample pairing (kick attack matching the 808), timing offset, and masking cuts first — Kenny Beats, [808 & Kick](https://youtu.be/4iAKvWWlCvY) → Sidechaining.
- **The kick owns sub-100 Hz** — hard low-cut the sub-100 junk out of everything that isn't kick/808 (guitars, keys, even hats): the instruments sound identical, the low end gets clean, the beat takes more level — Kenny Beats → Masking and Carving.

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

Optional analog pass when a sample feels sterile — UAD plugins acting as the console input, printed to audio:

- 🎬 *From video:* **parallel-distorted kick** — duplicate the direct/close kick to a second channel, run it through a guitar-distortion-pedal-style stage (Nick Launay uses a hardware SansAmp; owned stand-in Decapitator or Devil-Loc Deluxe), and blend under the direct signal for thickness — a named repeatable trick, not a one-off. Full recipe on Parallel Processing — Mix with the Masters (Nick Launay), Parallel distortion by Nick Launay.
- 🎬 *From video:* **tuned parallel-distorted kick, variant with a note.** Same SansAmp-duplicate idea, but driven for a musical NOTE instead of pure thickness: a very narrow, sweepable EQ tunes the distorted low end to the song's key ("I like to keep things musical"), then a gate (Drawmer DS201; owned stand-in Gate) shapes the note's length before it's blended under the clean, clear-topped close mic. Full recipe on Saturation and Distortion (effect) and Gate — Mix with the Masters (Nick Launay), Mixing Nick Cave & The bad seeds - Nick Launay.

### 1. UAD Neve 1073 — Preamp plugin
- Light iron drive · ~0 VU

### 2. UAD UA 1176LN — Compressor
- 1–2 dB on peaks, or skip on one-shots

### 3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — EQ
- The boost+atten @ 60 Hz trick for weight · print

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Shape
- HPF 25–30 Hz · define the thump (boost or notch ~50–60 Hz, wherever this kick's fundamental is) · cut box 250–400 Hz · click +1–2 dB @ 3–5 kHz if it needs attack definition
- 📖 *From book:* trap/808 alternative HPF — **40–60 Hz** (not 25–30) when an 808 owns the sub outright and this kick only needs knock; thump shelf **80–100 Hz**, snap **2–4 kHz**, click band **8–10 kHz** (printed as a "notch," almost certainly meant as a boost — see the caveat on Kick Design) — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
- 🎬 *From video:* if the kick reads "too loud and too quiet at the same time" with the low end already sitting right, the fix is usually a missing beater/attack transient, not more low end — add **1–3 kHz** presence for the "smack" of the beater hitting the head, A/B'd on/off before touching anything else. → TRANSIENT Slot, Kick Design — Andy Wallace (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Avenged Sevenfold - Andy Wallace
- **Why:** Decide the kick's fundamental *now* — the bass carve ([Electric Bass DI Track](#/chain/electric-bass-di-track)/[Digital Bass Track](#/chain/digital-bass-track)) is built around it.

### 2. Transient Master — Punch
- Attack +10–30% · sustain to taste (down = tighter, up = roomier) · trim output — added attack raises peaks
- **Why:** Transient designers add punch without compressor pumping — level-independent, works on every hit equally. Attack = a **depth knob**: more = toward your face, less = sits back.

### 3. FETish — Comp (optional)
- **Ratio 4:1** (②) · **Attack slow (~2, knob left)** (③ — lets the beater click through before clamping) · **Release fast (~6)** (④ — recovers before the next hit) · **HPF engaged** (⑤ — so sub doesn't over-trigger the detector) · **~2 dB GR** · **Mix 100%** (⑦) · **Output** to make up (⑧)
- **Why:** Only for uneven kicks (live or velocity-varied) — evens hit-to-hit level without dulling the transient. A consistent one-shot can skip this entirely.

### 4. kHs Clipper — Clip
- **Input to shave 1–2 dB off the peak** (① — drive to taste) · **Hard** (②) · enable **oversampling** (⑤) to hold true peak on the shaved transients
- **Why:** Clipping the transient trades inaudible peak for real loudness headroom — the modern hip hop/EDM standard, and why the drum-bus limiter won't have to work as hard. *(Owned substitute for Gold Clip Track — same transient-clip job.)*

## 5 — Track FX (optional)

- Usually nothing — kick character was decided at selection. Release automation for section energy (the [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag) short-kick trick: ~120 ms with release opening up) lives here when used.

## 6 — Bus / Send FX (optional)

Routing: **Drums Kick → [Drums Group](#/chain/drums-group) → [Drums Bus](#/chain/drums-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)**.

- **This track is the sidechain trigger** for Kickstart 2/duck sends on four-on-floor — better: split to a **dedicated inaudible trigger track** so added syncopated kicks don't stutter the pump (Sidechaining).
- No reverb, no width — the kick lives center and dry.

## Variations

- **Trap:** kick keeps the click + 60–100 Hz knock, HPF 45–50 Hz so the 808 owns the sub — layered low end needs strict lanes. End 808 patterns with a velocity-0 note so tails don't carry.
- **Four-on-floor EDM:** more Transient Master attack; trigger duty as above.

## From books

- **Kick EQ starting points, and one printed contradiction worth knowing about.** Low cut **40–60 Hz** (rumble — the trap/808 alternative to this chain's 25–30 Hz HPF) · low shelf **80–100 Hz** for thump · boost **2–4 kHz** for snap (this chain's own "click +1–2 dB @ 3–5 kHz" is the same move) · a band at **8–10 kHz** for click, printed as a **notch** despite "for click" being its stated reason — read as a boost, or as a narrow notch for a clicky resonance. Compare Lophiile's opposing rule above: don't low-pass the kick's top off, shelf the lower-highs down instead. See the inline 📖 line in §4 above. → Kick Design, EQ, Masking and Carving — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

## From videos

- **Diagnose "too loud and too quiet at the same time" as a missing beater/attack transient, fixed by boosting 1–3 kHz rather than touching the low end.** Andy Wallace, with zero upper-range EQ applied yet: "the too loud component can happen because when you have the low end feeling where it should be, you're not getting enough smack on it." See the inline 🎬 line in §4 above. → Kick Design, TRANSIENT Slot — Mix with the Masters (Andy Wallace), Mixing Avenged Sevenfold - Andy Wallace
- **A tuned variant of the parallel-SansAmp kick trick: the distorted low end is deliberately tuned to the song's key and gated for note length, then blended under a clean close mic.** Nick Launay, on a Nick Cave kick that was already good on its own: "I want it to have a little bit more clarity in the top end, so I'll get that from the close mic... and I usually tune that note to the song because I like to keep things musical." Full recipe with the Drawmer DS201 gate on §3 above. → Saturation and Distortion (effect), Gate, SUB Slot — Mix with the Masters (Nick Launay), Mixing Nick Cave & The bad seeds - Nick Launay
- **A dull, "cardboard"-sounding raw bass drum fixed by layering in a sample — no EQ/compression chain shown, just the added layer.** Bob Clearmountain, A/B'ing before/after on Squeeze's "The Knowledge": "that's the original bass drum, a bit dull, it sort of sounds like cardboard. I add that in and it just adds a bit of punch to it... a little point to the bass which is nice." → Kick Design, Sound Selection Guide — Mix with the Masters (Bob Clearmountain), Bob Clearmountain's mixing techniques
- **A named, repeatable parallel-distortion trick: guitar distortion pedal (SansAmp) on a duplicated kick channel, blended under the direct mic for thickness.** Nick Launay: "that trick I've explained before on other Mix with the Masters sessions" — confirming it's a standing go-to, not improvised for this session. Same shape reused one drum over on the snare (Distressor, low end only — see [Drums Snare-Clap Track](#/chain/drums-snare-clap-track)). No exact drive/blend amount given. → Parallel Processing, Saturation and Distortion, Drum Mic Technique, Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters (Nick Launay), Parallel distortion by Nick Launay
- **"Oliver Power Tools Vol. 3" (Splice) chosen specifically for a disco-poppy kit character, reused twice in the same beat — once for the main kick/hat foundation (a 4-step kick fill), and again later for the snare layer.** Genre-appropriate kit choice named as the reason for reaching for it, ahead of any processing. → Sound Selection Guide, Rhythm and Groove — loner, [making a billboard number 1 pop beat for post malone's next album from scratch!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WX_IB6K-xIo)
