- **"My Hi" kick is two full layers plus a clicky top-end layer, stacked over an already kick-heavy garage loop:** one kick tuned for punch/attack (low end mostly rolled off), a separate sub kick underneath for the felt weight and low-end "collapse," and a third short/clicky layer riding on top purely for transient click — three lanes doing three different jobs rather than one kick doing everything. → Layering and Stacking — Disclosure (Sol State), [In The Studio: Disclosure "My High" breakdown [Twitch]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hOJafQO-LyY)

- **The "car EQ" kick curve + 1k dip** — shelf (don't filter) the lower-highs, filter only the extreme top, ~1 kHz dip for boxy kicks; mono the sample; shorten the low tail for punch — Lophiile, [All About Basslines stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tnruvmw_OWc) & [Make Your Drums Slap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v4ZhwlhF5yE)
## Sources

Disclosure — [Latch](https://youtu.be/u-0Q41XB7U4) · [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8) · [Making Beats + Talk](https://youtu.be/1GhqAf9lc3A) · Kenny Beats — [808 & Kick + Subtractive EQ](https://youtu.be/4iAKvWWlCvY) · Kick Design for synthesis

chains.title: Drums Snare-Clap Track
chains.routing: Drums Snare/Clap → Drums Group → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** The backbeat. Snares/claps are the loudest transient in most modern mixes — crack + body + a tail that sets the mix's sense of space.

**Chain philosophy:** shape EQ → transient → color → level. Body-vs-crack balance first, dynamics after.

## 1 — Sound Selection

- **A snare that already crunches through raw needs almost no chain; a weak/airy one can't be EQ'd into hardness.** Audition in XO against the beat's *intent* — hard trap = crunchy digital, boom bap = live/dusty — before reaching for a single plugin.
- 🎬 **No sample fits? Build the snare from scratch** — Operator body oscillator (fixed frequency ~160–250 Hz + pitch envelope) + noise tail + texture layers (Shifter/Corpus/Grain Delay), grouped and saved as a reusable "snare starter" rack — see Snare Design for the full recipe — dnksaus, [craft UNIQUE snares](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeHN9GPokMA).
- 🎬 **Match transients across a loop** — one snare with a bad transient/pop gets chopped and replaced so it matches the rest — Disclosure, [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag).
- 🎬 **Hand Clap Studio "underneath claps"** — layered under the main clap for thickness (Clappers 4–8, a little Looseness for a human group, Close-mic'd/dry and fairly narrow so it reinforces without adding space) — Disclosure, [Remix Stems Stream](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8).

## 2 — Programming Best Practice

- 🎬 **UK garage bounce snares: 4 ticks off-grid, selected as a group.** Alongside the normal on-grid backbeat snare hits, place extra "bounce" snares in the gaps, then Select None → select just those extra hits → nudge right 4 ticks (arrow key ×4) — a specific, repeatable offset (not "a little late") credited as the actual source of garage's bounce feel. A clap layered on top with some hits landing ON the snare and some just BEFORE it adds further bounce. Full kit build order (hats, kick) on Genre Drum Patterns. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns — loner, [i combined r&b melodies with uk garage drums to make an insane beat (crazy bounce!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I4-jcoCVdC0)
- **Counter-snares and percs go in the GAPS** — balance, not overlap; the backbeat stays king.
- 🎬 **A clap slightly AHEAD of the beat** (drawn in the step sequencer) reads urgent and clean — the deadmau5 clap is "so ahead of the kick, so clean, cuts through everything" — Disclosure, [Remix Stems](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8) / [Prince Edit stream](https://youtu.be/hOvLf9nX500).
- **Trap stack:** layer snare + clap, EQ each to its lane (snare = body, clap = 1–4 kHz slap).
- Velocity-vary ghost hits; keep the main 2 & 4 consistent.

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

Optional analog pass when a sample feels sterile — printed to audio:

### 1. UAD Neve 1073 — Preamp plugin — light drive, ~0 VU
### 2. UAD UA 1176LN — 1–2 dB on peaks, or skip on one-shots
### 3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — broad body/air strokes
- 🎬 Kenny's live-snare order agrees: **Pultec first, before any dynamics**, then a gate for noise between hits — [Cook Up From Scratch](https://youtu.be/l7AjRTXex2U)
- 🎬 *From video:* **parallel comp on this exact pair, blended under the dry snare rather than run as a straight insert.** Bob Clearmountain: EQ-only pass first (this note's own Pultec top-end/700 Hz/low-end move) → the same signal additionally hit with the 1176 → blended with the untouched dry snare — "you get a little bit of the natural sound but you get that compression." Named payoff on a rolled passage: the parallel layer pulls up the quieter in-between/ghost notes along with the main hits. Full recipe on Parallel Processing. — Mix with the Masters (Bob Clearmountain), Bob Clearmountain's mixing techniques
- 🎬 *From video:* **parallel low-end-only distorted snare** — duplicate the direct/close snare (a 57) to a second channel, drive a compressor hard for character (Nick Launay uses a hardware Distressor; owned stand-in UAD UA 1176LN or Devil-Loc Deluxe), then EQ that channel top-rolled-off/low-boosted so it reads as a pure thuddy low-end layer, and blend it under the direct mic — a narrower target than the kick's full-signal parallel-distortion trick above. Full recipe on Parallel Processing — Mix with the Masters (Nick Launay), Parallel distortion by Nick Launay.

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Shape
- Body +1–3 dB @ 200–250 Hz (the "thwack") · cut mud 400–600 Hz · crack/presence 3–6 kHz · air 10 kHz+ for claps
- 📖 *From book:* add an HPF **100–200 Hz** ahead of the body boost — but set it *below* this snare's body, since the chart's own 200–300 Hz "umph" shelf overlaps the same range as the cut; crisp/crack alternative **5–7 kHz**; optional high cut 15–20 kHz (headroom only, not a harshness fix) — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
- **Why:** Body-vs-crack balance is the whole snare identity — set it before dynamics.

### 2. Transient Master — Snap
- Attack +10–25% · sustain down slightly for tight trap, up for roomy rock.

### 3. Saturn 2 — Color
- Tape or tube, single band, low-medium drive
- **Why:** Saturation rounds the harsh digital edge and fattens the body — a saturated snare sits *in* the track instead of on top of it.

### 4. Pro-C 2 — Level (optional)
- Punch style · slow attack · 1–3 dB GR on uneven hits — one-shots skip.

## 5 — Track FX (optional)

- Usually nothing; special-moment tricks (reverse-clap risers, filtered-verb clap tails à la [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag)) get automated per section.

## 6 — Bus / Send FX (optional)

Routing: **Drums Snare/Clap → [Drums Group](#/chain/drums-group) → [Drums Bus](#/chain/drums-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)**.

- **[Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room)** — the snare is the *main* customer of the room send; its tail defines the mix's space.
- 🎬 *From video:* on the clap specifically, treat the room send's **pre-delay** as a swing/timing control, not just a space control — nudge it to push the clap's felt placement against the beat, on top of (or instead of) moving the hit itself. See [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) for the full note. — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"
- **[Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send)** for size on hooks · **[Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap)** instead of reverb for the trap "pop."

## Variations

- **Trap:** the stack from §2, no reverb — slap delay for the pop.
- **Beatles/vintage:** Kramer Tape instead of Saturn, sustain UP, real room verb longer.

## From books

- **Snare EQ starting points — and the 200 Hz conflict against this chain's own body boost.** Low cut **100–200 Hz** ("more if necessary") · low shelf **200–300 Hz** for "umph" · boost **5–7 kHz** for crisp · high cut **15–20 kHz** ("remove harsh freq"). This chain instead **boosts +1–3 dB @ 200–250 Hz** for the thwack, so the HPF has to sit *below* this snare's body or it removes what the next band adds — high-pass by ear per sample, not at a fixed number. Treat the 15–20 kHz cut as headroom hygiene only; real snare harshness is 2–5 kHz (Soothe2). See the inline 📖 line in §4 above. → Snare Design, EQ, Masking and Carving — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

## From videos

- **A textbook parallel-compression A/B/C on a snare — dry, then EQ-only, then EQ+compression, then the compressed pass blended back under the dry original — see the inline 🎬 note in §3 above.** UAD Pultec EQP-1A (top end, ~700 Hz boost, a bit of low end) + UAD UA 1176LN, blended under the dry snare rather than inserted straight. Also, on the snare's "underneath"/bottom-mic signal specifically: raw described as "pretty nasty-sounding," fixed with a lot of top end plus a scoop-then-restore midrange move (cut mids, then add some back) for brightness rather than body. → UAD UA 1176LN, UAD Pultec EQP-1A, Parallel Processing, EQ (effect) — Mix with the Masters (Bob Clearmountain), Bob Clearmountain's mixing techniques
- **Reverb-send pre-delay used deliberately as a swing/timing tool on a clap — see the inline 🎬 note in §6 above.** → [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room), Pocket and Microtiming — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"
- **A dark-sounding top snare mic opened up decisively at the tracking stage, plus a bottom-mic level catch, before any mix-stage processing.** CLA's first listen on a live snare's top mic read "a little too deep" — opened it up rather than under-correcting, with the stated rule "never be shy with EQ, that's what it's here for"; separately, the bottom-snare mic was caught reading too loud in the level check and pulled down before moving on. Full mic-technique context on Drum Mic Technique. → Drum Mic Technique, EQ, Gain Staging — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Tracking live drums with Chris Lord-Alge
- **UK garage bounce-snare recipe: 4-tick off-grid nudge on extra bounce snares + on/before-the-beat clap layering** — see the inline 🎬 note in §2 above; also live-recorded hand claps (compressor → Cool Room-preset reverb → bandpass EQ) layered under the programmed snare/clap for extra texture and bounce. → Pocket and Microtiming, Genre Drum Patterns, Reverb — loner, [i combined r&b melodies with uk garage drums to make an insane beat (crazy bounce!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I4-jcoCVdC0)
- **Scoop the snare's fundamental frequency, THEN compress hard, for a fat-but-not-punchy character** — removing the fundamental first changes what the compressor actually grabs; the goal is "the close-mic sound of the snare but without so much of the punch, almost like the punch of an overhead." Finish with a touch of spring reverb. → [Drums Bus](#/chain/drums-bus), Snare Design — Zach Scholz, [I Tried Recording a Song Like It's 1976](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6kA1mWeTiZc)
- **Dual-mic snare trick for a live/hybrid source: a standard top mic + a second angled mic that doubles as a near-front kick mic** — second mic (same model as the first) positioned slightly above the shell, a bit further back, not quite side-snare — picked up more kick batter-head and kit ambience than a straight top mic alone; both summed to one input before the DAW. Driving both mics hot into an analog stage for deliberate clipping is a genre-appropriate lo-fi choice, not a mistake to fix. When the second mic directly faces the hi-hat and bleed is unavoidable, use **expansion instead of compression** to push the snare out and drop the bleed down, rather than compressing (which pulls bleed up toward the snare). → [Drums Group](#/chain/drums-group), Sidechaining — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Build a synth snare from scratch: Operator body + pitch envelope, noise tail, texture layers, saved as a "snare starter" rack** — see Snare Design for the full macro-mapped recipe (body/tail/texture/EQ) plus metallic Grain Delay and pitched-impact-one-shot variants. → Snare Design — dnksaus, [craft UNIQUE snares](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeHN9GPokMA)
- **Mono the snare, shorten the sample, saturate first** — Utility width 0 ("snares are dope mono"), clip the baked-in reverb off hit 1 (leave it on hit 2 for contrast), saturate a soft sample before reaching for a new one, EQ out the papery top — Lophiile, [All About Basslines stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tnruvmw_OWc) & [Make Your Drums Slap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v4ZhwlhF5yE)
## Sources

Kenny Beats — [Cook Up From Scratch](https://youtu.be/l7AjRTXex2U) · Disclosure — [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag) · [Remix Stems Stream](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8) · [Prince Edit](https://youtu.be/hOvLf9nX500)

chains.title: Drums Group
chains.routing: [Drums Kick, Drums Snare/Clap, Drums Hats Group, percs] → Drums Group → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** The kit summed (kick, snare, hats group, percussion). This is your current working drums chain (Step 1 Drums export), kept as the default — it's a solid EQ → comp → saturate → transient structure.

**Source note — all drums come from packs/loops** (no live kit): XO to browse/audition one-shots by similarity, Drum Rack/Simpler to play them, Serato Sample for chops. That means: (1) sound selection replaces mic technique as "Step 1 — Record" — swap samples before reaching for plugins; (2) samples arrive pre-processed, so track chains stay light; (3) **full loops**: split stems or slice into the Drum Rack when possible so kick/snare/hats can hit their own chains — an unsplit loop gets treated on this group directly (RC-20 Retro Color texture + the chain below).

## Chain overview
Corrective EQ → kit compression → color → punch restore. The Transient Master at the *end* is the clever part of your chain: it restores the attack that compression and saturation soften.

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Kit balance
- Broad moves on the summed kit: low-mid mud cut 250–400 Hz · any whole-kit tilt
- Per-drum EQ already happened on tracks — this is about the *kit* as one instrument.

### 2. Pro-C 2 — Kit compression
- Punch style · 4:1 · attack 20–30 ms (transients pass) · release 100–150 ms or auto — time it to "breathe" with the tempo · **2–3 dB GR**
- **Why:** Compressing the kit together is what makes separate samples sound like a *band's drummer* — they start moving each other's levels, which reads as cohesion.

### 3. Saturn 2 — Kit color
- Tape, single band or gentle multiband · low drive
- **Why:** Rounds the digital edges of the whole kit uniformly — shared harmonics are shared identity.

### 4. Transient Master — Punch restore
- Attack +5–15%
- **Why:** Both previous stages shave transients slightly; adding attack back *after* them gives you compression's glue AND the punch — order is the trick.

## Variations
- **Harder hip hop:** raise Pro-C 2 GR to 3–4 dB and lean on [Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send) blended under for size.
- **Live-feel/Beatles:** swap Saturn for Kramer Tape pushed harder, slow the Pro-C release, let it pump musically.

## From books

- **Tom EQ starting point — parked here because toms have no track note of their own in this system.** Four moves per tom, tuned *per drum* rather than across a tom bus: **low cut 60–200 Hz** ("stop clashing" — floor toms near 60, rack toms near 200, each filtered out from under the drum below it) · **cut 300–800 Hz** for boxiness (sweep a narrow +8–10 dB band through the range until the honk rings, then flip it to a 3–5 dB cut — *general starting point, the source gives no Q or gain*) · **boost 100–300 Hz** for low-end power (BASS Slot, top edge into the BED Slot) · **boost 5–10 kHz** for stick attack / high-end punch (LEAD Slot into the AIR Slot; a TRANSIENT Slot job by role). The low cut and the low boost overlap deliberately: cut *below* that specific drum's fundamental, boost *at* it. Set toms this way on their own tracks before this group's broad 250–400 Hz kit-mud cut, which will otherwise fight the tom body boost. → EQ, Pro-Q 4, Masking and Carving, Kick Design, Snare Design — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

## From videos

- **Four stackable drum-bus compression techniques, fully worked with settings.** Standard glue: slow-enough attack to preserve transients, release above ~20 ms (avoids low-frequency distortion), 3-6 dB gain reduction. Parallel: a unity-gain SEND (not an output change) to a separate heavily-compressed aux, blended back via fader to reveal masked low-level detail (snare buzz, stick rattle) without flattening the main bus. Emphasis/de-emphasis: EQ before the compressor attenuates a range you want spared (e.g. dip the kick's lows), letting the compressor bear down harder elsewhere, then an equal-and-opposite boost after restores tonal balance — a single-band-compressor workaround for frequency-selective (multiband-style) compression. Harmonic distortion before vs. after compression changes whether the added harmonics get compressed too; both at once is the most intense, deliberately reserved for drums that need to cut aggressively. Full breakdown: 4 Ways to Use Drum Bus Compression. → Compression Staging, Parallel Processing, Multiband Compression, Saturation and Distortion — Sage Audio, [4 Ways to Use Drum Bus Compression](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eY-vIUZzA4s)
- **A second live-tracking mic-technique lesson, JJP's this time — on-topic even though this chain runs from samples: mic layering, not just EQ/level philosophy, is the whole subject.** Full recipe on Drum Mic Technique — headline moves: a passive speaker used as a third mic on BOTH kick and snare (on snare, aimed specifically at a 200–400 Hz lower-mid fill + tail); a subtle SPL-style transient-designer pass on the underneath mic (Transient Master is the owned best-match — a third SPL use case on this vault); a heavily processed mono front/back "punch" pair judged only in the full blend, not solo; and cymbal spot mics layered under the overheads specifically for overtone/ring character. Complements the CLA session directly below (that one is EQ/level philosophy; this one is mic choice/layering). → Drum Mic Technique, Transient Master, Sound Selection Guide — Mix with the Masters (Jack Joseph Puig), Tracking drums with Jack Joseph Puig
- **Left the drums almost entirely alone because the source already sounded good — the same "don't fix what isn't broken" philosophy applied even more bluntly than usual, plus two standby (not default) transient/drive tools kept loaded for individual hits.** "I didn't do anything to the kicks. The drums I kind of left how they were because they sounded so good when I got them. Like, I just messed with the blend, I didn't change anything that didn't need to be changed." Light Decapitator Drive on hi-hats, A/B'd across the plugin's Style algorithms by ear; Decapitator, Transient Designer (SPL, unowned — Plugin Wishlist), and Transient Master all kept loaded on toms/drum loops "in case I need to do any transient love" — available tools, not blanket-applied processing. → Decapitator, Transient Master, Mix Handoff, Plugin Wishlist, [Dua Lipa Vocal Chain](#/chain/dua-lipa-vocal-chain) — Mix with the Masters (Josh Gudwin), Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
- **A live-tracking mic-technique lesson from CLA, on-topic even though this chain runs from samples: overhead-as-whole-picture, direct-vs-ambient EQ split, per-tom pan-not-EQ discipline, and "simple miking + a good drummer beats an elaborate setup."** Full recipe on the new Drum Mic Technique note — headline moves: overhead named the single most important mic ("that's the whole picture of the record"); EQ/comp effort reserved for kick/snare (direct mics) while overhead/room stay untouched; toms checked one hit at a time, each panned to its own position but kept EQ-consistent across the set; stated philosophy, "if you keep the miking simple and you have a good drummer, it's really easy — it's all about how you blend it," echoing this section's own Kenny Beats/Zach Scholz mic-placement entries below. → Drum Mic Technique, EQ, Gain Staging — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Tracking live drums with Chris Lord-Alge
- **Section-staged drum sample reinforcement: bass drum sample under the whole song, but snare/clap/tambourine reinforcement layers reserved for the chorus only — full recipe on Sound Selection Guide.** Tom Elmhirst, Adele's "Rolling in the Deep" — a small, deliberately section-specific reinforcement pass on top of one plain mic'd kit, not a blanket drum-replacement. → Sound Selection Guide, Layering and Stacking, Arrangement and Song Form — Mix with the Masters (Tom Elmhirst), Tom Elmhirst breaks down his mix of 'Rolling in the Deep' by Adele
- **Splice "Afrodancer" afrobeat kit + a groove loop layered on top + a drum fill named as the actual level-up move for the genre, plus a rim shot layered purely for texture (kept even though it wasn't audibly cutting through).** Genre-matched kit selection over a generic trap/hip-hop kit, consistent with the "match the kit to the genre" pattern already logged on Sound Selection Guide — the notable addition here is the explicit claim that fill quality, not kit quality, is what actually differentiates an afrobeats groove. → Sound Selection Guide, Rhythm and Groove — loner, [making a soulful afrobeats beat for rema & wizkid from scratch (use voice notes to start ideas!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e-KvnLXHAy4)
- **Dual-mic snare trick: a standard top mic + a second angled position that doubles as a near-front kick mic** — mic 1 in the usual top-snare spot a few inches off the batter head; mic 2 (same model) positioned slightly above the shell and a bit further back — not quite side-snare, chosen because it also catches the kick's batter head almost like a front kick mic, plus extra kit ambience. Both run into independent mixer channels, EQ'd separately, then get **summed to a single input** — a hardware pre-sum before the DAW. → [Drums Snare-Clap Track](#/chain/drums-snare-clap-track) — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Push mic input hard into an analog stage for deliberate clipping, kept as intentional lo-fi character, not gain-staged away** — both snare mics driven hot enough to clip an analog mixer produced "a very distorted snare" that read as a genre-appropriate choice in the context of a full lo-fi drum mix; the kick got the same treatment (EQ boosted hard around 60 Hz until it clipped) for a deliberately weird low end that "sounds really cool" once blended with the overhead. → Saturation and Distortion, SUB Slot — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **When a source can't go through the analog stage (no phantom power for a condenser overhead), emulate the same character in the box instead** — drive a preamp plugin hard on the direct-to-interface overhead to match the vibe of the already-driven kick/snare, rather than letting one mic sound cleaner than the rest of the kit. → UAD Neve 1073 — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Budget stereo-pair trick: cheap pencil condensers hung directly from the cable instead of mounted on stands** — light enough to skip buying stands entirely; used here as a subtle stereo-widening pair kept very low in the mix (the kit stays mostly mono), with extra top-end attenuation since cheap pencil condensers tend to read bright. → Stereo Field — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Ambience trick: a spare mic in an unrelated adjacent room, processed through an amp sim purely for reverb** — reads "more natural" for a bigger drum sound than throwing reverb on the drum bus directly; general takeaway — if there's a spare mic during a drum session, throw it somewhere far away and process it separately rather than leaving it unused. → Depth and Space, Reverb — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Snare/hi-hat bleed fix: expansion instead of compression on a bussed snare pair** — when a mic position makes hi-hat bleed close to unavoidable, expanding the dynamic range (rather than compressing, which would pull the bleed UP toward the snare) pushes snare hits further out and drops the hi-hat bleed between them down. Once separated this way, the snare can take additional distortion for extra lo-fi grit without dragging the hi-hat bleed along with it. → [Drums Snare-Clap Track](#/chain/drums-snare-clap-track), Sidechaining — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Group saturation IS the drum glue (and drums don't get limited)** — kick+snare+hats saturated together so hits interact; his control doctrine: saturate/distort drums, limit everything else; alternate section trick: print a "wavy" version of this whole group through filter+phaser+auto-pan performed by hand for verse 2 — Lophiile, [Make Your Drums Slap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v4ZhwlhF5yE) & [Maria Isabel breakdown](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RXrF27xqogg)
- **Scratch-kit chain order: Pultec EQ → Gate → Soothe2 on the GROUP → Devil-Loc Deluxe** — EQ first on the snare, gate the noise between hits, one Soothe2 resonance pass over the summed kit (not per mic), Devil-Loc for the crush; then warp the timing and **pitch the drums down** for weight (the sampled-break move on your own kit) — Kenny Beats, [Cook Up From Scratch](https://youtu.be/l7AjRTXex2U)
- **Four close mics, NO room mic** — U87 overhead placed low at knee height **between snare and floor tom, aimed at the kick, far from the hi-hat** (bright condensers near the hat only add ping; from there one mic hears the whole kit incl. kick) + ribbon over the kick + snare + kick-front. Rooms are optional, placement isn't — Kenny Beats, [Drum Recording Process 2023](https://youtu.be/HTbdB6rWHNI)
- **Mechanical bleed control beats gating** — snare mic ~1" above the rim aimed near-straight down, with a crash-guard shield blocking the hat; fix spill at the source, not with plugins — Kenny Beats, [Drum Recording Process 2023](https://youtu.be/HTbdB6rWHNI)

chains.title: Drums Hats Group
chains.routing: [Drums Hat tracks, shakers, percs] → Drums Hats Group → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Hats + shakers + top percussion summed — the mix's "top layer" treated as one texture.

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Sum cleanup
- HPF the whole group 300+ Hz · one broad tilt decision: how bright is the top layer vs the vocal air?
- **Why:** Hats and vocal air share 8–12 kHz — decide who owns it (usually vocal, in your genres) and shelf the hats accordingly.

### 2. Glue Compressor — Texture glue
- **Ratio 2:1** (②) · **Attack 1 ms** (③ — fast; hats have no transient worth protecting at group level) · **Release Auto** (④) · **Threshold for ~1.5 dB GR** (①) · **Makeup** to unity (⑤) · **Dry/Wet 100%** (⑦)
- **Why:** Makes hat + shaker + perc breathe as one instrument instead of three competing tickers. A fast attack is fine here — clamping the tick fronts evens the texture rather than dulling it.

### 3. S1 Imager — Width
- **Width +15%** (①) — top percussion is where width is cheap and safe (no mono-compat risk like low end).

## Variations
- **Trap:** skip the imager, keep hats fairly centered and dry — modern trap tops are narrow and upfront.
- 🎬 *From video:* Southside signature exception to "dry" trap hats — reverb specifically on the hats (named example: *Married to the Game*), as either the hats' own insert or a dedicated hi-hat send depending on the session. → Reverb — loner, [the secret samplemaker behind Southside's best beats!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WLOHe9CJChY)

## From videos

- **Reverb specifically on the hi-hats, as a recurring Southside signature** — named example: *Married to the Game*; a deliberate exception to the "keep trap hats dry" default above, worth reaching for on a Southside/Future-adjacent beat specifically. → Reverb — loner, [the secret samplemaker behind Southside's best beats!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WLOHe9CJChY)

- **"Always overdrive your shakers — ALWAYS"** — chasing the 7-inch-record breakup: distortion on shakers/cabasa as a rule, not a choice — Disclosure, [Prince Edit stream](https://youtu.be/hOvLf9nX500) → Saturation and Distortion
- **Pan and de-grid the extras** — hat rolls/open hats/percussion off-center and swung/off-grid; the core hat can stay center but the ornaments shouldn't stack on it — Kenny Beats, [Trap Drums More Interesting](https://youtu.be/fo-E8dY81Nw) → Width and Stereo
- **909 hat volume-envelope hold trick — one sample, two lengths.** Pull the volume envelope's hold stage all the way up: hold the key down and the hat sustains for as long as you hold it, release early and it stays short — one key gives you both a long and a short hat, no second sample needed. — Disclosure (Sol State), [How Disclosure Makes A Remix/Edit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jS9rs9y3kFs)

chains.title: Drums Bus
chains.routing: [Drums Group] → Drums Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** The drum section's final glue + loudness stage. Your current working chain (Bus_Drums export) kept as default — API glue into tape into density into color into a catch-limiter is a pro-standard structure.

## Chain overview
Glue comp → tape → density → color → peak catch. Compressor first so everything downstream saturates a *steady* signal; limiter last purely as a peak net.

## Chain

### 1. API-2500 — Glue compression
- 🎬 *From video:* build a four-aux parallel-send system off this bus — after crushing it hard through comp/limiting, rebuild ONLY what got lost via dedicated sends rather than backing off the crush. Jaycen Joshua: "with these four, I'm making up what I'm losing by hitting the compression and the limiter and the Black Box super, super hard." Aux 1 ("Transformer") = Decapitator (dark, mid-aggressive) → an SSL-style "Cross-Eyed" comp (Attack 30, Release 1, Ratio 2:1, ~8 dB GR — see Glue Compressor) → low end stripped, top-end "spark" only. Aux 2 = an MV2-style low-level enhancer as a front-to-back attention effect (unowned, see Plugin Wishlist). Aux 3 ("Transformer 2," on the kick specifically) = same Decapitator+comp recipe with Decapitator's Style E (Chandler-style) for a deliberately blown-out, Fruity-Loops-style hip-hop kick character — subtle here, pushable to full aggression on harder records. → Decapitator, Glue Compressor, [Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send), TRANSIENT Slot, Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters (Jaycen Joshua), [Jaycen Joshua on creative drum mixing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BELkgU5j2ww)
- 🎬 *From video:* a named alternative bus compressor reached for specifically to add impact rather than just glue: **UA 33609**, driven for obvious "extra sauce" that "really makes him hit" — a heavier-drive, presence-forward use distinct from this stage's default subtler glue role. Bypass-checked against the raw signal. Unowned — see Plugin Wishlist; owned equivalents in the same energetic-drum-bus-comp role are this chain's own API-2500 (pushed harder) or UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII — Mix with the Masters (Marcella Araica), Printing stems through analog equipment with Marcella Araica
- 🎬 *From video:* a contrasting light-touch alternative worth trying on a subtler mix: Jaycen Joshua runs his own drum bus through a **Shadow Hills Mastering Compressor** (plugin, A/B'd against hardware and preferred for automation flexibility) barely engaged — "I just kiss it," relying on the unit's character rather than gain reduction. Owned equivalents in the same subtle-glue role: Glue Compressor or Solid Bus Comp, driven for tone with GR kept minimal. See Plugin Wishlist for the Shadow Hills entry — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), [Jaycen Joshua's drum bus](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LY-vU5MwBvs)
- 🎬 *From video:* on "My Hi"'s drum bus, the API-2500 was pushed for a **brutal transient slam** at the entry point — driven hard enough that it's audibly aggressive on its own, then dialed back via the plugin's own mix knob rather than reducing the ratio/threshold (drive the circuit hard for its character, use Mix to tame the amount) — Disclosure, [First Twitch Stream Ever (Production Tutorial)](https://youtu.be/IObzp3OugtY)
- 🎬 *From video:* a SEPARATE shared parallel "kick-snare crush" send off this bus, downstream of this stage's own glue — a DBX-160-style compressor at **~4:1–4.5:1**, transient-triggered, not much GR, adding length and reshaping the attack rather than obviously squashing; stacked with two further parallel stereo drum-bus compressors (a Fatso-style unit for peak limiting, and a Fairchild-670-style "drum crush" run as two mono instances deliberately UNLINKED left/right) — full recipe on Parallel Processing — Mix with the Masters (Andrew Scheps), Mix buss & drum processing with Andrew Scheps
- 🎬 *From video:* an automated "drums dirt" push send off this bus (high-pass EQ → lo-fi/downsample → aggressive multiband clipper → an EQ cutting the mid-range mess that stage creates), muted everywhere except transitions and choruses — beefs up the whole kit in the moment without just raising the fader; room-mic tracks get the same automated in/out treatment for the same sections — Mix with the Masters (Andrew Scheps), Mix buss & drum processing with Andrew Scheps → Redux, Saturation and Distortion, Automation
- **Ratio 4:1** (②) · **Attack 30 ms** (③ — slowest step, the punch dial: slower = bigger transients) · **Release: click the knob to its final position for variable/Auto release** (④ — recovers faster after light compression, slower after deep hits; ~120 ms if set fixed) · **2.5 dB GR** on the beat
- Tone section: **Thrust = Loud** (⑤ — max low-freq detector filtering so the kick stops pumping the whole bus; drop to Med only if it thins the kick) · **Knee = Hard** (⑧ — "the 2500 sound") · **Type = New** (⑥ — feed-forward, snappy/modern punch; **Old** = warmer, laid-back vintage — pick per song)
- **Link 100%** (⑦ — unlinked, a hard left-side tom compresses only the left channel and shoves your centered kick/snare toward the right)
- **Mix 100%** (⑨) for straight glue; drop to **~75%** for the parallel transient-slam move (drive the circuit hard for character, tame the amount with Mix, not the ratio/threshold) · **Output** (⑩) to make up the 2–3 dB back to unity
- Output gain up until the drums fill the same space as bypassed, just tighter (or flip the auto-makeup switch)
- **Why:** The API-2500 is *the* drum bus compressor; Thrust is its superpower — without it, every kick hit ducks the snare/hats. The classic drum recipe: slow attack + fast release + aggressive ratio.
- **Alt use — one-plugin parallel:** high ratio, fast attack, fast release, slam it, then blend with the **mix knob** — instant "energy giver" without a separate crush send.
- 🎬 *From video:* complement bus glue by **faking hard compression at the source** — nudge a clap/hat ~10–13 ms *ahead* of the kick so its transient pokes through before the body (a comp always lets the transient through first). Don't quantize it — in-grid it sounds soft — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8) & [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ).

### 2. Kramer Tape — Tape stage
- 🎬 *From video:* on a heavy 4-on-the-floor drum bus, tape saturation is what "squashes the hi-hats in a lovely way" every time the kick hits — a GP9-style tape setting with lows rolled off, driven hard for squelch on the hats/percussion specifically, backed off if it starts losing overall dynamic range — Disclosure, [First Twitch Stream Ever (Production Tutorial)](https://youtu.be/IObzp3OugtY)
- Settings: **15 ips** (④) · **Flux driven hard** (① — the squelch) · **HP filter rolling off lows** (⑧ — GP9-style, keep the drive on mids/hats) · **Playback to unity** (③). **Flux is the real drive knob** — more flux = more tape compression/saturation at the same output. Or unlink record/playback and push record level (turn playback down to match).
- Speed: **15 ips** = tighter lows + lifted highs (default) · 7.5 ips = fatter lows, duller top (lo-fi/vintage drums) · bias Over = a little extra top
- A touch of wow/flutter + noise only if you *want* audible vintage; zero for clean glue
- **Why:** Tape after compression is the analog-record order (console comp → tape machine). Soft-clips the drum transients the API let through — free peak control that sounds like glue, not limiting.

### 3. Oxford Inflator — Density
- Effect 20–35%
- **Why:** Raises perceived loudness between the peaks — drums feel bigger at the same meter reading.
- 🎬 *From video:* Disclosure lean on Inflator (or the Oxford Limiter) here for a **forward push** even when it's barely engaging — the slight distortion is the point; the bus ends up reading *louder and fuller while the meter reads lower* — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ) & [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).

### 4. Saturn 2 — Final color
- Gentle, tape/tube, single band or subtle multiband
- **Why:** Last coat of harmonic paint on the finished dynamics — by this point it's seasoning, not cooking.
- 🎬 *From video:* think of stages 2–4 as **stacked gentle saturation across the whole bus** (tape → density → tube), each adding ~10% harmonics — the sum tames the transients that would push into the red, so the drums sound bigger at a *lower* meter. A touch of de-esser on the bus also tames harsh hi-hats — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ).

### 5. Ozone 9 Maximizer — Peak catch
- IRC IV · threshold for **1–2 dB GR on hits only** · ceiling −0.3 dB relative
- **Why:** A safety net so drum peaks don't eat the master's headroom — NOT a loudness stage; if it's working hard, back off upstream.

## Meters & gain staging
Your export shows the full meter sandwich (Utility + Swiss Army + mvMeter at both ends) — drums are *the* place for the "average around 0 VU" rule since peaks fly far above average.

## Variations
- **Trap knock:** API attack faster (10–15 ms), Gold Clip instead of Maximizer (Threshold to shave ~3–4 dB of transient, Softness low/hard, Oversampling on, Mix 100%) — clipped transients are the modern knock sound.
- **Big live rock:** more Kramer drive, API release slower, blend [Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send) up underneath.

## From videos

- **A crush room-mic layer, tracked in parallel and run hard through an opto tube compressor purely for character, feeding this bus alongside the clean kit.** Sylvia Massy's tracking-stage version of the same "crush a room/character mic hard" idea this bus already applies at the mix stage — a ribbon mic through a Teletronix LA-2A. Direct owned match: UAD Teletronix LA-2A. → UAD Teletronix LA-2A, Parallel Processing, Drum Mic Technique — Sylvia Massy (Mix with the Masters), Analog Recording workflow - Sylvia Massy
- **A dense, mostly-parallel layered treatment for this bus: a shared kick-snare crush send, an automated "drums dirt" push effect, two stacked stereo parallel drum-bus compressors, tom/snare short-ambience reverbs (one pitch-shifted), and a reamped-guitar-amp ambience track — individually each layer sounds artificial or subtle in isolation, but together it reads as one drummer rather than a stack of processing.** Full per-stage breakdown inline at stage 1 above and on Parallel Processing, Reverb (effect), Saturation and Distortion; a mix-bus "happy face" broad EQ + a barely-engaged always-on Oxford Limiter (4–5 dB GR on kick/snare peaks despite reading as inaudible) sit on the MASTER bus feeding this one — see UAD Pultec EQP-1A, Limiting. Explicit design philosophy: "the more I sort of treat and process, the less natural they sound individually, but together it still sounds like a drummer, it doesn't sound like samples being built up." → Parallel Processing, Reverb, Saturation and Distortion, Automation, Kick Design — Mix with the Masters (Andrew Scheps), Mix buss & drum processing with Andrew Scheps
- **A per-element Lo-Fi/sample-rate-reduction pass across nearly every drum channel (kick/808, snare, hats, layered vinyl samples) for a dark, "not in your face" album-wide character, plus a standing cymbal-pocket habit: a subtle quarter-note delay + long reverb on any downbeat cymbal, every time.** Full recipe on Redux and Reverb (effect). Drum-bus compression workflow note: built from a "Heavy Drum" preset then tweaked (lower the mix, nudge a parameter) rather than dialed from scratch — "I use presets all the time cuz plugins come with presets, use them." → Redux, Reverb, Delay, Compression — Mix with the Masters (Kieron Menzies), Drum programing with Kieron Menzies
- **The full four-aux subtractive-then-additive drum-bus system, in one place: crush this bus hard via compression/limiting, then rebuild ONLY the specific qualities lost (transient life, tonal attention, kick character) through dedicated parallel sends rather than softening the crush itself.** Jaycen Joshua's governing philosophy alongside the system: "I always try to remove stuff so things can be on its own and separated — the bass has its frequency region, the loop has its frequency region, and so on and so forth, and when they all work together it absolutely sounds beautiful." Full aux-by-aux breakdown logged inline on stage 1 above and on Parallel Processing. → Parallel Processing, Decapitator, Glue Compressor, Masking and Carving — Mix with the Masters (Jaycen Joshua), Jaycen Joshua on creative drum mixing
- **A second, gentler bus insert shape for a percussion stem, run alongside (not instead of) a parallel comp send: a restrained compressor plus a transient designer nudged and then blended back in only lightly.** On the aux the percussion stem was already routed through: a compressor with a fairly fast setting, deliberately **not** driven hard ("don't quite want to hit it as hard as that"), followed by a Sonnox Oxford Envolution transient designer — praised for sensitivity/threshold on grabbing internal transients "a little bit better than some of the other ones can." Pushed "a little bit over the top," Attack up and Sustain trimmed reads "a nice amount of attack" but "a little bit process sounding" at full strength — the fix was mixing in "just a tiny bit" of the processed signal rather than running it fully wet. Closed with a critical-listening pass on individual elements that caught a specific frequency undermining the new snap (flagged, not fixed on screen) — worth doing as a final check any time a bus-stage move is chasing "more snap." Owned best-match for the transient designer: Transient Shaper (its own Mode/Sensitivity control matches the language used here). → Transient Shaper, TRANSIENT Slot, Masking and Carving, [Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send), Parallel Processing — Mix with the Masters (Alan Meyerson), Adding impact to percussions with Alan Meyerson
- **Tracking-stage precedent for this chain's own hardware-Fairchild/vintage-limiter references above: a real engineer checking a bus limiter live while getting drum sounds up, and running a room mic through nothing but Fairchild bus compression (no reverb).** While tracking, CLA runs a limiter check directly on the drum bus before mixing even starts ("take our bus limiter, make sure you're doing right"), and processes the room mic with just light Fairchild compression — "I got a Fairchild and it kicks ass, so why not use it... this is no reverb, just a little bus compression." Corroborates this chain's existing Disclosure "a limiter still earns its place on the drum bus" entry below and the Oxford-Limiter-as-Fairchild-substitute reasoning on Limiting — worth reaching for on the **Big live rock** variation above when the source is genuinely a mic'd kit rather than samples. → Drum Mic Technique, Limiting, Vintage Gear Worklist — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Tracking live drums with Chris Lord-Alge
- **A named UA 33609 added right at this bus's compression stage specifically for impact, driven differently here than on the matching music bus in the same session.** "On both of these buses I'm going to add a 33609 from UA — this really brings extra sauce on the drums that really make him hit." Comes immediately after individually printing each drum's analog-board processing back as its own stem (kick and snare each processed with EQ + an SPL transient designer, printed one by one even though they shared output channels going out) — see Committing and Printing. Contrast with the lighter, "breathing" dial-in used on the music bus for the same plugin — see [Inst-Synth Bus](#/chain/inst-synth-bus) and Compression Staging. → Committing and Printing, Compression Staging, [Inst-Synth Bus](#/chain/inst-synth-bus), Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters (Marcella Araica), Printing stems through analog equipment with Marcella Araica
- **A full alternate light-touch drum bus chain, mastering-engineer style: subtle compression → noise-floor gate → broad EQ dip + presence boost → mid/side pocket carve → mono maker → matched mid/side EQ recovery.** In order: (1) Shadow Hills Mastering Compressor-style glue barely engaged, unowned — see Plugin Wishlist and §1 above; (2) a Gate used purely for noise-floor control (not dynamics) — hold + release combined ~1 second so it never chatters between hits, since a heavy compression/plugin chain raises the audible noise floor even when there's nothing left to gate musically; (3) a broad EQ dip **~1100 Hz and below, ~2.5 dB**, to tame a "heavy" low-mid that was over-driving upstream harmonics, followed by a small presence-region boost — "I'm a dipper," cut before you add; (4) a **mid/side EQ dip on the bus's CENTER image** to carve a pocket for the vocal, since the drums live mostly in the mid/center image on this mix (Pro-Q 4 M/S mode); (5) **Mono Maker** — collapse everything below **~61 Hz** to mono/center (owned: Ozone 9 Imager's Mono Maker control); (6) a **matched cut-center/boost-sides move at the SAME frequency (~112 Hz)** — remove it from the vocal's center pocket, then put it back on the outside/side image so the energy isn't lost, run extremely lightly ("kissed it, barely feel it"). Every stage deliberately subtle — worth reaching for on a vocal-forward mix where the drum bus needs to leave the center image open rather than dominate it, distinct from this chain's default heavier-glue structure above. → Gate, EQ, Pro-Q 4, Ozone 9 Imager, Width and Stereo, Compression, Masking and Carving, Plugin Wishlist — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), [Jaycen Joshua's drum bus](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LY-vU5MwBvs)
- **A much harder, "level every peak to the same height" bus compression target for a vintage acoustic-soul drum sound, distinct from this chain's default lighter glue.** The waveform of a reference Marvin Gaye drum track shows peaks sitting at nearly the same level throughout — a heavier compression than a typical modern bus-glue pass; matched on a recreated soul-flip kit (Addictive Drums, hand-played/unquantized for swing) with a compressor pushed hard enough to flatten the peaks that far. Worth reaching for on this bus specifically when the goal is "recorded to tape in one take," not "glued but still dynamic." *(general starting point — no ratio/threshold given)* → Compression, Pocket and Microtiming, Sound Selection Guide — loner, [these 1970's soul secrets will change how you make melodies!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRLzsshf6yg)
- **Two mid/side moves for this bus, both routed via the duplicate-channel M/S trick and both called out as working "especially" on drums.** (1) A transient expander on the isolated **side** image restores a percussive quality the sides often lack — insert after this bus's glue stage, blend in carefully so it doesn't overdo the effect (owned starting points: Transient Master, kHs Transient Shaper). (2) Parallel compression + limiting + overdrive blended into the isolated **mid** image only (demoed with unowned Invigorate, see Plugin Wishlist) — a mid-only variant of this chain's existing §1 API-2500 glue stage, worth trying when the kit needs more center-weight density without also driving the sides. → Width and Stereo, Parallel Processing, Plugin Wishlist — Sage Audio, [Mid Side Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SHxih1xc5yM)
- **"My go-to drum bus level": peak at -8 dB, framed as a reference point for knowing where every other bus should sit relative to it** — same "think like a mastering engineer with the stem" order as the rest of this chain (compression → saturation → resonance control → limiter), but with a lighter glue variant on this song: API-2500 slow attack starting at **2:1 ratio** (rather than the 4:1 documented above from "My Hi") before tape/Inflator/Saturn tube. **Soothe dialed to a 50/50 mix specifically to tame a resonant tambourine** — an ear-informed, targeted fix rather than a default setting. Limiter preference confirmed as **Oxford Limiter** (Ozone 9 Maximizer or a vintage-style limiter as fallbacks). Bypassed-vs-processed check: not louder in peak terms, just more body/weight — reinforces the existing "reads louder while the meter reads lower" theme already documented below. → Soothe2 — Disclosure, [GO TO Drum Bus (8 Step Method)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tRDJRCoDXPg)
- **When most of the character was already driven in at the mixer/mic stage, keep this bus deliberately light** — a lo-fi drum session run almost entirely through an analog mixer (hard-driven snare/kick clipping, breakup on every mic) needed only subtle EQ and a little compression at the bus stage — his own point being that most of the "sound" was decided at the source, not here. A useful check before reaching for heavier bus processing: if the tracks already carry real character, this bus's job is just light glue, not a rescue. — Zach Scholz, [Recording Old School "Hip-Hop" Drum Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R14N3T5AikU)
- **Signature snare trick: scoop the snare's fundamental frequency, THEN compress hard** — removing the fundamental first changes what the compressor actually grabs, producing "the close-mic sound of the snare but without so much of the punch, almost like the punch of an overhead" — a fat-but-not-punchy character, finished with a touch of spring reverb. → [Drums Snare-Clap Track](#/chain/drums-snare-clap-track), Snare Design — Zach Scholz, [I Tried Recording a Song Like It's 1976](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6kA1mWeTiZc)
- **Mix THROUGH the crush + the second-bus escape hatch** — put the MPC-style crush/distortion on the drum bus early and build the beat through it ("it needs noise, needs wrongness"); when one element suffers (their hi-hat), route the distorted bus into a clean **post-distortion bus** and move the sends/next effects there — staged buses let one element escape a group treatment — Disclosure, [Remix Stems Stream](https://youtu.be/IOSPhXcXT_8)
- **EQ → saturation/tape-weirdness → THEN compress** — Kenny's hardware return order on live drums (Terry CEQ → weird tape echo/saturation → compressor): compressing the already-dirty signal glues the dirt in. Inverse of Disclosure's comp → tape (tape as transient limiter) — pick by intent: comp-last glues character, comp-first tames peaks — Kenny Beats, [Drum Recording Process 2023](https://youtu.be/HTbdB6rWHNI) → Compression Staging
General tips pulled from production breakdowns (via `/music-enrich`), newest-first.

- **"My Hi" drum bus chain, in order:** API-2500 (hard transient slam, tamed via Mix knob) → tape saturation (GP9-style setting, lows cut, driven for hi-hat squelch) → Oxford Inflator (touching red, clip button toggled off/on for extra flavor) → subtle master-style EQ cut (a few unwanted frequencies removed) → a limiter for a few dB of natural-sounding overdrive, leaving headroom — the throughline is **stacked saturation across multiple stages** rather than one heavy hit anywhere — Disclosure, [First Twitch Stream Ever (Production Tutorial)](https://youtu.be/IObzp3OugtY)
- **A/B every saturation stage at once, not one at a time** — Disclosure's live sound engineer builds confidence in a "does-nothing-alone" plugin like Oxford Inflator by bypassing every instance across the whole session simultaneously and toggling back in — the cumulative difference (drums + bass + vocals + master all inflating together) is obvious even when any single instance in isolation seems to do nothing — Disclosure, [First Twitch Stream Ever (Production Tutorial)](https://youtu.be/IObzp3OugtY)
- **Send the whole kit through reverb** (an "H-Verb across the drum bus" signature) for space/glue — feels dead without it; pair with EQ over Soothe2 here because EQ is more transparent and lets you shape transients — Disclosure, [Deeper (with Leon Thomas)](https://youtu.be/SM0FZ58ckVw)
- **Stack gentle saturation across the whole bus** (tape + tube + a third), each ~10% harmonics — reads louder/fuller while the meter reads *lower* (6.9 vs 8); tame the transients that would sum into the red — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ)
- **Oxford Inflator/Oxford Limiter on the drum bus** for a forward-push distortion, barely engaging (safety) — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ) & [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8)
- **Fake hard compression by nudging transients ~10–13 ms early** (clap/hat before the kick) rather than actually squashing — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8) & [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ)
- **De-ess the drum bus** a touch to control harsh hi-hats — Disclosure, [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ)

chains.title: Exponential Groove Drum Rack
chains.routing: Drum Rack (per-pad Simpler) → [[2 Drums Group|Drums Group]] → [[3 Drums Bus|Drums Bus]] → Master
chains.reference: asd (ableton sound design, YouTube breakdown channel)
plugins: loop settings copied to all siblings)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** an evolving, self-mutating drum groove built from a completely ordinary drum pattern — the pattern itself never changes, but a single macro rides every pad's sample-loop length at once, so the groove constantly stretches, compresses, and drifts into audio-rate texture while the underlying beat stays recognizable. Part of asd's five-part "Exponential Rhythms" series; the sibling clip-level technique (Texture warp mode, no instrument needed) is Texture Mode. The through-line across the whole series: use a percentage-based (not fixed-time) parameter as the modulation target, so the same automation/macro produces genuinely different, evolving results rather than a locked-in repeat.

**Signal source:** built entirely from stock Ableton devices (Drum Rack, Simpler ×N, Reverb, Compressor) — nothing here needs an unowned plugin, see Plugin Wishlist (nothing added from this video).

## Chain (build order)

### 1. Drum Rack — kit container, one Simpler per pad
Load a Drum Rack with a handful of drum one-shots (impact/kick/snare/hat character samples); Drum Rack auto-creates one Simpler instance per pad, each with its own spatial/pan variation by default.

### 2. Program the pattern — legato, ordinary
Write a simple, unremarkable drum pattern first — the groove's evolution comes entirely from the macro modulation layered on top, not from a complex pattern. **Every note set to Legato** so notes sustain long enough for the per-pad Simpler loops to actually cycle rather than being cut short.

### 3. Simpler loop setup on one pad, then **copy value to all siblings**
On a single pad's Simpler: enable **Loop**, disable **Zero Crossing Snap**, set **Sample Start = 0**, **Loop = 100%**, **Length = 100%**, nudge the sample's end marker in toward the tail. Right-click that Simpler → **copy value to all siblings** to push the identical settings to every other pad's Simpler in one action, rather than repeating the setup by hand per pad.
- **Why:** establishes the same loop-capable baseline on every pad before any macro mapping happens — the macro step below depends on every pad already having Loop enabled and a usable Start/Loop/Length setup.

### 4. Map **Length** to a rack macro, then **map to all siblings**
Map one pad's Simpler **Length** parameter to a rack macro; right-click → **map to all siblings** so the same macro now drives every other pad's Length parameter simultaneously. One knob rides loop length across the whole kit.
- 🎬 *From video:* fine-tune each pad's individual **Start/End** afterward so every sample's "sweet spot" for the shared macro range still lands right — not every one-shot loops musically across the exact same macro range without this per-pad correction.
- **Why it's free polyrhythm:** Simpler's Length is a **percentage of each individual sample's own Start–End span, not a time value** — so the identical macro position produces a genuinely different loop rate on every pad (a short sample and a long sample never sync to the same rate at the same macro value). See Rhythm and Groove (Polyrhythms) for the general mechanism. → Simpler, Rhythm and Groove

### 5. Ride the macro live against the pattern
Trigger the ordinary drum pattern while moving the Length macro. The exponential/evolving-rhythm movement superimposes onto the existing beat rather than replacing it — the pattern's backbone stays audible while the loop rates underneath constantly shift. Framed in the source as "only creating the illusion of things falling apart," not actual chaos — the balance point between control and disorder is the point of the whole series.

### 6. Extra movement layers (optional, stack freely)
- 🎬 *From video:* map **Transpose** on the hi-hat pads specifically to their own macro — since loop rate is pitch-coupled on a real audio loop, this adds pitch-driven rhythmic movement just to the hats, distinct from the shared Length macro.
- 🎬 *From video:* extend the arrangement's sequence loop length and draw in Length-macro automation across the longer span so the groove keeps evolving rather than repeating a short cycle.
- 🎬 *From video:* deliberately **lengthen some MIDI notes** so they overlap — overlapping notes trigger overlapping looped samples, which reads as genuinely overlapping/layered rhythm rather than one clean pattern.
- 🎬 *From video:* map **Loop** (region start) to a second macro and **Fade** (crossfade) to a third — Loop combined with the existing Length/Transpose automation can push samples further past the audio-rate-looping threshold; Fade smooths the audible clicking that shows up once loop regions get very small.

### 7. Harmonic backdrop + finishing
Layer in one or two additional melodic/harmonic samples for a chordal backdrop under the rhythm (not part of the Drum Rack's percussive pads). Finish with a spacious Reverb and a healthy amount of Compression on the arranged sequence. *(general starting point — exact reverb/compression values not stated in source)*

## Macro rack summary

| Macro | Target | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Length | Simpler Length, mapped to all siblings | shared loop-rate control across the whole kit; per-pad rate differs because Length is % of each sample's own length |
| Hi-Hat Transpose | Simpler Transpose (hi-hat pads only) | pitch-coupled loop-rate movement, isolated to the hats |
| Loop | Simpler Loop (region start) | pushes further past the audio-rate-looping threshold, combined with Length automation |
| Fade | Simpler Fade (crossfade) | smooths clicking on very small (near-audio-rate) loop regions |

## Variations

- **Any kit, not just impacts** — the reusable idea is the copy/map-to-all-siblings workflow plus the percentage-based-Length mechanic, not the specific impact-sample kit. Works on any Drum Rack built from one-shots with enough sustain to loop musically.
- **Pair with the Texture-warp-mode approach** — Texture Mode reaches a related-but-distinct family of results at the clip level (no Drum Rack/Simpler needed); the two can be combined on different elements of the same arrangement — one drum kit via this Simpler-macro method, one melodic/textural clip via Texture warp.
- **Pair with the Free-Rate Arpeggiator approach** — [Free-Rate Arpeggiator Resampling Rack](#/chain/free-rate-arpeggiator-resampling-rack) (part 1 of the same series) reaches the audio-rate-crossover phenomenon via Arpeggiator's fixed-time Rate parameter instead of Simpler's per-sample-relative Length, and adds a resample-to-new-MIDI-track workflow for locking a rhythm in permanently — usable on any MIDI instrument, not just a Drum Rack.
- **Dial back for a usable mix element** — as built, this is a generative/experimental patch. For a track-ready groove, keep the Length macro's range narrower and reserve full audio-rate excursions for transitions/breakdowns rather than the whole arrangement.

## Notes

- All-stock-plugin build — nothing to add to Plugin Wishlist from this video.
- Sibling technique note: Rhythm and Groove (Polyrhythms section) documents the general "percentage-based parameter = free polyrhythm across differently-sized samples" mechanism this chain relies on.

**Sources:** asd, [ableton sound design | EXPONENTIAL RHYTHMS [2/5] Sample Looping in Simpler](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QRj6sxdimkQ) — video-derived, 2026-08-11.

chains.title: Free-Rate Arpeggiator Resampling Rack
chains.routing: MIDI track (sample/instrument) → [[Arpeggiator]] (Rate Mode = Free) → instrument → new armed MIDI track (MIDI From = arpeggiated track, records the resampled rhythm) → [[2 Drums Group|Drums Group]] or downstream instrument/bus
chains.reference: asd (ableton sound design, YouTube breakdown channel)
plugins: Rate automation (drawn over a legato note)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** rhythms that stretch and compress "like a rubber band" instead of sitting on a fixed BPM grid — the entry point of asd's five-part "Exponential Rhythms" series, and its most straightforward method. The sibling chains reach related territory a different way: [Exponential Groove Drum Rack](#/chain/exponential-groove-drum-rack) (part 2) uses Simpler's percentage-based Length parameter across a whole Drum Rack; Texture Mode (part 3) uses clip-level warp settings. This chain instead decouples Arpeggiator's Rate from BPM-synced time divisions entirely, then — the technique's real power move — resamples the arpeggiator's live MIDI output onto a new track so the result becomes permanent, editable rhythm material rather than a one-off performance.

**Signal source:** built entirely from stock Ableton devices (Arpeggiator, Random, Scale, instrument-internal LFO, optionally Corpus/Grain Delay) — nothing here needs an unowned plugin, see Plugin Wishlist (nothing added from this video).

## Chain (build order)

### 1. Arpeggiator on any sample/instrument, Rate Mode = Free
Drag any sample onto a MIDI track (any MIDI instrument or VST works — demoed on a kick sample), load Arpeggiator as a MIDI effect, and set **Rate Mode = Free**. This decouples Rate from BPM-dependent divisions and instead sweeps a raw **10 ms–1000 ms** interval range — holding a note and moving Rate live stretches/squishes the rhythm in real time.

### 2. Draw Rate automation over a legato note for precision
Build a 2-bar MIDI clip with a single note on middle C, press **Legato** so the note sustains to the clip's end, and draw a Rate automation curve directly over it. Different curve shapes produce distinctly different rhythms; crossing a certain Rate threshold flips the result from discrete rhythmic hits to a continuous pitched tone (the series' recurring audio-rate-crossover phenomenon).
- **Why:** live performance (step 1) is good for finding a range; drawn automation is what makes the result repeatable and refinable.

### 3. Resample to a new MIDI track — lock the rhythm in
Create a new MIDI track, arm it, and set its input/**MIDI From** to the arpeggiated track, then record. Every arp hit is captured as a distinct, permanently editable MIDI note event — stretch, compress, or chop individual hits in the new clip's note editor.
- 🎬 *From video:* asd used exactly this to build a song's central rhythm — resampled the arpeggiated MIDI output from a **hi-hat** track, then reused that resulting MIDI clip to drive the rhythms of the **bass, strings, and vocal** elements elsewhere in the same track. One resampled rhythm became the backbone for multiple, otherwise-unrelated parts.
- **Why:** this is the step that turns Arpeggiator from a live-only modulation effect into reusable, arrangeable material — the technique's real value over just riding Rate live.

### 4. Secondary shaping parameters (optional, stack freely)
- 🎬 *From video:* modulate **Gate** for note-length variation relative to the current Rate value.
- 🎬 *From video:* feed **chords** into Arpeggiator instead of single notes for pitch variation across hits, plus variation for any key-tracked downstream parameters; the **Style** parameter changes how the chord gets interpreted/ordered.

### 5. Optional generative-melody layer: Random → Scale
For tonal/harmonic instruments, chain a Random MIDI effect right after Arpeggiator (re-transposes each generated hit), then a Scale device after that (quantizes the randomized result into a chosen scale) — turns the arp into a self-generating melodic line that stays in key.

### 6. Optional per-hit modulation: instrument-internal LFO trigger mode
For instruments with a built-in LFO: enable its note-on/trigger mode with wave = Random or Sample & Hold, so every incoming arp hit retriggers the LFO to a fresh random value assignable to pitch, filter cutoff, or other synth parameters. Distinct from the Max for Live LFO device — this uses the instrument's own internal LFO.

### 7. Optional correlated-movement finish: copy Rate automation to a second parameter
Copy the drawn Rate automation curve and paste it onto a second parameter's automation lane (e.g. filter cutoff), then reshape to taste on the new target.
- 🎬 *From video:* demoed on the kick-sample instrument — pasted the Rate curve onto a **resonant high-pass filter's cutoff**, pitched the sample up, and tightened the amplitude envelope for a tighter, "clicky" sound. *(general starting point — exact filter/pitch/envelope values not given in source)*

### 8. Optional resonator finish
As a further textural layer, run the result through a resonator effect — asd names Corpus and Grain Delay as personal go-tos for this, flagged as "an entirely different rabbit hole" with no specific settings given (a dedicated resonators series was stated as planned).

## Macro rack summary

| Stage | Target | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Rate Mode | Arpeggiator Rate | Free = 10–1000 ms raw range, decoupled from BPM |
| Rate automation | Arpeggiator Rate, drawn over a legato note | precise, repeatable stretch/squish shaping |
| Resample track | New MIDI track, MIDI From = arp track | locks the arpeggiated rhythm into permanent, editable MIDI |
| Gate | Arpeggiator Gate | note-length variation relative to Rate |
| Random → Scale | post-Arpeggiator MIDI chain | generative-but-in-key melody on tonal instruments |
| Copied Rate curve | a second parameter (e.g. filter cutoff) | correlated movement from one drawn shape |

## Variations

- **Any MIDI instrument, not just drums** — the demo uses a kick sample, but the technique is instrument-agnostic; asd's own use case (resampling a hi-hat's arp output to drive bass/strings/vocals) shows it working across an entire arrangement, not just percussion. Filed under `2 Drums/` alongside its sibling [Exponential Groove Drum Rack](#/chain/exponential-groove-drum-rack) for series continuity, but equally applicable via `5 Inst & Synth/`.
- **Pair with the sibling techniques** — combine this Arpeggiator-based method on one element with [Exponential Groove Drum Rack](#/chain/exponential-groove-drum-rack)'s Simpler-Length method on a Drum Rack, or with Texture Mode's clip-warp method on a melodic clip, for a fuller "exponential rhythms" arrangement across multiple elements.
- **Live-performance vs. drawn-automation are two distinct modes** — live Rate-riding is fast for finding a range/feel; drawn automation + resampling is what makes a result repeatable and reusable elsewhere in the arrangement.

## Notes

- All-stock-plugin build — nothing to add to Plugin Wishlist from this video.
- Sibling technique note: Rhythm and Groove (Polyrhythms section) cross-links this chain's audio-rate-crossover mechanism against the sibling Simpler-Length method.
- Resonators (Corpus, Grain Delay) are named as a further finishing layer but with no settings given in source — see those plugins' own notes for their independently-documented techniques from other videos.

**Sources:** asd, [ableton sound design | EXPONENTIAL RHYTHMS [1/5] Free Rate Arpeggiator](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WXzDesXWA3I) — video-derived, 2026-08-11.

chains.title: Drums FX Track
chains.routing: Drums FX → FX Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Sweeps, impacts, risers, reverses, foley percussion — drum-adjacent ear candy. Routes to the [FX Bus](#/chain/fx-bus), not the drums bus: these are *texture*, not groove — they shouldn't hit the drum-bus compressor and make it pump.

**Chain philosophy:** fit → character → tame.

## 1 — Sound Selection

- **Selection IS the recording step** — audition in XO / pack browser. Human-touch sources beat stock sweeps: 🎬 Disclosure use **Splice acapella vocal shouts + a white-noise sweep as impact tools**, and **self-recorded tambourines at different speeds** (varispeed) that lock when pitched together — [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag) → Sampling and Sound Selection.
- 🎬 **Layer many small risers instead of one Splice riser** — a freq-mod build + delay build + filtered clap-verb + two tambourines drifting in early, all cresting together — Disclosure, [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag).

## 2 — Programming Best Practice

- FX earn their place at **section boundaries** — risers into drops, impacts on downbeats, reverses as pre-echoes. One per transition; more = noise.
- 🎬 **"Sneaky stuff":** heavily distorted, near-silent accent layers under loud kick/snare, pumped hard by the sidechain so you never consciously hear them — "all they do is bring out the hi-hat." Texture you feel, not hear — Disclosure, [Making Beats + Talk](https://youtu.be/1GhqAf9lc3A) → TEXTURE Slot.

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

Rarely needed — texture wants character, not fidelity. If a sample is sterile: UAD Neve 1073 driven harder than usual → print. (The Sony TC-630 loop is the better sterile-fix for this lane.)

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Fit
- HPF aggressively (usually 100–300 Hz — FX rarely deserve low end) · LPF if the element fights vocal air
- **Why:** Ear candy earns its place at the spectral edges; full-range FX mask the money elements.

### 2. RC-20 Retro Color — Character
- Any flavor that separates it from the clean kit — texture is the point. (Hardware lane: Sony TC-630; Kenny's Generation Loss pedal is this same job — [Guitar Recording Process](https://youtu.be/VruZ-A0_aZk).)

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Tame
- Fast catch of unpredictable peaks (impacts/risers vary wildly) · 2–4 dB GR.

## 5 — Track FX (optional)

- Reverses, granular smears (Crystallizer/Echobode), pitch drops — this whole track IS the FX lane; go wild, then gain-stage it back down.
- 🎬 **Drop "womp" one-shots: reverb → OTT → multiband compression** — drown a plain synth zap (or a bass hit) in Hybrid Reverb, run OTT after it, then a multiband compressor on top — turns a basic zap into a huge-impact drop-transition one-shot; works on sub-bass despite the usual low-end caution. Native granular smear alternative to the wishlisted Portal: Granulator 3 on a resampled kit/clip loop (Cloud mode, Variation up) — dnksaus, [reverb can be POWERFUL](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gi_y81NmoGg) & [granulate EVERYTHING](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVLM1XMT6Z0)

## 6 — Bus / Send FX (optional)

Routing: **Drums FX → [FX Bus](#/chain/fx-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)** (deliberately NOT the drums bus).

- **Risers into drops:** automate [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) up through the riser and cut it dead at the downbeat — the silence-slam trick.
- Sidechain-duck the whole track to the kick when it's a bed rather than an event.

## Variations

- **Percussion loops as texture:** crush harder (RC-20 mix 50%+) and tuck way under the programmed kit.
- **Ambient/indie:** field-recording beds instead of sweeps — see Ambient Texture and Field Recording.

## From videos

- **Drop "womp" one-shots: reverb → OTT → multiband compression** — drown a plain synth/bass zap in Hybrid Reverb, run OTT after it, then a multiband compressor — turns a basic hit into a huge-impact drop-transition one-shot. → OTT — dnksaus, [reverb can be POWERFUL](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gi_y81NmoGg)
- **Granulator as a native granular-smear alternative** — Granulator 3 (Cloud mode, Variation up) on a resampled kit/clip loop covers the same "granular smear" role as the wishlisted Portal, for risers/texture built entirely from stock devices. → Granulator 3 — dnksaus, [granulate EVERYTHING](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVLM1XMT6Z0)

## Sources

Disclosure — [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag) · [Making Beats + Talk](https://youtu.be/1GhqAf9lc3A) · Kenny Beats — [Guitar Recording Process](https://youtu.be/VruZ-A0_aZk) · dnksaus — [reverb can be POWERFUL](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gi_y81NmoGg) & [granulate EVERYTHING](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVLM1XMT6Z0)

chains.title: FX Bus
chains.routing: [Drums FX, transitions, ear candy] → FX Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Sums the *sound-effect elements* ([Drums FX Track](#/chain/drums-fx-track), risers, impacts, transitions, foley). Distinct from the send returns ([Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) etc.), which are shared spaces — this bus is for elements that ARE effects.

## Chain

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Containment
- HPF 100–200 Hz and LPF ~12 kHz on the sum — FX get the mid window, the spectral edges belong to the music.

### 2. Glue Compressor — Tame
- **Ratio 4:1** (②) · **Attack 10 ms** (③ — fast-ish, grabs unpredictable spikes) · **Release Auto** (④) · **Threshold for ~2.5 dB GR** (①) · **Makeup** to unity (⑤) · **Dry/Wet 100%** (⑦)
- **Why:** FX elements (delays, risers, one-shots) are unpredictable by nature; a firm 4:1 with a fast attack keeps their collective level civilized so no single throw jumps out of the mix.

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Duck vs lead vocal
- External sidechain from the lead vocal · 1–2 dB
- **Why:** Ear candy should never cost a lyric. Ducking the whole FX lane under the vocal means you can be generous with candy and never mask the money.

## Variations
- **Instrumental/EDM:** re-key the duck from the lead synth instead.

chains.title: Digital Bass Track
chains.routing: Digital Bass → Bass Group → Bass Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** 808s, synth bass, sub bass — the programmed low end. Treated like an instrument per the process: same stages a recorded bass gets, with UAD plugin equivalents standing in for the hardware pass.

**Chain philosophy:** tone EQ → saturation → control comp → sidechain duck → mono. Saturation *before* the compressor here (unlike the recorded chains) because on an 808 the saturator is *generating* the tone — you want the comp to level the harmonics it creates.

## 1 — Sound Selection

**Selection is the real recording step — a great 808 sample needs almost nothing.**

- 🎬 **Juno-emulation synth bass written by following the chord roots + extra bounce notes, written EARLY in the build "so I can make sure it's right," then Decapitator for crunch.** Building an 80s synthwave/pop beat, the bassline doubles the chord progression's own root notes with extra notes layered in purely "to give it a bounce and rhythm," then Decapitator runs afterward just for crunch (no exact Style/Drive given). A third confirmed sighting of loner's root-following-plus-embellishment bass-writing pattern on this vault (see the Bryson Tiller reuse logged below); the explicit "write bass early" ordering and the added Decapitator crunch stage are the new information here. → Decapitator, Bass Design, Synthwave — loner, [how to make an 80's synthwave/pop beat for the weeknd.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dWhh27UFWhY)
- 🎬 **CS80 one-shot bass from a personal one-shot kit ("Nami's kit," a repeat go-to bass source), pitched up, then given a ShaperBox volume preset so it pulses instead of sitting flat.** Building a beat around a found a cappella: the bass one-shot's pitch is brought up (and the underlying chord's root note dropped, since it tracked too high otherwise), then a **ShaperBox volume preset ("set to a half")** is added so the bass "pulses a bit more" rather than being constantly present — the closing chord's timing gets nudged slightly afterward because the pulse read as too jolty/in-your-face. Owned-lane mapping for the volume-pulse stage: Shaper. → Shaper, Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist — loner, [we made a crazy r&b trapsoul song!? (making a beat from scratch around an acapella)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=39aHjEJ5-FU)
- 🎬 **Kontakt Scarbee Rickenbacker bassline written by following the chord roots + added licks, sample pitch-shifted down as a whole after tracking too high.** On an afrobeats build, the bass part is the chord progression's own root notes played back, with extra melodic licks layered on top; register came in too high on playback, so the whole recorded take is pitch-shifted down rather than re-tracked lower — paired with an AmpliTube amp preset layered on top for color. → Kontakt 7, Bassline Writing, Sound Selection Guide — loner, [making a soulful afrobeats beat for rema & wizkid from scratch (use voice notes to start ideas!?)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e-KvnLXHAy4)
- 🎬 **A two-part bass system: a plucked synth patch filling only the GAPS between chords (never doubling the main line), plus a finger-picked "Moto Bass" (near-certain auto-caption garble of IK Multimedia MODO Bass, unowned — see Plugin Wishlist) carrying the actual bassline.** A dedicated ending flourish — a run pitched down six semitones — gets its own light Decapitator drive + EQ pass afterward specifically to make it "stand out a little more" than the rest of the part. → Bass Design, Decapitator, EQ, Sound Selection Guide — loner, [making a billboard number 1 pop beat for post malone's next album from scratch!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WX_IB6K-xIo)

- **Ramzoid 808 Cooker** — purpose-built trap 808 design: base tone, drive/character in-instrument, done. → Ramzoid 808 Cooker — Trap 808
- **808 samples from packs** (SpinZ/Zay-type industry sounds) — pick ones with **real front-end attack**: enough attack and the kick becomes optional ("a lot of the best shit right now is no kick" — Kenny Beats, [808 & Kick](https://youtu.be/4iAKvWWlCvY))
- **Serum 2** — reese/growl/design bass (EDM lane): sine sub osc + saw/wavetable above, sub osc unprocessed. → Serum 2 — Reese Growl Bass
- **Operator** — clean FM sub (sine + slight 2nd harmonic); a plain sine patch ("Huge Sine Base") is the reliable fallback under a characterful bass — Disclosure. → Operator — Clean FM Sub
- **Drift / Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer** — analog-style synth bass (indie/synthwave). → Drift — Analog Synth Bass / Model 84 — Juno Bass
- **Bloom Bass Impulse** — production-ready basses when speed wins.
