**The verse is the same sample, reversed and dropped an octave.** Stage 8 above is the whole arrangement method — no second sample is written. Reverse and re-chop the mallet part to its original rhythmic pattern, pitch the entire thing down twelve semitones, and that *is* the verse section.

| Section | Source |
|---|---|
| Hook | the sample as built — five melodic layers + vocal chop |
| Verse | the same sample, reversed + octave down |
| Late variation | the last two vocal-chop slices reversed |

**The move — transform, don't write.** One recorded idea covers every section. Cheapest possible arrangement, and it guarantees the sections belong to each other.

**Density: 5–6 layers, constant.** Sections differ by pitch and direction, not by count — a **timbre** genre in the Genres Index sense.

## Variations

- **The reverse-and-pitch-down-an-octave verse trick generalizes to any melodic sample flip** — a cheap way to signal a section change using only the material already built, no new instrumentation required. Directly comparable to the half-time/kick-out toggles used for the same purpose on [Southside Dark Synth Trap Chain](#/chain/southside-dark-synth-trap-chain) and [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) — a third distinct "signal the section via processing, not new parts" mechanism on this vault.
- **Skip-the-kick-when-the-808-already-hits is a reusable rule, not specific to this beat** — any build where the bass/808 has a strong front-end attack is a candidate to drop the kick entirely rather than fight for space.
- **Extracting a bassline from a finished bounce (instead of writing a fresh 808) is worth trying whenever a sample's own low end already reads right** — see Sampling and Sound Selection for the owned-lane equivalent (Melodyne-based note extraction).

## Notes

- No exact EQ frequencies, reverb decay/mix percentages, or delay time/feedback values were given on screen beyond the qualitative descriptions above — treat every device's setting as a starting point to dial in by ear.
- Two low-confidence items from auto-caption garble: the stab-bass preset name ("knits her base"/"knitter bass") and the declick/degrade tool name used after heavy chopping ("generic bleeding") — neither could be confidently identified, so no owned-tool guess was made; see Plugin Wishlist for the stab-bass gap.
- Analog Lab (shaker+bowl preset) is the only unowned source in this build — see Plugin Wishlist for its now-eighth confirmed sighting on this vault. Every processing stage (EQ, reverb, delay, tremolo/modulation, pitch/formant) is fully owned-tool coverable.

**Sources:** loner — [how jetsonmade makes bouncy/melodic beats for playboi carti & lil keed (from scratch)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQZbvASWIQE) (00:09:18, 2020-10-29) · full note: loner - how jetsonmade makes bouncy-melodic beats for playboi carti & lil keed (from scratch)

chains.title: Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain
chains.routing: Piano + mallet one-shot + 2 synth layers + 3-layer vocal stack → [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] / [[2 Main Vocal Group|Main Vocal Group]] → [[3 Inst-Synth Bus|Inst-Synth Bus]] / [[3 Vocal Bus|Vocal Bus]] → Master
chains.reference: Kendrick Lamar / Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers-era piano samples — a from-scratch vintage sample-flip build
plugins: King's Microphones, Waves EQ x2, mallet one-shot (stretch mode), Analog Lab synth layer 1 (ValhallaDelay + Decapitator), Analog Lab synth layer 2 (EQ + reverb + delay + shaper), 3x vocal takes (Auto-Tune + compressor + Little AlterBoy + EQ, each with one distinguishing extra stage), final slicer chop (pitch + attack + micro-timing)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch "vintage soul sample" built to sound like a genuine Kendrick Lamar-style piano-led flip (inspired by the piano-forward tracks on the *Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers* era) rather than a chopped real record. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, [how to make the most realistic vintage soul samples for kendrick lamar!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oMbeATqXOww). Unlike [Beatles Psych-Rock Sample Chain](#/chain/beatles-psych-rock-sample-chain) (real-gear research into owned/replica hardware), this build leans on VST sources with no owned equivalents — see Plugin Wishlist for every unresolved plugin.

## Chain overview

Five elements stack into one sample: a piano chord bed, a mallet counter-layer, two synth texture layers, and a 3-take vocal harmony stack — finished by bouncing the piano+vocal portion into a slicer for a chop/pitch/micro-timing pass. The build's two biggest reusable ideas: **spread/low-velocity chord voicing on the piano** (theory-level "vintage" before any processing touches it) and **a 3-take vocal stack sharing one base chain, each take earning exactly one distinguishing extra stage** (not three fully separate chains, not a plain doubled take).

## 1. Piano — Cinesamples Blue

- **Instrument:** Cinesamples Blue (Contact bank) — "probably my favorite piano vst." No owned equivalent, see Plugin Wishlist.
- **Chords:** VI–III–v–VII in B natural minor — **Gmaj9 → Dmaj9 → F♯m → Amaj7** (spoken on-screen as "6-3-5-7"). Full theory writeup: Chord Progressions.
- **Voicing:** root low, then the rest of each chord (including the 7th/9th) spread up a full octave — "helps to create such a different vibe... much more emotion out of your chords." The second chord (Dmaj9) repeats the exact same major-9 shape but is re-voiced slightly differently (F♯ brought up) purely for variety between two structurally identical chords. → Chord Inversions
- **Velocity:** dropped to near-zero on every note, deliberately — "the texture sounds better doing this... when the velocity is super high the notes can be a bit too harsh."
- 🎬 *From video:* try a whole chord part at very low velocity before reaching for EQ/compression on a harsh-sounding source — a general lesson worth applying beyond this chain.

## 2. Piano FX chain — "go-to piano chain" (4th confirmed instance)

- **Waves King's Microphones** — vintage mic emulation. No owned equivalent; closest is UAD Century Tube Channel Strip / UAD Neve 1073 ahead of an EQ roll-off. → Plugin Wishlist
- **Waves EQ #1** — a "snare" preset auditioned by ear (not chosen by name), brings out a lot of high end for vintage character.
- **Waves EQ #2** — cuts some low end, boosts a little high end. Owned-lane stand-in for both EQ stages: EQ Eight.
- Same three-stage shape as an earlier loner video's "go-to piano chain" (see Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist) — now confirmed a 4th time.

## 3. Mallet layer

- **Source:** a one-shot from the (then-unreleased) "Layers Volume 2" pack, set to **stretch mode** — plays back at a fixed length regardless of octave/pitch. Owned-lane equivalent: Ableton Simpler in Complex/Complex Pro Warp mode.
- **Part:** copies the piano's chords, hitting rhythmically in between the piano's own notes.
- 🎬 *From video:* pitching a length-locked one-shot into a higher octave (rather than a normally-pitched sample) is what produces the "really cool textures" — the stretch-mode step matters, not just the pitch shift. → Sampling and Sound Selection

## 4. Synth layer 1 — delay + drive

- **Source:** "chiclets" preset, Arturia Analog Lab's Impulse bank (per prior-video name resolution, see Plugin Wishlist). One chord copied, hit on the second bar.
- **ValhallaDelay** — set super long/dragged-out, to rescue a too-quiet/too-thin layer before any drive stage.
- **Decapitator** — Drive up, Mix pulled back from full-wet, a modest Low Cut. Credited to a producer named Louis, "puts it on a bunch of his synths."

## 5. Synth layer 2 — texture + shaper

- **Source:** a second Impulse-bank preset ("the Machinist"/"Dying," exact name unconfirmed in auto-captions). A simple counter-melody, one note.
- **EQ** — cut low, boost high.
- **Reverb** — very short but heavy (strong wet, fast decay).
- **Delay** — FL Studio's stock "fruity delay," owned-lane Echo/Delay.
- **Shaper box** — owned-lane Shaper/Transient Shaper; a dedicated multiband shaper remains a wishlist gap, see Plugin Wishlist.

## 6. Vocals — 3-layer harmony stack

The real centerpiece of the build. **Three genuinely different vocal takes** (distinct melody + harmony each, not one take doubled three times), placed **center / hard right / hard left**.

**Shared base chain (all three takes):**
1. Auto-Tune (Auto-Tune Pro)
2. A Waves compressor (unnamed product) — "really brings the vocal out, makes it stand out really well." Owned-lane stand-in: Glue Compressor / API-2500.
3. Little AlterBoy — neutral/"very standard" setting.
4. EQ — cut low end, a little high boost (lighter cut than the producer's usual).

🎬 *From video:* processed deliberately to read as a **real song's vocal**, not the usual filtered/distant sample-vocal treatment — "this time I wanted to make it sound like a real song, and obviously that means the vocal is going to be much more present." → Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Vocal Tuning

**Per-take distinguishing stage (each take gets exactly ONE extra):**
- **Take 1 (center):** Little AlterBoy switched to its "vocal dub" preset.
- **Take 2 (hard right):** Little AlterBoy switched to its "vocal chorus" preset instead.
- **Take 3 (hard left):** base chain kept, **ValhallaVintageVerb** added on top — "just to slightly switch it up, give it a different sound."

## 7. Finishing chop pass (piano + vocal only)

1. Bounce the piano+vocal portion.
2. Load into a slicer (Fruity Slicer — owned-lane Simpler in Slice Playback Mode).
3. Pitch down a few semitones.
4. Raise the attack.
5. **Micro-timing pass:** zoom all the way in, nudge every individual note's start time back very slightly — "you almost can't hear it but it just adds a little bit of bounce, a little bit of variety." Concrete real-world example for Pocket and Microtiming's "laying back" concept.

## 8. Arrangement — two-half contrast

- **First 8 bars:** the chopped/pitched sample from stage 7, synth layers (stages 4–5) dropped out entirely — vocals + piano are the sole focal point.
- **Second half:** the same sample playing naturally/unchopped, WITH the synth layers reintroduced.
- 🎬 *From video:* "each half of the sample sounds completely different, it feels different" — a structural contrast built entirely from processing/arrangement choices on the SAME source material, not new content. → Arrangement and Song Form

## Variations

- **Any minor-key soul/neo-soul piano bed** — the reusable core isn't the specific Gmaj9/Dmaj9/F♯m/Amaj7 chords, it's the VI–III–v–VII root motion (see Chord Progressions) plus the spread-voicing/low-velocity approach.
- **The vocal-stack shape generalizes past this exact chain** — one base chain, three takes, one distinguishing stage per take — reusable on any hook/vocal-heavy sample even without the specific plugins named here.

## Notes

- No exact settings (drive amount, EQ frequencies/gains, reverb decay, delay time/feedback, semitone/ms values on the final chop) were given on screen beyond the qualitative descriptions above — treat every device's setting as a starting point to dial in by ear.
- All-unowned instrument sources (Cinesamples Blue, Arturia Analog Lab's Impulse bank, Waves King's Microphones) — see Plugin Wishlist for the current gaps; the processing stages after them (EQ, delay, reverb, saturation, vocal tuning/pitch-formant) are fully owned-tool coverable.

**Sources:** loner — [how to make the most realistic vintage soul samples for kendrick lamar!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oMbeATqXOww) (00:08:20, 2022-05-26) · full note: loner - how to make the most realistic vintage soul samples for kendrick lamar!?

chains.title: PARTYNEXTDOOR Jazz Sample Chain
chains.routing: Piano + electric guitar + bass + brass + minimal drums → [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] / [[2 Guitar Group|Guitar Group]] / [[2 Bass Group|Bass Group]] / [[2 Drums Group|Drums Group]] → bounce/pitch/flip stage → Master
chains.reference: PARTYNEXTDOOR's "Joy" (P3) — a from-scratch vintage jazzy R&B sample-flip build
plugins: Teletone Audio "Postcard Piano" (Reels tape + Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 + EQ)
Kontakt "Evolution Strawberry Bank" guitar (valve comp + Cassette crunch + delay + EQ
Splice brass loops (bandpass EQ + heavy reverb + delay)

minimal drums (bandpass-EQ'd kick+snare, low hats, reverbed/delayed ride, open hat, ~50% swing), full bounce pitched down 1 semitone + EQ + comp, Melodyne flip-and-pitch-up-2-3-semitones + new bass part
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch vintage jazzy R&B instrumental built to chase the mood of PARTYNEXTDOOR's "Joy" (off *P3*) — real jazz harmony (minor 9ths, minor 7ths, an inverted major 9th), an unusual 6/8 time signature identified by ear from the drums, and an arrangement built entirely by subtracting elements rather than adding new ones. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, [how to make moody vintage r&b samples for partynextdoor (sounds like a real jazz sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wD4RzEKo7vU). Companion build to [Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain](#/chain/kendrick-lamar-soul-sample-chain) and [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) — same vintage-sample-flip lineage, jazz-forward voicings instead of soul/trap.

## Chain overview

Five elements (piano, guitar, bass, brass, drums) build a single instrumental sample, then the whole thing gets bounced, pitched, and flipped as a second-pass demo. The two biggest reusable ideas: **identify an odd time signature (6/8) by ear from the drums, not the melody**, and **arrange by subtraction across four 8-bar sections** rather than writing new material per section — bass and guitar are toggled off/on and brass drops out for the final section, explicitly reasoned to leave room for whoever eventually flips the sample.

## 0. Time signature — set before writing anything

- **Identify 6/8 by ear from the drums:** "Joy" counts in groups of three (one-two-three, one-two-three) rather than four — the tell for 6/8 over 4/4.
- Owned-lane equivalent of the FL Studio numerator/denominator field: Ableton's time signature, set alongside tempo at the top of Arrangement/Session View (or per-clip in Session View).
- 🎬 *From video:* the same chords in 6/8 vs. 4/4 read as a genuinely different bounce against a metronome click — 6/8 changes the feel, not just the count.

## 1. Piano — Teletone Audio "Postcard Piano"

- **Instrument:** Teletone Audio "Postcard Piano" — chosen for vintage character/imperfection over a clean modern piano. No owned equivalent tracked; second confirmed use of this library. → Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist
- **Voicing:** roll the chord's bass note slightly ahead of the rest of the notes (not block-triggered) for a natural, bouncy feel. → Pocket and Microtiming
- **Progression:** Bm9 (×2, filler notes added) → C♯m7 (×2, top-line notes added) → bars 5–7 repeat bars 1–2 → C♯m7 again → resolves on **Amaj9**, voiced **A as bass note, B (the 9th) inverted up to the top** rather than left in a plain root-position stack. → Chord Progressions, Chord Inversions
- **FX chain:** "Reels"-style tape emulation (Baked preset, hiss/motor down) → **Ghz Vulf Compressor 3** (owned) to tighten → EQ cutting low end. → Kramer Tape, EQ Eight

## 2. Electric guitar — filling the gaps

- **Instrument:** Kontakt "Evolution Strawberry Bank" — fills empty space before/between piano chord hits. → Kontakt 7, Sound Selection Guide
- **FX chain:** valve compressor (UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII) → Cassette-style crunch → delay → EQ cutting low end and harsh mid-range.
- 🎬 *From video:* the LAST bar of the guitar part is time-stretched slightly, then reversed, for a unique cadence into the next section — a cheap way to punctuate a section boundary without new material.

## 3. Bass — Scarbee Rickenbacker

- **Instrument:** Kontakt "Scarbee Rickenbacker" — kept deliberately simple/clean, the odd one out against the busier piano/guitar/brass build. → Kontakt 7, Sound Selection Guide
- **FX chain:** a tube pre-amp preset only (UAD Century Tube Channel Strip) — no other processing.

## 4. Brass — sourced, not synthesized

- **Source:** Splice loops, not a programmed brass VST — realistic brass is hard to fake convincingly.
- **Treatment:** layered chops, reversed and left dry (no FX on the reversed pass itself), then all on ONE mixer channel: bandpass EQ (cut low + high) → heavy reverb (mix pushed near 100%) → delay for extra space. → EQ, Reverb (effect), Delay (effect)

## 5. Drums — minimal, deliberately simple

- **Kick + snare on one mixer channel**, kick hitting only the downbeat of every bar, both through a bandpass EQ (cut low + high).
- **Hi-hat** turned way down — present but barely audible.
- **Ride** hits only on the "one," pushed through heavy reverb to extend the hit, plus delay to fill space.
- **Open hat** as the final drum element.
- **Swing knob to ~50%** — a standing habit for "unique" drum feels (afrobeats, jazzy 6/8 material). → Rhythm and Groove

## 6. Arrangement — subtraction across 4×8-bar sections

- **Bars 1–8:** everything in (bass, guitar, piano, brass).
- **Bars 9–16:** bass OUT — reasoned explicitly to leave room for whoever flips the sample to add their own bass.
- **Bars 17–24:** guitar OUT, bass back IN, for a more spaced-out section.
- **Bars 25–32:** bass OUT again AND brass OUT, for the sparsest final section.
- Pure subtraction — no new material per section, only elements toggled off. → Arrangement and Song Form

## 7. Bounce & finishing

1. Bounce the entire sample to one audio file.
2. Pitch the whole thing down 1 semitone.
3. EQ: cut real low end + a few mid-range frequencies.
4. Compressor: tighten and shave peaks.

## 8. Flip demo — a second-pass example

1. Open a new project, load the bounce, **Melodyne it** to find its actual bass notes (found: B♭, C, B♭, C, A♭). → Plugin Wishlist (Melodyne — #1 tracked gap, reinforced by this instrumental use-case)
2. Extracted notes read too low → pitch the ENTIRE sample up 2–3 semitones before writing a new bass part.
3. New bass part includes a couple of "glidy" (portamento) notes rather than plain static hits.

## Variations

- **The subtraction-arrangement move generalizes past this exact instrumentation** — any multi-element sample build can use the same "toggle elements off across fixed-length sections, reason each removal around what a flipper needs" approach, independent of the jazz/R&B genre lane.
- **The 6/8-by-ear-from-drums identification method** is reusable on any reference track suspected of an odd meter, not just this one.

## Notes

- No exact EQ frequencies/gains, reverb decay, or delay time/feedback values were given on screen beyond the qualitative descriptions above — treat every device's setting as a starting point to dial in by ear.
- All-unowned instrument sources (Teletone Postcard Piano) — see Plugin Wishlist; Kontakt-based sources (Evolution Strawberry Bank, Scarbee Rickenbacker) are owned via Kontakt 7.

**Sources:** loner — [how to make moody vintage r&b samples for partynextdoor (sounds like a real jazz sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wD4RzEKo7vU) (00:10:16, 2026-08-11) · full note: loner - how to make moody vintage r&b samples for partynextdoor (sounds like a real jazz sample)

chains.title: Smooth R&B 6-8 Chain
chains.routing: Kontakt guitar (amp-sim chain) + simple root bass + piano bed + Kontakt Session Horns + strings → [[2 Guitar Group|Guitar Group]] / [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] → [[3 Guitar Bus|Guitar Bus]] / [[3 Inst-Synth Bus|Inst-Synth Bus]] → Master
chains.reference: loner's from-scratch "smooth/sexy R&B in 6/8" build — a genre/feel target (Kehlani/Ty Dolla $ign-adjacent vibe), not a specific record
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch "smooth/sexy R&B in 6/8" beat build, reverse-engineered from loner's own breakdown, [making a smooth/sexy rnb beat in 6/8 time signature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mMZaktspUAA). Not a specific record recreation — the target is a genre/feel (name-checked as "Kehlani/Ty Dolla $ign"-adjacent) built around a single structural lever: the whole project runs in **6/8** instead of 4/4, which reshapes the chords, the drum programming, and the guitar's processing depth. The guitar chain here (9 stages) is the deepest single processing chain logged from this channel to date — most of the "reusable" value in this chain lives in that ordered device list.

## Chain overview

Kontakt guitar (4-chord harmonic-minor progression) carries the harmonic/melodic weight through a 9-stage FX chain. A simple root-following bass gets one widening move. Piano thickens the bed. Kontakt Session Horns and Spitfire Studio Strings (demo) are reserved for the hook only — the verse runs on guitar + bass alone to leave room for a vocalist. Drums are the other half of the "6/8-ness": same physical snare placement as a 4/4 beat, reinterpreted entirely by counting in 3s instead of 4s.

## 1. Foundation — project time signature

- **Options → Project → General Settings → Signature → 6/8** (3/4 named as the alternative). Set BEFORE writing any parts — every subsequent chord/drum decision is built around counting in 3s. → Rhythm and Groove

## 2. Guitar — Kontakt chord source + the 9-stage FX chain

- **Instrument:** Kontakt 7, unnamed guitar patch. 4-chord progression in harmonic minor (chords 1–2 same, 3–4 switch up). Played dry first to hear the raw tone.
- **FX chain, in order:**
  1. **Bias FX (Positive Grid) amp sim** — tone source. Unowned, see Plugin Wishlist.
  2. **Reverb** (early-chain, smaller) → Reverb
  3. **Chorus #1** + an EQ move boosting some frequencies
  4. **EQ Eight** — cut lows, boost some highs, cut mids *(qualitative only — no exact Hz/dB stated)*
  5. **TAL-Chorus-LX** — "the Juno chorus," a SECOND separate chorus stage, named as a repeat go-to across multiple loner videos → Modulation
  6. **Compressor** — "rhythm guitar" preset, input knob dialed to shave peaks, tightening only → Compression
  7. **Kramer Tape** — "Reels" preset, run alongside another chorus pass, for width + vintage depth, **hiss/noise turned UP** (contrast vs. other loner builds where Reels' hiss is usually pulled back) → Saturation and Distortion
  8. **Kickstart 2** — pulled back (mix low), just enough to make the part "flow in and out," not an obvious pump
  9. **Reverb** (final, heavy) — closes the chain, distinct from stage 2's smaller reverb

## 3. Bass — simple root line + one widening move

- **Root notes only, copied directly from the guitar's chord roots** — no independent bassline, no extra notes. → Bassline Writing
- **Ghz Midside 3 — boost the Side channel** to widen the bass and fill the stereo frequency picture. *(general starting point — no exact dB given)* → Width and Stereo

## 4. Piano — depth layer

- A piano part layered underneath the guitar/bass foundation purely for depth, with added top-line notes for a small extra melodic hook in the background.

## 5. Brass — Kontakt Session Horns (hook only)

- **Kontakt Session Horns**, a short pattern, velocities pulled DOWN specifically because higher velocity read as "more harsh" and didn't complement the beat's soft character. → Kontakt 7, Sound Selection Guide

## 6. Drums — the 6/8 groove itself

- **Snare:** same physical grid position as a straight 4/4 beat — the "6/8-ness" comes from counting in 3s around it ("one-two-three, one-two-three"), not from repositioning the hit. Reverbed percussion layered underneath. → Rhythm and Groove, Genre Drum Patterns
- **Hi-hat 1:** pitch down, shifted off-grid more aggressively than a 4/4 pattern would tolerate — licensed by the slower 6/8 tempo/lower hit density. → Pocket and Microtiming
- **Hi-hat 2:** intermittent, hits "every now and then," with a roll at the end for variety.
- **Kick:** minimal/spaced through most of the pattern, landing on the downbeat each pass, breaking into a 3-hit flourish only at the very end of the phrase. → Kick Design

## 7. Strings — Spitfire Studio Strings (hook only)

- Demo version (~15-min session limit) — enough to lay one pattern and bounce to audio. Violins chosen from several available articulations. No owned equivalent tracked — see Plugin Wishlist.

## 8. Arrangement — the hook/verse split

- **Strings + horns reserved for the hook only.** The verse/main groove runs on guitar + bass alone, deliberately, to leave the singer room to work. → Arrangement and Song Form

## Variations

- The 9-stage guitar chain (amp → reverb → chorus → EQ → chorus → comp → tape → sidechain-pump → reverb) generalizes to any "vintage, wide, sexy" guitar/keys part — the width specifically comes from stacking THREE separate devices (2 choruses + tape), not one wide-sounding plugin.
- The snare-stays-put / recount-in-3s trick is the cheapest way to test whether an existing 4/4 idea has a usable 6/8 or 3/4 alternate feel before rebuilding a pattern from scratch.

## Source

- loner, [making a smooth/sexy rnb beat in 6/8 time signature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mMZaktspUAA) — full breakdown: YouTube note

chains.title: Soulful Sample Stacking Chain
chains.routing: Electric piano + bass + 2 synth textures + accent synth + piano bed → [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] / [[2 Bass Group|Bass Group]] → sample-stack pass (perc loop, strings, guitar, brass, all Splice) → bounce/consolidate → [[3 Inst-Synth Bus|Inst-Synth Bus]] → Master
chains.reference: loner-style Rhodes-led soulful sample, built as a 6-element bed then finished with outside-sample stacking
plugins: AAS Lounge Lizard EP + spring reverb + Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 + EQ + ValhallaDelay
Kontakt Scarbee Rickenbacker bass + Guitar Rig crunch + small mono spring reverb + 50 Hz low cut
Arturia Juno "Girl in Africa" preset texture
Arturia Jupiter-8 "Give Me a Sign" (Layers Analog Lab bank) + heavy reverb + Cassette Crushed
Kontakt "Gentleman" piano + Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 + EQ + spring reverb (near-mono)
Splice string loop (chop/reverse/key-match/stretch) + Cassette Lo-Fi Drums + heavy reverb + delay + mono
Splice brass sample (reversed) + half-time + 100% wet vintage reverb + hard pan
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a Rhodes-led "soulful sample" built in two clean stages — first a six-element instrumental bed (electric piano, bass, two synth textures, an accent synth, a second piano), each processed with its own small effects chain that leans on **spring reverb** as the vintage-color constant across every layer; then a **"sample stacking"** finishing pass that reaches for outside Splice samples (a perc loop, strings, a "wire guitar," brass) layered on top of the finished bed for accents/melodies/textures the bed itself can't easily produce. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, [use this easy technique to take your samples to the next level!? (making a soulful sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vN0fgGDxp6E). The reusable idea distinguishing this chain from [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) and [Afro Sample Chain](#/chain/afro-sample-chain): **sample stacking as a named, deliberate workflow** — don't force every element from a VST when a real recorded performance (violin, guitar, brass) is one Splice search away; source it, then shape it around what you've already written rather than composing and processing it yourself.

## Chain overview

Ten elements total: six written/programmed (electric piano, bass, two synth textures, an accent synth, a second piano), then four sample-stacked on top (a perc loop, a strings sample, a guitar sample, a brass sample). The bed elements share a consistent processing language — spring reverb + a compressor + EQ + delay, at varying intensities per element's role (sustained chord bed vs. single-note accent) — while the stacked samples share a consistent SOURCING language (Splice search → chop → reverse where useful → confirm key → time-stretch → shape with reverb/EQ/delay to sit in the mix, usually pushed toward mono for its own pocket).

## 1. Electric piano — AAS Lounge Lizard

- **Instrument:** AAS Lounge Lizard, chosen directly after watching a "K1" breakdown video that used a real Rhodes — see Plugin Wishlist (repeat-use unowned electric-piano VST on this vault).
- **Processing:** spring reverb (short, pushed toward mono) → Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 (tight compression, loud/close-together) → EQ (cut lows, boost some highs) → ValhallaDelay (short mix, feedback pushed high, Wow/Flutter left on for detune character, delay time kept short enough that it reads "almost like a chorus effect" rather than a distinct echo).
- 🎬 *From video:* a short, high-feedback, unsynced-ms delay is a deliberate chorus substitute — the same short/high-feedback pattern also documented on ValhallaDelay from a different loner build (dark synth trap counter melody). Worth reaching for whenever a part wants chorus-like thickening without an actual chorus device.

## 2. Bass — Kontakt Scarbee Rickenbacker

- **Instrument:** Scarbee Rickenbacker in Kontakt 7 — "I use this all the time," the most repeat-used instrument on this vault's sample-flip breakdowns (see Sound Selection Guide).
- **Processing:** Guitar Rig 7 FX (crunch, to help the bass stand out in the mix — unowned, demo-only) → a very small spring reverb (all-the-way short, all-the-way mono, mix brought well down so it doesn't muddy the low end) → low cut around 50 Hz to remove "stubby" sub-adjacent frequencies.
- 🎬 *From video:* "you don't want to muddy out your low end with too much reverb, but it just adds a nice little bit of texture" — the mono + short + low-mix combination is the whole trick for putting any texture on a bass without smearing the low end. → BASS Slot, Bass Design

## 3. Synth texture — Juno, "Girl in Africa" preset

- **Instrument:** owned-lane Roland Juno-106 territory (Softube Model 84 / TAL-U-NO-LX), preset "Girl in Africa" (name as given in the video — no owned VST ships this exact preset; treat as a starting-point character).
- **Processing:** filter cutoff/frequency brought down a little for less high end, then a simple original melody played on top.
- 🎬 *From video:* a synth added purely as "a little textural part," not a lead — kept deliberately understated relative to the piano/bass foundation. → TEXTURE Slot

## 4. Accent texture — Portal, "Backfire" preset

- **Device:** Portal — "Backfire" preset, plus a half-time device to pitch/tempo it lower.
- 🎬 *From video:* a brand-new purchase used on the very first project after buying it — reached for immediately rather than deep-dived, consistent with Portal's other logged "browse presets, print what sounds good" workflow (see Portal's Techniques section).

## 5. Accent synth — Jupiter-8, "Give Me a Sign" (Layers Analog Lab bank)

- **Instrument:** owned-lane Roland Jupiter-8 territory (Arturia Jup-8 V in the source, via Analog Lab, "Layers" third-party preset bank) — "Give Me a Sign" preset, used for exactly ONE note across the whole track.
- **Processing:** a really heavy reverb (mix at 81, very heavy decay) → Cassette "Crushed" preset, deliberately pushed hardest of any element in the build "to make it really stand out within the mix."
- 🎬 *From video:* the single most heavily processed layer in the whole bed is also the one doing the LEAST — a one-note accent, not a sustained part. Save your most extreme processing for the smallest, most attention-grabbing element rather than spreading heavy treatment evenly across every layer.

## 6. Second piano — Kontakt "The Gentleman"

- **Instrument:** "The Gentleman" patch in Kontakt 7 — a second confirmed use of this exact patch on this vault (see Kontakt 7's Techniques section for its other, differently-processed use on a 2000s R&B sample).
- **Processing:** Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 again, dialed less harsh than on the Rhodes ("didn't want it too crazy") → EQ (cut lows around 200 Hz) → spring reverb again, mix pushed higher than the other layers, decay length brought up a little. Mixer track pushed closer to mono than the rest of the bed for its own pocket.
- 🎬 *From video:* the same compressor plugin dialed to two different intensities across two layers in one build (Rhodes = tight/aggressive, this piano = gentler) — treat plugin choice and plugin SETTING as two separate decisions, not "pick the tool once and reuse the preset." → Width and Stereo

## 7. Sample stack 1 — perc loop

- An unnamed perc loop placed underneath the finished bed purely "to give it a little bit more." → Sampling and Sound Selection

## 8. Sample stack 2 — Splice strings

- **Source:** a Splice string loop — reached for instead of composing/processing a realistic string melody from a VST, "obviously it's really hard to replicate realistic sounding violins and strings."
- **Prep:** chop the wanted part → reverse it → confirm it's in-key → time-stretch to tempo.
- **Processing:** Cassette "Lo-Fi Drums" preset (a filtering/character role on a melodic layer, not on drums — cross-role reuse) → heavy reverb (to drown it out) → a medium-sized delay (FL Studio "Fruity Delay" in the source; owned-lane: Delay) → pushed to mono for its own pocket.

## 9. Sample stack 3 — "wire guitar" (loner's favorite element of the video)

- **Source:** a Splice sample searched by the term "wire guitar," auditioned until a fitting melody was found, then dropped in.
- **Prep:** pitched and time-stretched to key/tempo, a specific section chosen by ear.
- **Processing:** reverb (to drown it out a bit) → EQ (cut some lows + specific mid-range frequencies described as "kind of a bit annoying").

## 10. Sample stack 4 — brass

- **Source:** a Splice brass sample, added because the build "just needed one more thing."
- **Prep:** reversed, pitch kept intact (a different texture than a straight reverse-and-repitch).
- **Processing:** half-time device → vintage reverb at 100% wet mix ("really drowned out") → panned hard to one side.

## Arrangement

**Two stages, and the second one is the arrangement.** Six written/programmed bed elements first (EP, bass, two synth textures, accent synth, second piano), *then* four sampled layers stacked on top (perc loop, strings, guitar, brass).

| Stage | Elements | Slots |
|---|---|---|
| The bed | 6, written | BASS · BED · MIDS |
| The stack | 4, sampled | MIDS · AIR · TEXTURE |

**The move — write the bed, sample the top.** The written layers share one processing language (spring reverb + compressor) so they read as one instrument; the sampled layers arrive already sounding like a record. That split is what makes ten elements cohere instead of pile up.

**Density: 10 — the densest build in this folder.** It works because the bed is uniform. If the six written elements had six different reverbs, this would be mud.

## Variations

- **The core reusable idea — sample stacking — generalizes past this exact build.** loner explicitly frames it as direction-agnostic: start from your own written material and layer outside samples on top (this build), OR start from an outside sample (e.g. a simple guitar chord progression) and write your own material on top of THAT instead. Either direction is "sample stacking."
- **Spring reverb as a single-tool vintage-color signature** — used on all six bed elements in this build, at varying mix/decay per role. A simpler, more consistent version of the "one reverb type, tuned per layer" idea also seen on [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) ("use room presets... especially with real-instrument samples").
- **Match processing intensity to the element's job, not a house style** — the loudest/most-processed layer here (Jupiter-8 accent) is also the smallest (one note); the most-understated layer (Juno texture) does the least standalone work. Process for the role, not out of habit.

## Notes

- No exact reverb decay times, compression ratios/attack-release, or EQ Hz figures were given for most stages beyond the qualitative descriptions above (spring reverb settings, Vulf Compressor amounts) — treat every device setting as a starting point to dial in by ear. Confirmed exact figures: bass low cut ~50 Hz, second-piano EQ cut ~200 Hz, Jupiter-8 reverb mix 81%, brass reverb mix 100%.
- Unowned/best-match sources: AAS Lounge Lizard (electric piano — see Plugin Wishlist), Guitar Rig 7 FX (demo-only on this machine), Arturia Juno emulation + Analog Lab "Layers" bank (Jupiter-8 preset pack) — see Plugin Wishlist. Everything else (Kontakt instruments, ValhallaDelay, Cassette, Portal, EQ, general reverb/delay) is fully owned.

**Sources:** loner — [use this easy technique to take your samples to the next level!? (making a soulful sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vN0fgGDxp6E) (00:08:19, 2021-11-28) · full note: loner - use this easy technique to take your samples to the next level!? (making a soulful sample)

chains.title: Southside Dark Synth Trap Chain
chains.routing: Main pad + low-fill pad + counter melody + hook stab + drums → [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] / [[2 Drums Group|Drums Group]] → [[3 Inst-Synth Bus|Inst-Synth Bus]] → [[Master Chain|Master]]
chains.reference: Southside-style dark synth trap beat for Future/Roddy Ricch, built from scratch
plugins: Analog Lab "Providence/Selena" pad → reverb + half-time 1/8 delay + EQ + volume/filter/width Shaper stack
Analog Lab "Lost/Loophole" low-fill pad → release/filter tweak + band-pass EQ
Kontakt "Tape Synths" counter melody → ValhallaDelay + vintage reverb + Reels tape
copied-chord hook stab → reverb + delay + EQ
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch dark synth trap instrumental in the style of Southside's work for Future/Roddy Ricch. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, [how southside makes dark synth trap beats for future from scratch (dark melody music theory)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TVjyuF5-xUo). Unlike [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) (a 9-element vintage sample built, bounced, and chopped into a beat), this is a straight synth-pad trap instrumental — two layered synth pads carry the harmony, a Kontakt counter melody and a copied-chord stab round out the melodic content, and drums come from a personal one-shot kit rather than a sample flip. The centerpiece idea is the **dark chord voicing**: 2–3 note shapes built around an internal semitone clash, the same underlying trick already logged on Chord Progressions and [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain) — the near-identical D♯m/G♯m shape recurring across two different loner videos strongly suggests it's his go-to teaching example for this style, not a coincidence.

## Chain overview

Two Analog Lab pads (a dark unusual-texture main pad + a low-end-filling second pad) carry the 3-chord dark voicing; a Kontakt counter melody and a copied-chord hook stab add melodic interest without adding new harmonic material; drums are simple and built in a fixed order. Arrangement does most of the remaining work — no kick for 8 bars, a half-time toggle for energy contrast, and an octave-pitched-down bounce to signal the verse.

## 1. Main pad — Analog Lab "Providence" bank, "Selena" preset

- **Instrument:** Arturia Analog Lab, "Providence" bank, "Selena" preset — a dark, unusual texture, "sounds a bit mad" completely dry. → Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist
- **FX chain:** heavy-but-short reverb → half-time delay set to 1/8 (not a straight subdivision) → EQ (heavy low-end cut — the raw preset's low end was "just a textural element") → a **triple-role Shaper stack**: volume shaper (base pulse) → filter shaper (gradually brings the high end in) → width shaper (stereo → mono → stereo cycle). → Reverb, Delay (effect), EQ, Shaper, Width and Stereo
- 🎬 *From video:* "I love the texture of it and I knew that I could flip it into something more usable" — the raw, slightly-broken-sounding preset IS the source material; the FX chain is what makes it usable, not a cleaner starting patch.

## 2. Chord voicing — the dark theory

- **Chord 1:** D♯ minor triad, top note pulled from F♯ down to F — two chord tones (D♯, F) a semitone apart.
- **Chord 2:** the same shape reduced to just F/F♯ — the whole chord IS the semitone clash.
- Variation notes (an extra F, a G♯) layered in for melodic movement; the 2-chord shape repeats for 6 bars.
- **Chord 3 (bars 7–8):** G♯ minor (the **iv** chord), top note (D♯) dropped an octave to stay in register.
- → Chord Progressions (full worked example), Melody Writing

## 3. Low-fill pad — Analog Lab "Lost," Loophole bank

- **Instrument:** "Lost" preset, "Loophole" bank (Louis of Loophole) — added because the main pad's texture doesn't cover the low end. → Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist
- **Settings:** release raised from default (was too short), filter cutoff brought down slightly.
- **FX:** band-pass EQ, cutting some high and low end so the two pads occupy separate bands. → EQ, Masking and Carving

## 4. Counter melody — Kontakt "Tape Synths"

- **Instrument:** Kontakt, "Tape Synths" library (Fono Loop). → Kontakt 7, Sound Selection Guide, Plugin Wishlist
- **FX chain:** ValhallaDelay (heavy feedback, time set in ms not a synced subdivision, kept short — reads "almost like a chorus") → heavy vintage reverb → "Reels" tape, "Excited Tape" preset (harshness + wow/flutter up, for detune/vintage color) → half-time, automated in at certain points only.
- → Automation

## 5. Hook stab — copied chord

- Copy the first chord voicing (D♯m from stage 2), place on bar 1 and bar 5 only.
- **FX:** reverb → very heavy delay → EQ cutting the lows.
- 🎬 *From video:* used as the hook-arrival signal in place of a riser or crash cymbal. → Arrangement and Song Form

## 6. Drums — personal kit

- Own unreleased "2022 essentials" kit (not a sourceable pack).
- **Build order:** room → bounce snare → hi-hat (two-step base) → hi-hat rolls → second hi-hat layer for bounce → percs (plain, ambient, and a drum-fill perc with pulled-down velocity + panning) → hard/distorted 808 → hard kick.
- → Genre Drum Patterns, Rhythm and Groove

## 7. Arrangement

1. **Intro:** the two pads only.
2. **Hook:** kick OUT for the first 8 bars, then in; half-time counter-melody effect engaged for the hook's first half, switched OFF for the second half — both toggles land at the same moment for an energy jump.
3. **Verse:** bounce the main pad to audio, pitch the bounce down an octave — signals the section, not a tone change.
4. **Extend:** repeat the structure rather than writing new material.
- → Arrangement and Song Form, Pitch and Formant

## Variations

- **The 2–3 note semitone-clash voicing generalizes to any minor key** — same shape as [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain)'s D♯m/G♯m trick; treat it as loner's standard dark-trap chord recipe, not tied to this specific key.
- **The kick-out/half-time-toggle hook move is reusable arrangement grammar** independent of the synth-pad instrumentation here — any halftime trap beat can borrow "remove the kick, toggle one effect off" as a cheap energy-contrast tool.

## Notes

- No exact reverb decay/mix percentages, delay feedback amounts, or EQ frequencies were given on screen beyond the qualitative descriptions above — treat every device's setting as a starting point to dial in by ear.
- All-unowned instrument sources (Analog Lab "Providence" and "Loophole" banks, Fono Loop "Tape Synths," "Reels" tape plugin) — see Plugin Wishlist for current gaps; the processing stages (reverb, delay, EQ, Shaper) are fully owned-tool coverable.

**Sources:** loner — [how southside makes dark synth trap beats for future from scratch (dark melody music theory)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TVjyuF5-xUo) (00:08:43, 2022-01-09) · full note: loner - how southside makes dark synth trap beats for future from scratch (dark melody music theory)

chains.title: Tory Lanez Underwater Synth Chain
chains.routing: Reversed one-shot synth pad + texture layers + vocal chop + hook flute → [[2 Inst-Synth Group|Inst-Synth Group]] / [[2 Main Vocal Group|Main Vocal Group]] → [[3 Inst-Synth Bus|Inst-Synth Bus]] / [[3 Vocal Bus|Vocal Bus]] → Master
chains.reference: Tory Lanez ("Take Care")-style melodic R&B — a from-scratch build, name-checking Chris Brown/Drake in the same lane
plugins: late hook flute (massive reverb + big delay)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch "underwater synth + vocal chop" melodic R&B beat, reverse-engineered from Tory Lanez's "Take Care," name-checking Chris Brown and Drake as the same stylistic lane. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, [how to make melodic r&b beats for tory lanez & chris brown (underwater synth/vocal sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JCup6FVW5o). Unlike the richer multi-take builds in [Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain](#/chain/kendrick-lamar-soul-sample-chain) or [Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain](#/chain/future-style-vintage-sample-chain), this beat is deliberately minimal — only two melodic elements (the synth pad and the vocal chop) for almost the entire runtime, with a flute added only to salvage a weak hook late in the build.

## Chain overview

A single reversed one-shot, hand-trimmed and driven by a repeating 4-chord progression, is processed into a submerged-sounding pad; a Splice vocal chop gets a parallel heavy-processing treatment; two low-level texture layers sit underneath both; a 3-layer hi-hat kit plus a bounce-varied kick and long 808 carry the drums; a flute is bolted on late purely to strengthen the hook. The reusable core idea: **reverse + hand-trim a one-shot for pulse, then bury the result under progressively heavier filtering/reverb until it stops reading as a clean synth** — the "underwater" character is entirely a processing choice, not a special patch.

## 1. Synth pad — reversed/trimmed one-shot

- **Source:** an ambient/synthy one-shot from the producer's own ("Nami's") one-shot kit, chosen because it matched the "watered down synth" heard in the Tory Lanez reference.
- **Reverse + trim:** reverse the one-shot, then hand-adjust its start point and length until the reversed tail's natural swell pulses in and out on its own — no LFO/modulation device involved.
- **Chords, D minor tonal center, one per bar:** **Dm7 → D♯maj7 (♭II7 borrowing) → Gm7 (top two notes dropped an octave) → Fmaj (C dropped an octave)**. Full theory: Chord Progressions.
- **Rhythmic pattern:** each chord hit **four times per bar** — combines with the reversed-tail swell to produce the track's signature pulse.
- 🎬 *From video:* reverse-and-hand-trim is a zero-extra-plugin way to generate rhythmic pulse before reaching for a dedicated modulation device. → Sampling and Sound Selection

## 2. Synth pad FX chain — "underwater" processing

1. **EQ low-cut** — remove the low end first.
2. **Long, always-active reverb** — auto-captioned "an intensity reverb… the infinity preset," which "comes on as soon as you open it up." Exact product unconfirmed, see Plugin Wishlist.
3. **Ghz Loh1 3** (HI-cut side) — reached for because the reverb stage left the pad "way too bright."
4. **Shaper** — Mix pulled to ~50%, used purely to filter out more high-end frequencies rather than as a full effect; gives the pad a "choppy," sample-like feel. Eleventh confirmed reuse of the owned ShaperBox lane, see Plugin Wishlist.
- 🎬 *From video:* the "underwater" read is built entirely from a sequence of progressively darker filtering/reverb stages, not one special plugin. → Ghz Loh1 3, Shaper, Reverb

## 3. Texture layers (unprocessed)

- **Perc loop** — from XO ("this perc loop from x y," near-certain auto-caption garble of XO), dropped in with no processing — "sounded really good as it is."
- **Rain noise** — a texture one-shot from the same personal one-shot kit, layered for atmosphere.
- → Ambient Texture and Field Recording, XO

## 4. Vocal chop

- **Source:** a Splice vocal chop, hand-edited down to the liked parts.
- **Chain:** bandpass EQ (cuts high AND low end) → an **automated half-time rhythmic device on its "quarter" preset** (unconfirmed product, see Plugin Wishlist) → a medium-sized reverb ("just to give it a bit of space") → a **heavy ValhallaDelay**, reached for explicitly to fill space since the pad and this chop are the only two melodic elements in the whole beat.
- **Automation:** the half-time device is fully engaged for the first 4 bars (pre-hook, lower energy), then partially lifted for the hook (audibly brighter). → Automation, Arrangement and Song Form

## 5. Drums

- **Snare:** single sample, no elaborated processing given.
- **Hi-hat 1:** "old-school, more acoustic" character.
- **Hi-hat 2:** shifted noticeably off the timing grid for a natural, live-feeling swing. → Pocket and Microtiming
- **Hi-hat 3:** modern-sounding, with rolls.
- **Kick:** velocities varied per hit, several hits panned, purely for bounce. → Kick Design
- **808:** long, very subby, sustaining under the pattern.
- 🎬 *From video:* three differently-timed/processed hi-hat layers stacked together fakes a hybrid boom-bap/modern feel without programming three full patterns. → Genre Drum Patterns

## 6. Hook-strengthening pass (added after the base beat)

- **Flute** one-shot (same personal kit) → massive reverb → really big delay, added specifically because "the hook just needs something else."
- A **counter-melody**, added for the same reason.
- → Sound Selection Guide, Reverb, Delay

## 7. Arrangement — pure subtraction, no new material per section

1. **4-bar intro:** pad + textures only, no drums.
2. **Pre-hook:** full drums enter, vocal half-time device kept fully on (lower energy).
3. **Hook:** half-time device lifted (brighter, more energy).
4. **Verse:** vocal chop muted entirely — the mute itself signals "verse, write here" to the artist.
5. **Second pre-hook variation:** hi-hats + snare removed, kick + 808 kept, for contrast on repeat.
- 🎬 *From video:* the whole song's structure comes from selective muting/toggling of just two melodic elements — no new musical material was written per section. Stated philosophy: a catchy chord progression + strong sound selection + bouncy drums is enough; you don't need to keep adding elements. → Arrangement and Song Form

## Variations

- **The reverse-and-hand-trim pulse trick generalizes to any ambient one-shot**, independent of the specific Dm7–D♯maj7–Gm7–Fmaj progression — the reusable core is the trim-for-pulse technique plus the four-hits-per-bar chord repetition.
- **The "only two melodic elements + heavy processing" minimalism is itself a reusable arrangement constraint** — worth trying deliberately on a beat that's starting to feel over-stacked.

## Notes

- No exact numeric settings (reverb decay/wet%, delay time/feedback, EQ frequencies, half-time device parameters) were given on screen beyond the qualitative descriptions above — treat every device's setting as a starting point to dial in by ear.
- Two plugins named in the source video remain unresolved: the "intensity/infinity" reverb and the half-time "quarter preset" device — both logged on Plugin Wishlist, not guessed here.
- Sibling in the same lane: [2000s R&B Piano Sample Chain](#/chain/2000s-r-b-piano-sample-chain) — a fuller, four-melodic-source build (piano+counter-melody+strings+vocal) rather than this chain's deliberately minimal two-element approach, also from a Ne-Yo/T-Pain/Chris Brown-referenced era and flipped for Tory Lanez/Bryson Tiller. The "Intensity" reverb gets a third confirmed sighting there, on a lead vocal this time.

**Sources:** loner — [how to make melodic r&b beats for tory lanez & chris brown (underwater synth/vocal sample)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JCup6FVW5o) (00:08:07, 2022-04-03) · full note: how to make melodic r&b beats for tory lanez & chris brown (underwater synth-vocal sample)

chains.title: Acoustic Guitar Track
chains.routing: Acoustic Guitar → Guitar Group → Guitar Bus → Master
chains.mics: Neumann TLM 102 (12th fret) + Shure SM57 (body/bridge, optional 2nd mic)
chains.body:
**Role:** Mic'd Yamaha FG730S — strummed beds or fingerpicked features.

**Chain philosophy:** phase-align → de-noise → subtractive EQ → gentle leveling → resonance tame → sweeten. Acoustic guitar is a *subtractive* instrument in a mix — it covers the entire spectrum, so the job is removing what fights everything else, not adding character.

## 1 — Recording Setup

- **Guitar:** Yamaha FG730S, fresh-ish strings — dead strings = dull takes no EQ fixes. Decide *before* setting up. **Source rule: instrument > mic > preamp.** No onboard pickup on the FG730S, so there's no DI option — this is a mic-only chain.
- **Mic 1 (always): Neumann TLM 102 → 12th–14th fret**, 8–12" out, angled ~45° toward the neck/body joint. String detail + air without the soundhole boom (Beato's go-to single-mic spot). Shock mount, 48V on, no pop filter needed.
- 🎬 *From video:* independent validation of this exact spot — a large-diaphragm cardioid condenser (his Warm Audio WA-87 R2, same mic class as the Neumann TLM 102) landed by ear at ~45° off-axis, roughly 10" from the end of the fretboard, after physically moving the mic while playing the actual part rather than starting from a formula. His stated philosophy: "most of that is going to come from up here" (the playing), not the mic — don't chase a gear upgrade before the part itself is dialed in. — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)
- 🎬 *From video:* a second, more aggressive close-mic option when boominess (not detail/air) is the problem — mic right by the **last fret**, not the soundhole, about **2½–3 inches away**: "I like to mic it right by the fretboard... I'm trying to eliminate some of the boominess from the body of the guitar... you're eliminating the possibility of extra boom." Closer and more fretboard-specific than the ~10"-off-the-fretboard-end default above; reach for this variant instead when the ~45°/10" spot is still reading boomy. A modern affordable mic recommended for the job: Shure KSM 141 (~$600, combines an AKG 451's brightness with a Neumann KM 84's vintage voicing, 20 dB pad, switchable omni/cardioid) — "does a very lovely job on recording acoustic guitars, percussion, any of that stuff." — Eddie Kramer, [Eddie Kramer's story behind "All Along The Watchtower" by Jimi Hendrix](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6m019pawms)
- **Mic 2 (optional, for the stereo-pair variation): Shure SM57 → body/bridge**, aimed at or slightly behind the bridge — NOT straight at the soundhole (that's where the boom lives). Adds warmth under the TLM's detail.
- **Mic 3 (optional, room): Neumann TLM 102 or Shure SM57 at 2–3 ft**, for natural room tone rather than detail. Only worth it in a room you actually like — in an untreated space this captures the boxiness the close-mic advice above is designed to avoid, and reverb is cheaper. Blend under the close mic and add [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) for depth. *(From Nate's own tracking notes, filed 2026-08-09.)*
- **Fake stereo without a second mic:** duplicate the mono close-mic take, hard-pan the copies L/R and delay one by **~10 ms**. Cheap width when only one mic was available — but it is a Haas trick, so **mono-check it**; see Artificial Double Tracking (ADT) for the version that survives a fold-down.
- **3:1 rule** when both mics are up: mics ~3× as far from each other as each is from the guitar. Polarity-check anyway (flip ø, keep the fuller low end) — see Phase Alignment.
- **Room:** phone silenced, fan/HVAC off, window closed. If a scratch take sounds boxy, move 2–4" *closer* and thin the proximity warmth later with a low cut — don't back off into the bad room.
- **Monitoring:** Audio-Technica ATH-M50x closed-back — no click bleed into the mic.
- **Interface:** Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII, input gain set on the *actual part at performance energy* — peaks **−12 dBFS**, average ~−18 (see Gain Staging).

## 2 — Tracking Best Practice

The decisions that shape the mix later — pick the variation *before* pressing record and label clips with the Sound Palette slot (`BED` / `MIDS`).

- **Default answer: yes, double-track strummed parts. Never copy-paste a take** — the micro-timing/tuning differences ARE the width. Duplicated takes just get louder, not wider (Width and Stereo).
- **Takes discipline:** 3 takes per part max, then a listen-back; comp in Ableton rather than chasing one perfect take. Record path `AcGtr_<song>_<take>`.

**Variations — pick one:**

1. **Wide double (the modern default, strummed bed):** 2 full takes of the same part, TLM 102 only (mono each), panned **40L / 40R** (Live's pan runs 0–50 per side). Occupies the BED Slot; mix HPF's it ~120 Hz, so don't chase bass while tracking.
2. **"Four of everything" (dense pop/produced records):** 4 takes — **2 hard-panned 50L/50R + 2 at ~22L/22R** — fills the whole field instead of leaving a hole between hard-panned doubles. Straight from Disclosure's stems session (Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems). Vary take 3–4: capo up + higher chord voicings (the Beatles trick — same part, different octave color) so the layers stack instead of comb-filtering.
3. **Stereo pair, single performance (fingerpicked feature):** Neumann TLM 102 neck + Shure SM57 bridge, panned ~25L/25R "player perspective." One expressive take beats stacked takes when the part is the feature — flirts with the MIDS Slot; move the TLM 4" closer and drop gain 3 dB to keep transients clean.
4. **Mono center (sparse/folk):** one take, one mic, dead center. If the arrangement is voice + guitar, mono is *more* intimate — pan "like you're looking at a stage," not for width's own sake (Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems).
5. **Tape character layer (optional, any of the above):** print one extra take through the Sony TC-630 loop (line out → tape → back in) — a hardware RC-20 Retro Color double to tuck under the clean takes.
   - 🎬 *From video:* treat this as a distinct, LATER, more consequential step than any in-the-box tape-modeling plugin already on the track — not a redundant extra. One documented session ran a deliberately "wonky" pre-EQ (mid scoop + shelf boosts, there specifically to provoke a bigger reaction out of the plugin stage) into an ITB tape-saturation plugin first, and only THEN moved to the physical tape print — described as "we are ready for tape" only once the plugin pass was already dialed in. The tape pass itself was praised for how it *compresses* the signal, on top of whatever the plugin stage did. His framing: "tape is commitment" — the plugin stage is like shooting flat log footage, the physical print is the color grade. **Budget time to manually realign the return** — tape bounces don't land back sample-accurately — and consider a match-EQ pass afterward (Ozone 9 Match EQ) if a pre-tape balance you liked needs to survive the print. See Committing and Printing. — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD Console)

Printed on the way in via Console — conservative, because printed is forever. EQ comes *after* compression on the way in, desk-style (Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems).

### 1. UAD Neve 1073 — Unison preamp
- Mic gain: lowest position that reaches level (the TLM 102 runs hot); output trim for −18 dBFS average, peaks −12
- EQ flat on the way in (high shelf +1 dB @ 12 kHz max if the guitar sounds dark at the mic) — the 1073's gentle iron adds body to acoustics
- **Alt:** UAD UA 610-B for a rounder tube flavor, or no Unison plugin for fully neutral.

### 2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — Tracking compressor
- Comp mode · Peak Reduction for **≤3 dB GR on the hardest strums, never more on the way in** · Gain to unity
- The "one-LA" rule: threshold + gain only; hit it harder = higher effective ratio (Disclosure - Ultimatum Breakdown + Breakbeat — their reach-for on tracked guitar "for shine")
- **Alt:** UAD UA 1176LN (4:1, attack 3–4, release 6–7, 2–4 dB GR) when the part is percussive strumming rather than smooth fingerpicking.

### 3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — Broad-stroke EQ
- Low ATTEN **2–3 @ 60 CPS** (rumble/boom out before the converters) · Low BOOST 0 · High BOOST 0–2 @ 12 KCS broad, only if the guitar sounds dark at the mic
- Leave real sweetening to Ableton where it's undoable.

🎬 *From video (if monitoring through Ableton plugins instead of Console):* buffer **128**, driver error compensation to ~0 ms, and arm a ghost **latency track** per mic — no plugins, monitor off, routed to a spare hardware out instead of the master; keep the ghost takes, they land on the grid (two mics = four tracks armed) — Kenny Beats, [Recording Without Latency](https://youtu.be/Gj4_IvHFn6g) → Latency-Free Tracking

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

Corrective, bounceable. Utility + mvMeter2nogpu meter sandwich at head/tail — ~0 VU (−18 dBFS) through everything.

### 1. Align Delay — Phase (two-mic takes only)
- On the Shure SM57 body mic: **Unit = samples** (②), **start at 13 samples** (① — ≈4 in of 57-vs-condenser spacing @ 44.1k, ~3–4 samples per inch) and nudge while both mics play; keep whatever makes the low end fullest. **Check polarity flip first** — it's free, and if a flip alone nulls the comb you may need almost no delay (Phase Alignment).

### 2. RX Voice De-noise — Noise floor
- **Adaptive mode ON · Reduction 4 dB** starting point (range 3–6) · learn on pre-count-in room tone
- Condenser self-noise + room hiss is far quieter than amp hiss — go lighter than the electric chain's 6–10 dB
- **Why:** every downstream stage (LALA, Soothe2) raises the floor with the signal — clean it before anything amplifies it.

### 3. Pro-Q 4 — Subtractive EQ (Joe Gilder's "3 cuts + 1 boost")
1. **Rumble:** HPF **45 Hz, 24 dB/oct** always; move it up to **120–150 Hz, 12–18 dB/oct** in a dense mix
2. **Thump:** bell **−3 dB @ 150 Hz, Q 1.5** — the percussive down-strum "djembe" bump; boost to find it, cut to balance, don't delete it (it's the warmth)
3. **Plastic:** bell **−2.5 dB @ 650 Hz, Q 1.2** — sweep 500–800 Hz for the cheap/boxy buildup; a small cut opens both lows and highs ("grown-up smiley EQ — a smirk, not a smile")
4. **Air:** shelf **+1.5 dB @ 8 kHz** — pick sparkle that cuts a dense mix. Small; overdoing this is the classic tell.
- **Why:** acoustic covers the whole spectrum; these four target exactly what fights the mix. EQ sits *before* Soothe2 so any brightening gets caught downstream (Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems).

### 4. LALA — Gentle leveling (or none)
- **Exposed part: bypass it.** ~90% of exposed acoustics sound better with EQ and NO compression — compression audibly squashes the harmonics.
- **Bed in a dense mix:** Peak Reduction for 2–3 dB GR (①), Comp mode (③), **Mix 100%** (⑤), makeup to unity (②)
- **"Butter compression" alternative (beds):** threshold all the way down, ratio crawled up from 1:1 to just **1.2–1.5:1**, attack **30 ms**, release **50 ms** — always-on ultra-shallow leveling, 5–6 dB of control with no grab-and-release pumping (Gilder)
- **Why:** opto/slow attack lets the pick through; fast heavy compression turns strumming into cardboard (Compression Staging).

### 5. Soothe2 — Pick/string harshness
- **Depth 3 · focus 2–6 kHz** (pull the side bands down out of the way) · **Sharpness ~50 · Selectivity ~40 · Speed 50%**
- **Wet/dry ~75%** — the Disclosure master-bus trick scaled to a track: tame the spikes, keep the life (Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems)
- Delta-listen: you should hear *only* uneven string zing, not the whole guitar
- **Why:** strummed steel spikes unevenly; dynamic taming beats a static cut that dulls the whole part.

### 6. Pro-Q 4 — Sweeten
- Shelf **+1.5 dB @ 10 kHz** only if the part is featured · skip for background strumming
- Featured fingerpicked part: optional bell **+1 dB @ 5 kHz, Q 1** for fingertip detail.

## 5 — Track FX (optional)

Most acoustic parts want nothing here — character was decided at the mic.

- **RC-20 Retro Color** — lo-fi bed under a produced track: Wobble 10–15%, Noise off, Distort 5%, MIX ~30%. Use it as an effects box, not a crusher (Disclosure - 'Never Enough' Twitch Breakdown).
- **Chorus-Ensemble** — last-resort width on a single take that *should* have been doubled: Amount 15%, Rate 0.3 Hz, Dry/Wet 20%. A real double (§2) always beats this.

## 6 — Bus / Send FX (optional)

Routing: **Acoustic Guitar → [Guitar Group](#/chain/guitar-group) → [Guitar Bus](#/chain/guitar-bus) → [Master Chain](#/chain/master-chain)** — carve against other groups happens at [Guitar Group](#/chain/guitar-group), tape/glue finish at [Guitar Bus](#/chain/guitar-bus).

- **[Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room)** — send **−15 to −12 dB** (modest); acoustics carry their own room already
- **[Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long)** — fingerpicked features only, send to taste from −20 dB, pre-delay 20–40 ms so the pick stays upfront
- **[Delay Send Slap](#/chain/delay-send-slap)** — rare; a 60s color on mono-center folk parts
- **[Width Send](#/chain/width-send)** — skip it: real double-tracking (§2) beats artificial width on acoustics, and fake-wide acoustics fall apart in mono.

## Variations (mix-stage quick recipes)

- **Strummed bed under full band:** HPF 150 Hz, LPF ~10 kHz, LALA 3–5 dB GR, pan per §2 option 1–2
- **Solo/fingerpicked feature:** stereo pair (§2 option 3), minimal EQ, [Reverb Send Long](#/chain/reverb-send-long) to taste

## From videos

- **Close-mic right by the last fret (not the soundhole), ~2½–3" away, specifically to eliminate body boominess — a second, more aggressive close-mic option than this chain's default §1 spot, for when boominess itself (not detail/air) is the problem.** Eddie Kramer: "I like to mic it right by the fretboard... I'm trying to eliminate some of the boominess from the body of the guitar... get up away from the hole of the actual guitar, right by the last fret — you're eliminating the possibility of extra boom." Also the story behind a famous track's guitar blend: two guitarists' live parts (12-string + 6-string) printed to one blended stereo track with drum bleed, bass rolled off one part to clear the other's low end, kept dry to preserve crispness — see Layering and Stacking, Masking and Carving. Modern mic recommendation for this close-mic role: Shure KSM 141. → Shure KSM 141, Layering and Stacking, Masking and Carving — Mix with the Masters (Eddie Kramer), Eddie Kramer's story behind "All Along The Watchtower" by Jimi Hendrix
- **A structural width-automation move: the mono/narrower demo acoustic guitar runs from the top of the song through the first pre-chorus, then the recording switches to a newly re-tracked, deliberately WIDER acoustic guitar performance from the pre-chorus onward.** Paul Epworth, on Adele's "Rolling in the Deep": "we've actually got the original... acoustic from the Logic demo on the front up to the first pre-chorus, and from then on it switches to... a new acoustic performance which we recorded to make it a bit wider... so you get this nice change of width of image." The wider re-track uses a **binaural head** specifically for its width — muting the close mic "scoops a lot of room-y-ness out," confirming the binaural signal carries most of the perceived width, with the close mic filling in detail on top. A concrete, real-record example of width as an *arrangement* device (narrower verse → wider pre-chorus arrival) rather than a fixed per-song setting — same family as this vault's other section-staged width/effects builds (see Arrangement and Song Form). → Width and Stereo, Arrangement and Song Form — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"
- **Mic placement found by ear, physically moving the mic while playing, lands on almost this exact spot** — a large-diaphragm cardioid condenser at ~45° off-axis, ~10" from the end of the fretboard — direct validation of this chain's §1 default. → Neumann TLM 102 — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)
- **A vintage-era "wonky" pre-EQ move: broad mid scoop + low-shelf and high-shelf boosts, sounds thin soloed on purpose** — exists specifically to provoke a bigger reaction out of a following saturation/tape stage, not to sound good dry. → Saturation and Distortion, BED Slot, MIDS Slot, AIR Slot — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)
- **Vintage pitch-drop capture trick: track slightly fast, then slow the take down afterward (tempo+pitch together)** — reproduces a classic tape-era move without needing tape; in Logic this is Flex Time's Speed FX mode specifically (links pitch+tempo the way real tape-speed change would) — the same relationship Varispeed 3.0 recreates live. → Varispeed 3.0, Pitch and Formant — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)
- **Match-EQ discipline after a tape print, when the goal is glue without a big tonal shift** — pull the tape-returned signal back toward a pre-tape mix balance that was already working, rather than letting the tape stage overwrite it. → Ozone 9 Match EQ — Zach Scholz, [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)
- **Explicitly not a universal default** — this level of vintage processing (wonky pre-EQ + tape print) is a deliberate, "a little extreme" character choice for period-correct material, not the guitar tone for every mix. Worth remembering before reaching for the full chain on a part that doesn't call for it.

## Sources

Rick Beato (mic placement) · Joe Gilder (3-cuts-1-boost, butter compression) — links in [FX Chain System](#/chains/system) · Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems (four-of-everything panning, stage panning, EQ-before-Soothe, desk order) · Disclosure - Ultimatum Breakdown + Breakbeat (LA-2A one-knob tracking) · Zach Scholz — [Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQuuXtnyZy8)

chains.title: Electric Guitar Amp Track
chains.routing: Electric Guitar → Guitar Group → Guitar Bus → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Mic'd amp — the real-amp tone lane. Fender Stratocaster → Fender Blues Junior → two mics blended: Shure SM57 close for mids/lows, Neumann TLM 102 for the airy top.

**Chain philosophy:** phase-align → de-noise → corrective EQ → tube color → broad tone → comp. Blend the two mics into one picture *first* (they're one instrument), then process the blend.

## 1 — Recording Setup

- **Run the decision tree before every take** (Kenny's habit): what guitar is working, what does the song want — DI + amp sim for speed? real amp? pedals → DI? pedals → amp? one mic or two balanced? Choose consciously instead of defaulting to yesterday's chain — [Guitar Recording Process](https://youtu.be/VruZ-A0_aZk).
- **Amp: Fender Blues Junior at LOW volume** — Kenny's most-recorded amp is a '64/65 Blackface Vibro Champ barely turned up ("even at a really low volume just sounds so good"). Small vintage-voiced Fender driven quietly beats a cranked amp for recording. Pedals in front per the board order: wah → dirt (Big Muff Pi/Boss DS-2) → delay (Line 6 DL4).
- 🎬 *From video:* a third independent source confirms the same clean-platform-first amp philosophy — "that's how I like to set an amp generally... it gives you a really nice platform to start adding pedals and effects, and it kind of works equally well with every guitar." Set the amp clean with a touch of reverb *before* engaging any pedals, on a mid-'60s Fender Princeton Reverb (Eminence speaker) — same small-clean-blackface-Fender lane as the owned Fender Blues Junior. — Jack Ruch, [My Home Recording Setup for Guitar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYTGFneEJ2A)
- 🎬 *From video:* a fourth confirmation of the small-clean-Fender-platform pattern, this time with the actual pedal *dial-in* method spelled out. Studio amp volume ≈ 3–4 (Princeton Reverb/Headstrong), live volume higher with more headroom for a louder band (Pro Reverb) — "all these old Fender amps have a great balanced, clean tone and are a really nice starting place for adding pedals." **Boost/overdrive volume-balancing method (new, reusable):** set a clean-boost pedal's volume *slightly louder* than clean rhythm volume (live use: helps melody/solo parts cut through the mix without breaking up, given headroom); with an overdrive, set gain to taste but push the pedal's own volume louder than feels necessary solo, to compensate for the *perceived* volume loss its own compression causes once a full band (especially drums/cymbals) is playing — "it might sound loud when you're playing by yourself... but you're going to notice that perceived volume loss with the compression of an overdrive" once the band comes in. Also: an overdrive's main job isn't just grit — it adds compression (sustain, "squishier" feel under the fingers) and typically cuts high end, taming a bright clean guitar/amp combo. **Tone controls set per pickup/guitar, not fixed** — a brighter guitar, brighter amp, or bridge-pickup use wants different pedal tone-control settings than a darker neck-pickup tone. **Amp volume changes the whole downstream calculation** — a louder/cranked amp is already compressing on its own tubes/speaker, shrinking available headroom, so pedal boost/overdrive volume settings need to come back down from wherever they sat at bedroom volume; re-tune the board any time the amp's own volume changes rather than assuming one dial-in transfers across sessions. → Fender Blues Junior, Boss DS-2 — Jack Ruch, [Dial In Your Amps and Pedals for Great Clean and Overdriven TONES!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=45s77xBLZBU)
- **Speaker map:** dust cap center = brightest/harshest · middle of the cone = balanced · outer edge = dark, low-heavy, least articulate.
- **Shure SM57:** close (1–3"), middle of the cone as the start. This mic is the body of the tone — wear headphones in front of the cab and move it; an inch genuinely changes the tone.
- **Neumann TLM 102:** the air layer. Two safe options: (a) next to the SM57, **capsules equal distance from the cone** (avoids comb-filtering); or (b) 1–3 ft back for air + room, then align in §4.
- 🎬 *From video:* a third confirmation of the two-mic-blend pattern, this time with a ribbon standing in for the condenser's air role: **Shure SM57 (dynamic, mid-rangey/cutting) + Royer 121 (ribbon, warmer/fuller, not owned)** — "the warmer, fuller sound of the Royer ribbon mic combined with the more focused mid-rangey harsher sound of the 57, which really cuts through the mix." Positioning stated as by-ear, not formula: "I just kind of positioned those a little bit off the center of the cone of the speaker, back an inch or two off the grill cloth. Basically, just move it around until it sounds good" — a looser framing of this stage's own "an inch of movement changes the tone" rule. — Jack Ruch, [My Home Recording Setup for Guitar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYTGFneEJ2A)
- **Pink-noise phase alignment (Dan Austin method):** play pink noise through the amp, set the SM57, then **flip the TLM's polarity and physically move it until the summed pair cancels hardest** (thin "windy" sound = perfectly aligned), flip back — phase-locked, blend freely. **Polarity-check every setup regardless:** flip ø, keep the fuller low end (Phase Alignment).
- 🎬 *From video:* a DI layer summed with a mic'd amp signal needs the same polarity check as two mics — "always want to check the phase of DI versus amp." A DI fuzz/pedal track on Muse's guitars was out of phase against its mic'd counterpart; flipping it "brought all the bottom back" and let the DI layer add real heat instead of cancelling low end. Full note on Phase Alignment — Mix with the Masters (Chris Lord-Alge), Mixing Muse Guitars - Chris Lord-Alge.

## 2 — Tracking Best Practice

- **Always print the clean DI too** — even when committed to the amp: it's the re-amp safety net, and you can *see* transients in a DI for editing that saturated takes hide.
- **Two mics = four tracks armed** — each mic gets its monitored FX track + its ghost latency track (no plugins, monitor off, out to a spare hardware pair); keep the ghost takes — [Recording Without Latency](https://youtu.be/Gj4_IvHFn6g) → Latency-Free Tracking.
- **Rhythm double-tracking (the real width move):** record the part twice, pan **35–50 L/R** (Live's pan runs 0–50 per side) — beats any widener. Vary take 2: different pickup position or capo'd voicing so the layers stack instead of comb-filtering.
- **Hardware echo as part of the tone, printed** — Kenny keeps Space Echo/Echorec-style boxes ON the amp and records them; owned lane: EchoBoy tape mode or the Sony TC-630 loop *before* commit, instead of always saving delay for sends — [Guitar Recording Process](https://youtu.be/VruZ-A0_aZk).
- **Bonus texture — the crushed room mic:** on big rock moments, a bright condenser a few feet back, **preamp slammed into breakup**, HPF'd hard, blended low *on its own track* (never summed into the close pair).
- **Tone-first rule:** if the mix needs massive EQ later, the fix is here — amp gain (too much eats note definition in a mix) and presence, or a different mic spot. **Re-record over re-sculpt.**

## 3 — Source → Ableton (UAD Console)

### 1. UAD Neve 1073 — Unison preamp (per mic)
- The guitar-amp classic; light drive, ~0 VU. (Alt: UAD UA 610-B, or a UAD Marshall/Fender Unison amp if going direct-ish.)
- 🎬 *From video:* the plain statement of the hot-but-not-clipping discipline this stage already runs, re-tuned per outboard preamp: "I just set the preamps right until they're... not clipping. So, as loud as they can get without hitting the red... you want to hit your recording software, the computer, with as much signal as possible. That's going to give you a nice loud full sound." Stated as a real, audible upgrade over interface-only gain, not just a habit: "I've done it without the mic preamps and there's a noticeable difference." → Gain Staging — Jack Ruch, [My Home Recording Setup for Guitar](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KYTGFneEJ2A)

### 2. UAD UA 1176LN — Compressor (optional)
- 2–3 dB GR max on peaks · 4:1 · skip entirely for dynamic blues/edge-of-breakup playing.

### 3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — EQ
- HPF-duty only (low ATTEN @ 60 Hz) · print conservative — the amp + mic *is* the sound.

## 4 — Ableton Initial Processing

### 1. Align Delay — Phase alignment (on the TLM track, if spaced)
- **Unit = samples** (②), **start ~13** (①) and nudge until the low end is fullest with both mics playing; polarity-flip check first
- **Why:** A spaced pair arrives at different times = comb filtering no EQ can fix. Align first; every downstream move assumes a coherent source.

### 2. RX 11 Voice De-noise — Noise floor
- Learn on a gap · 6–10 dB reduction, adaptive
- **Why:** Amp hiss + single-coil hum gets multiplied by every later compressor/saturator.

### 3. Pro-Q 4 — Corrective EQ
- HPF 80–120 Hz — **the guitar's fundamental lives ~100 Hz; don't HPF past it** (up to 200 Hz on layer/lead parts only) · cut mud 250–700 Hz as needed · **notch the 3.5–4.5 kHz nastiness** (narrow, a few dB)
- Magic boost map when the part needs it: **1 kHz** upfront/full · **2.5 kHz** edge/bite · **5 kHz** definition · **8 kHz** airy lift — but never boost the same ones on every guitar layer; stack them across different frequencies or they fight and mask the vocal.
- **Why:** Cuts before compression. Leave the 100 Hz–1 kHz "meat" mostly alone — heavily-EQ'd distorted guitar hurts more than it helps.
