**Role:** The "big moment" space — plate/hall tails for hooks, vocal features, ballad moments. Where [Reverb Send Room](#/chain/reverb-send-room) is invisible glue, this one is *audible* as an effect.

## Signal chain

### 1. ValhallaPlate — The tail
- **Mix 100%** (②) · **Decay 2.4 s** (③ — 1.8–3.0 window) · **Pre-delay 35 ms** (④ — longer than the room: big spaces have late first reflections, and the longer gap keeps the lyric intelligible under a long tail)
- Plate for vocals (dense, bright, no early-reflection clutter) — swap ValhallaVintageVerb hall for orchestral/ballad size.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter
- HPF 250–350 Hz · LPF 6–8 kHz (slightly brighter than the room — plate sparkle is the point) — same band-limiting logic as the room send.
- 🎬 *From video (clarity):* a narrow dip around **1.5–3.5 kHz** on top of the HPF/LPF keeps a long, audible tail from burying the lyric — pair with pre-delay in the **10–50 ms** range (this send already runs 35 ms) so the transient clears before the tail arrives — Sage Audio, [Reverb Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1ME30K2ro)

### 3. Pro-C 2 — Duck the tail (sidechain from lead vocal)
- 2:1 · **2–3 dB GR** keyed from the dry lead · slow release
- **Why:** The pro trick for big-but-clear: the tail tucks *while the singer sings* and blooms in the gaps between phrases. You get cathedral size with dry-vocal intelligibility.
- 🎬 *From video (creative sends):* the **George Michael trick** — invert a **de-esser** and use it to *drive* this send, so only the **S's** trigger the reverb (sibilance as a crash cymbal) — Disclosure, [Higher Than Ever Before](https://youtu.be/9XkHSronZck). And **reverse-reverb "dream" swells** — print a part full-wet, reverse the audio → a rising wash into a hit — Disclosure, [You've Got To Let Go](https://youtu.be/1iRPvK1gaOI). (These often live as **track inserts**, not just this send.)

## Usage
- Lead vocal on hooks (automate the send up for choruses) · harmonies · featured guitar/piano moments · risers.
- 🎬 *From video:* introduce this send at a SPECIFIC section rather than leaving it running from the top — on Adele's "Rolling in the Deep," the verse runs a tape delay only (no reverb at all), and this send is switched on for the first time at the bridge, one section before the chorus's delays arrive — a clean three-step example of staging each vocal-effect send to a different structural landmark. → Arrangement and Song Form, [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other), [1 Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) — Mix with the Masters (Tom Elmhirst), Tom Elmhirst breaks down his mix of 'Rolling in the Deep' by Adele

## Variations
- **Shimmer moments:** swap in ValhallaShimmer for the pitched-up wash (intros/bridges/outros).

## From videos

- **Confirms this send's own §3 sidechain-duck design as the universal recipe: aux + compressor keyed off the DRY vocal, ducking the attack/decay and blooming back in the gaps — the general version of exactly the Pro-C 2 stage this chain already runs.** Pair with the return's existing 1.5–3.5 kHz clarity dip; a broader version of the same masking carve is 200–400 Hz specifically. → Sidechaining, Masking and Carving — Sage Audio, [The 5 MOST IMPORTANT Vocal Mixing Tips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXk1lvT6AhU)
- **Reverb held back until the bridge, one section before delays arrive at the chorus — see the inline 🎬 note in Usage above for the full three-step build.** → Arrangement and Song Form, [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other), [1 Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) — Mix with the Masters (Tom Elmhirst), Tom Elmhirst breaks down his mix of 'Rolling in the Deep' by Adele
- **Clarity move for a long, audible tail: dip ~1.5–3.5 kHz on the return EQ, keep pre-delay in the 10–50 ms window** — this send's existing 35 ms pre-delay and Pro-Q 4 band-limiting already follow the general principle; the added specific is a narrow attenuation around 1.5–3.5 kHz so the lyric-intelligibility band stays drier under a long tail, worth reaching for whenever a hook-moment reverb is fighting the vocal for clarity. → Pro-R 2 — Sage Audio, [Reverb Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1ME30K2ro)
- **The Kenny long-verb recipe: ValhallaRoom 3.0 s decay · 100% wet on the return · depth ~90% · EQ on the return channel** — send-level scale from his template: Travis-style washed ad-libs = heavy send, wet main vocal = moderate, "pretty much dry" = barely cracked open — Kenny Beats, [Vocal Template](https://youtu.be/X_iDENABLmk)
- **2022 update: long tier swapped to ValhallaVintageVerb** ("just like the way it's been sounding on vocals") — Kenny Beats, [New Vocal Chain 2022](https://youtu.be/-SvBNOBWJ_8)

chains.title: Reverb Send Room
chains.routing: Return track — receives sends from any track/group → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** The mix's shared "room" — the default space most elements send to. One room for everyone is what makes separate recordings sound like they happened in the same place.

**Send/return theory:** returns run **100% wet**; the *send knob* is the dry/wet control. One reverb shared by ten tracks beats ten inserted reverbs — cheaper, and more importantly *coherent*: every element sits in the same acoustic space.

## Signal chain

### 1. ValhallaRoom — The room
- **Mix 100%** (②) · **Decay 1.0 s** (③ — 0.8–1.2 window) · **Pre-delay 20 ms** (④ — 15–25) · **High Cut ~5–6 kHz** (⑦)
- **The controls that matter, in order: Mix, Decay, High Cut** (then pre-delay, then everything else). Workflow: set **Early Size first** (it defines the room's perceived size/attack), then fine-tune Late Size (default ~15 is fine); Depth balances early-vs-late character.
- Mode picks: **Large Room / Bright Room** = the do-everything modes (Bright Room even works on bass) · Dark Room/Dark Chamber = washier, more chorused · **Nostromo/Narcissus** = great on keys.
- Low Mult below 1.0 to tighten the reverb's low end at the source (on top of the return HPF).
- **Why pre-delay matters:** 0 ms glues the reverb onto the dry signal and blurs it; 15–25 ms separates the dry transient from the tail — the source stays upfront *and* sounds placed. The #1 amateur reverb fix. (Fast rhythmic sources like busy bass lines want it shorter, ~10 ms, or the timing smears.)

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter the return
- **HPF 200–300 Hz · LPF 4–6 kHz**
- **Why:** Low reverb energy = mud, high reverb energy = harsh sizzle that fights vocal air. The "Abbey Road filter" trick: a band-limited reverb adds *space* without adding *frequency content* — you can run more of it before the mix notices.
- 🎬 *From video (clarity):* on a vocal fighting to stay clear through this send, add a narrow dip around **1.5–3.5 kHz** on top of the HPF/LPF — a general clarity move, separate from the wide-band filtering above — Sage Audio, [Reverb Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1ME30K2ro)

## Usage
- Snare is the main customer (its tail defines the space) · vocals low send · guitars/keys to place them · never send bass, kick, or 808s (low end + reverb = mud, always).

## Variations
- **Drier modern trap:** decay down to 0.5–0.7 s — a "small booth" flavor just for glue.

## From videos

- **The general recipe behind this send's ducking mechanism, stated as a universal build: put the reverb on an aux, add a compressor sidechained to the DRY vocal, and it ducks the return for the vocal's attack/decay then blooms back in the gaps — usable on ANY reverb/delay plugin, not just ones with built-in ducking.** Combine with an EQ dip around the vocal's 200–400 Hz masking range on the return afterward for the fuller fix — see Sidechaining for the full recipe this send could add if it doesn't already run a sidechain stage. → Sidechaining, Masking and Carving — Sage Audio, [The 5 MOST IMPORTANT Vocal Mixing Tips](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXk1lvT6AhU)
- **Reverb send pre-delay used deliberately as a groove/timing tool on a clap, not just for space.** Paul Epworth, opening the clap reverb in his Adele "Rolling in the Deep" session: "you can see how we're using the pre-delay to try and give a little bit of swing and timing to the feel of the rhythm track as well." No exact pre-delay value given (qualitative), but the framing is distinct from this note's own pre-delay rule above (dry-transient-vs-tail separation) — here the pre-delay amount itself is treated as a rhythmic push, shifting the clap's perceived placement relative to the beat, not just keeping it upfront. Worth trying on a backbeat element when a static grid feels stiff: nudge the send's pre-delay rather than (or alongside) moving the MIDI/audio itself. → [Drums Snare-Clap Track](#/chain/drums-snare-clap-track), Pocket and Microtiming — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"
- **The "zombie vocal" ceiling — if the send reads as audible reverb rather than body, it's too hot.** CLA peels a vocal's reverb send back to roughly **5% wet** specifically so it never announces itself: "I have it set so low I really [don't] hear reverb... let me see if I can just get it to not be a zombie." A concrete, low number to anchor this send's "you don't really hear it" philosophy (see Kenny Beats' bullet below) against. → Reverb (effect), [1 Main Vocal Track](#/chain/main-vocal-track) — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Chris Lord-Alge processing vocals
- **Clarity move for this send's return EQ: dip ~1.5–3.5 kHz in addition to the HPF/LPF, and keep pre-delay in the 10–50 ms window** — this room send's Pro-Q 4 stage already band-limits (HPF 200–300 / LPF 4–6 kHz); the added clarity trick is a narrow attenuation around 1.5–3.5 kHz so that intelligibility band stays drier, paired with the pre-delay already on this note (20 ms sits inside the general 10–50 ms window this technique recommends) — the transient passes through dry before the reflections arrive. → Pro-R 2 — Sage Audio, [Reverb Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1ME30K2ro)
- **The short tier is body, not audible space** — "you don't really hear it"; his 2022 short verb is Pro-R 2 preset *Vocal Backings Bright* (he used the original Pro-R at the time — the preset name may differ in Pro-R 2) (lightly tweaked) — set it so muting it thins the vocal rather than removing a reverb sound — Kenny Beats, [New Vocal Chain 2022](https://youtu.be/-SvBNOBWJ_8)

chains.title: Saturation Send
chains.routing: Return track — vocals, bass, drums → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Parallel dirt — a filthy copy blended under clean sources for density and attitude. Same parallel logic as [Parallel Comp Send](#/chain/parallel-comp-send): keep the clean signal intact, add controlled wreckage underneath.

**Why parallel instead of insert saturation:** an insert saturator has one drive knob per source; a saturation *send* gives every track a blendable dirt knob (the send level) into one consistent flavor — and the dirt can be EQ'd separately from the source.

## Signal chain

### 1. Decapitator — The dirt
- **Style E** (① — Chandler/EMI TG, aggressive but keeps low-end weight + airy top; the parallel-attitude default) · **Drive 6.0** (② — genuinely dirty; subtle defeats the purpose on a parallel path) · **Low Cut 150 Hz** (⑥ — keep flabby lows out of the saturation circuit) · **Tone slightly Bright, ~1 o'clock** (⑦) · **High Cut 10 kHz** (⑧ — tame fizz at the source) · **Thump off · Steep off** · **Auto on** (⑩ — output stays level-matched) · **Mix 100%** (⑪ — the send level is the parallel blend, so the plugin runs full wet)
- **Punish (③): off by default — punch it in for a hook / rap-verse attitude moment**, then print the result. Alt **Style P** (Culture Vulture pentode) for thicker, odd-harmonic grit.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Shape the dirt
- **HPF 200–300 Hz** (saturated lows = instant mud) · LPF 6–8 kHz (fizz control)
- **Why:** Mid-focused distortion is what reads as "attitude"; full-range distortion reads as "broken."

## Usage
- **Lead vocal:** blend under for hooks/rap verses — density that EQ can't buy.
- **Bass:** parallel grit lets the Hofner keep its clean low end while the mids snarl.
- **Snare/full drums:** an alternative flavor to the 1176 crush — try both, pick per song.

## Variations
- **Lo-fi flavor:** swap Decapitator for RC-20 Retro Color (adds wobble/noise, not just drive).
- **Tape flavor:** Kramer Tape slammed (input hot) — softer, rounder dirt for the Beatles lane.

chains.title: Width Send
chains.routing: Return track — vocals, synths, guitars → Master
chains.body:
**Role:** Parallel stereo thickener — the classic "pitch-shift widener" (a.k.a. the H3000 micro-pitch trick on every pop vocal since the 80s). Splits the signal to L/R copies detuned a few cents apart with tiny delays, creating width that doesn't exist in the mono source.

## Signal chain

### 1. MicroShift — The widener
- **Style I** (① — the classic H3000 recipe) · **Detune & Delay at 100% default** (②/③ — push toward 200% only for deliberately phasey/crazy moments) · **Mix 100%** (⑤ — return)
- **Focus knob** (④): set the crossover ~100–200 Hz — everything below stays mono *inside the plugin*, so the widening never touches the low end
- Audition all three styles per source — same trick, subtly different phase behavior
- **Why a send:** at 100% wet on an insert, micro-pitch makes the source blurry; as a *blend under* the dry center image, the dry keeps the focus and the shifted copies pure width. Focus + size simultaneously.

### 2. Pro-Q 4 — Keep it out of the way
- **HPF 250–400 Hz** (belt-and-suspenders on top of the focus knob) · LPF ~10 kHz.

## Usage
- **Lead vocal hooks:** automate the send up in choruses — verse stays intimate/mono-ish, chorus blooms wide. The cheapest "chorus lift" in pop.
- 🎬 *From video (mono→wide drop):* make a chorus feel bigger **without turning it up** — keep the verse mono, then on the drop fade this send (or a chorus/rotary) up so it opens to full width; the fastest one-knob version is the **RC-20 Retro Color "Whip"** control, or just switch on a flanger/chorus/phaser for the drop — Disclosure, [Talk](https://youtu.be/PBbnvElf9ac).
- **Mono synths/guitars** that need to feel doubled without re-recording.
- 🎬 *From video:* direct confirmation of the exact hardware this send's "H3000 micro-pitch trick" is modeling — a real Eventide H3000 set to ±4 cents split L/R as a guitar-solo widener, run alongside a second H3000 on a subtle custom flange for character. Full technique on MicroShift — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Muse Guitars - Chris Lord-Alge.
- Never on bass, kick, or anything whose mono low end matters.

**Mono-compatibility check:** flip the master to mono (Utility) — the widened element should get quieter but not disappear or comb-filter. If it vanishes, drop the send or raise the return's HPF.

## Variations
- **Subtle tape-chorus flavor:** Chorus-Ensemble on the return instead — more vintage motion, less surgical width.
- **Extreme trap vocal width:** MicroShift Style II + higher send, panned doubles on top.

chains.title: Glitch Delay Rack
chains.routing: Track insert (or a send return) — [[Delay]] (time-mapped, Random-LFO-modulated) → nested mono/[[Delay]] Ping Pong sub-rack → [[Limiter]]
chains.reference: asd (ableton sound design, YouTube breakdown channel)
plugins: mapped to Delay Time + Feedback + Rate + Curve macros)
nested rack (mono Delay chain / stereo Ping Pong Delay chain
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a from-scratch custom Audio Effect Rack built from only two delays and one LFO — proof that a single well-chosen modulation source (an LFO mapped to delay time) produces the entire range of results from subtle stutter to full deconstruction, with everything else in the rack (feedback, dry/wet, stereo width) as supporting macros. Built and demoed by asd (2017) using the era's separate "Simple Delay" / "Ping Pong Delay" devices — both are the same device family unified today in Delay (Live 11+). Companion technique note: Randomized Rack Design (the chain-volume-fade dry/wet macro and nested-rack-shared-macros patterns this build relies on are documented generally there).

**Signal source:** built entirely from stock Ableton devices (Delay ×2, LFO, Limiter) — nothing here needs an unowned plugin. LFO 2.0 is a free Ableton Max for Live device if not already installed. Nothing added to Plugin Wishlist from this video.

## Chain (build order)

### 1. Prove the concept by hand
Loop a percussion-based sample on an audio track (busy transient content shows the effect most clearly). Drop Delay on the track: **Stereo Link on** (bypasses the right channel's own time, applies the left channel's setting to both sides), mode **Time** (not Beat sync), **Dry/Wet 100%**. Play the loop and manually drag the delay-time slider around — this manual drag alone is the entire foundation of the rack; everything after this step exists to automate that one gesture.
- **Why:** confirms the ear-catching effect before any device/macro complexity gets added — the rest of the build is pure automation of this one motion.

### 2. Group into a rack, map Delay Time + Beat Division to a macro
Group the delay into an Audio Effect Rack. Map **Delay Time** to a macro; also map **Beat Division** to that *same* macro (so the synced and free-time behaviors move together). Map the **delay-mode button** (Beat sync / Time) to a separate macro — a performable toggle rather than a fixed choice.

### 3. LFO → the time macro, at "full modulation"
Map LFO to the delay-time macro (Map → click macro). Set **Control = 0.5** (macro's center/default value) and **Amount = 0.5** (swing range from center) — together this is "full modulation" of the mapped macro, the starting point worth trying before hand-tuning further. Switch **Wave = Random** (stepped, unpredictable per-cycle values) and **Rate ≈ 5 Hz**.
- 🎬 *From video:* **Beat sync** delay mode + this LFO setup reads as more rhythmically "locked"/relevant — a crude beat-shuffling effect — than free **Time** mode with the identical LFO settings.
- **Why:** Random wave at a mid-fast rate is what turns smooth modulation into "glitch" — a sine/triangle LFO on the same macro would read as a sweep, not a stutter.

### 4. Feedback macro
Map **Feedback** to its own macro. Higher feedback = a more metallic character layered on top of the LFO's rhythmic chaos — a one-knob "how extreme" control.

### 5. Dry/wet macro — built as a two-chain crossfade, not the Dry/Wet knob
Create a **dry chain** (empty passthrough) and a **wet chain** (the delay) inside the rack. Open the **Chain Select editor**, stretch both chains' zones to span the full 0–127 range, adjust each chain's **fade range** and **zone range** so 0 = fully dry, 127 = fully wet, smooth crossfade between. Map the **chain selector** to a macro.
- **Why this instead of the delay's own Dry/Wet knob:** leaves the rack able to accommodate a *second* delay inside the same wet path later (step 6) — the chain-selector approach scales to more devices, a plain knob doesn't. This is the same mechanism documented generally on Randomized Rack Design as "the chain-volume-fade dry/wet macro."

### 6. Nest a Ping Pong sub-rack for stereo width
Group the mono delay into **its own** audio effect rack (nested inside the outer rack). Inside that inner rack, build a **mono chain** and a **stereo chain** using the same two-chain zone-stretch technique as step 5. Drop a Delay instance in **Ping Pong** mode into the stereo chain, map its time/feedback/mode parameters to the **same macros** already driving the mono delay (both delays track together, no independent control needed), fully expand its **band-pass filter** section, and set its own Dry/Wet to 100% (the outer rack's macro already handles the overall blend).
- **Why:** nested rack + shared macros is the reusable idea — adds a parallel processing variant without duplicating the control surface. → Width and Stereo

### 7. Finishing macros: LFO Rate + Curve
Map the LFO's **Frequency/Rate** to its own macro, ranged **5–30 Hz** (arbitrary starting range). Map the LFO's **Curve** to a second macro, ranged roughly **0.3 and up** — Curve skews the LFO's *output-value distribution*: at 1 unaffected, below 1 more low values, above 1 more high values. Net effect: Rate controls glitch speed, Curve controls whether the randomization leans subtle or extreme.

### 8. Limiter — protect the output
Drop a limiter at the very end of the chain. Jump-mode transitions and high feedback can get loud fast; the limiter is a safety net before pushing the rack to its extremes.

## Delay-mode behaviors (right-click the delay's title bar)

| Mode | Character |
|---|---|
| Re-Pitch | Tape-throw pitch-bend on time changes — smoother, more musical glitch |
| Jump | Audible clicks on every time change — harder mangle/distortion |

## Usage

- **Percussive loop** — the obvious, foundational result (what the build is designed around).
- **Melodic content (piano comp, etc.)** — noticeably subtler than percussion; switching to the Ping Pong/stereo path specifically adds "interesting and busy" movement even here.
- **Full song / mix** (both rhythmic and harmonic elements present) — produces the wildest, most extreme results of the three source types.

## Variations

- **Skip the Ping Pong nesting for a lighter/mono-only build** — steps 1–5 alone (delay + LFO + feedback + dry/wet macro) already deliver the core glitch character; the nested stereo rack is an add-on for width, not a prerequisite.
- **Swap Random for Sample & Hold or a custom shape** — the general LFO-on-delay-time mechanism generalizes beyond Random wave; see Delay and Randomized Rack Design for related LFO-on-delay techniques from other sources (S&H random-slicer, Stray-shape vinyl wobble).
- **As a send instead of an insert** — the video builds this as a track insert; nothing about the macro/chain structure prevents running it on a return the way [Delay Send Other](#/chain/delay-send-other) does, if the goal is a shared glitch texture across multiple tracks.

## From videos

- **A genuine "happy accident" alternative to a designed glitch rack: push a synth-into-delay signal chain past the software's real-time calculation limit for real, unrepeatable glitches.** Justice ran a mono synth through a digital delay and sped the tempo up until Ableton's delay could no longer calculate the taps in real time — the resulting glitches are a literal one-take recording of the software failing to keep up, not a simulated effect. Deliberately used for a specific dramatic goal (turning a "sunny" outro into "a feverish nightmare"), and kept once discovered — an example of treating a genuine technical limitation as a compositional device rather than a bug to avoid. Distinct from this rack's LFO-on-delay-time approach: no macro control, no repeatability, found by pushing a real signal chain past breaking rather than designed. — Justice, Behind the Track - 'Dear Alan' by Justice

## Notes

- All-stock-plugin build (LFO 2.0 is free Ableton content) — nothing to add to Plugin Wishlist from this video.
- Sibling technique: Randomized Rack Design documents the chain-volume-fade dry/wet macro and nested-rack-shared-macros patterns generally (that note's other examples are sourced from a separate, later dnksaus video — this chain is an earlier worked example of the same core Ableton trick).
- Plugin notes carrying this video's techniques: Delay, LFO.

**Sources:** asd, [Ableton Sound Design | Glitch Delay Audio Effect Rack](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=95e5bfB8th8) — video-derived, 2026-08-11.

chains.title: Sparkle Texture Rack
chains.routing: Track insert (fully wet, no dry pass-through) — Delay/Reverb (tape preset) → [[kHs Pitch Shifter]] (+1 octave) → [[Portal]] (texture) → chorus → half-time → [[EQ Eight]] (low-pass)
chains.reference: loner (YouTube breakdown channel)
chains.body:
**Reference/vibe:** a fully-wet, 6-stage "one or two knob pedal" built from stock/owned plugins to replicate the character of chased-after hardware guitar pedals (Chase Bliss Thermae, Hologram Microcosm, Chase Bliss Blooper, Cooper FX Arcades — pure name-drops in the source, no settings given) without the rarity/cost/learning-curve tax of hunting real hardware down. Built in FL Studio's **Patcher** (a routing/container plugin hosting a chain of other plugins with a custom macro-knob surface); the direct Ableton equivalent is an **Audio Effect Rack** with Macro knobs — see EffectRack for the same "save FX-rack chains as reusable sounds" lesson from a different video, and Randomized Rack Design for the general macro-mapping mechanics. Saved and named "Sparkle" in the source, then dragged onto a fresh 130 BPM perc loop on a new mixer track to prove instant recall.

**Signal source:** built from a mix of stock and owned tools plus two unowned Waves plugins swapped for owned equivalents below — nothing here blocks an owned-tools build.

- Reverb/delay opening stage → owned lane: ValhallaDelay (Tape/BBD mode) or EchoBoy/Kramer Tape feeding Echo.
- Pitch shift → source names "Waves SoundShifter" (unowned, Plugin Wishlist); owned lane kHs Pitch Shifter (±12 semitones covers the octave move).
- Texture stage → **Portal** (owned).
- Chorus stage → owned lane TAL-Chorus-LX or kHs Chorus (source plugin name garbled in captions, "Clever" — unconfirmed, medium confidence).
- Half-time stage → **Cableguys HalfTime** (unowned, Plugin Wishlist) — already the established owned-adjacent gap for every other half-time chain on this vault (see Little AlterBoy, Phaser-Flanger).
- Low-pass EQ → **EQ Eight** (owned, Band 7 set to Low Pass).

## Chain (build order)

### 1. Warm-up build — chorus-modulated reverb (2-3 macros, dry path kept)
Reverb (ValhallaVintageVerb-style) chained output-to-input into a chorus (TAL-Chorus-LX) set to a **flanging preset**. Macros: reverb **Mix**, reverb **Decay**, chorus **Mix** — three knobs. Recreates one feature of the KMA Cirrus hardware pedal ("a chorus modulated reverb setting"). Closing EQ cut on the low end (no exact frequency given). Dry signal stays in parallel with the wet chain throughout.
- **Why the extra chorus instead of the reverb's own internal modulation:** "you can modulate the reverb inside Valhalla but that's not giving you a unique sound, everyone can do that" — an arbitrary second device is what makes the combination personal rather than a factory setting anyone could reach for.

### 2. The full build — fully wet, no dry pass-through
Unlike step 1, this chain drops the dry signal entirely — everything downstream is meant to sit as "more of a textural element on top" of the underlying part, not a replacement for it.

1. **Tape-flavored "space echo" reverb/delay preset** — described only as "nice little reverb, a bit of a tape effect as well." Owned lane: ValhallaDelay Tape/BBD mode.
2. **Pitch shift +1 octave** — owned lane kHs Pitch Shifter (Pitch = +12 semitones, Mix full wet).
3. **Portal** — loaded with a preset from its "pitch" category, "make it super textural."
4. **Chorus** — loaded with a **"vocal chorus" preset**, run fully wet (no dry blend dragged in for this stage either).
5. **Half-time device** (Cableguys HalfTime lane) — its Mix parameter mapped to a macro named **"Half Time,"** the first of only two macros exposed on the whole rack.
6. **Low-pass EQ** (EQ Eight Band 7, Filter Type = Low Pass) — its **Frequency** mapped to the second and last macro.

### 3. Expose only 2 macros on the whole 6-stage chain
- **Half Time** (mix of the half-time stage) and **low-pass cutoff frequency** — those are the ONLY two performable controls; every preset choice and internal setting on stages 1-4 stays baked in and unmapped.
- **Why:** "I want to make this kind of like a one or two knob pedal... this is the effect it's going to give you, but I want to let the person decide" — the design goal is a simple front panel, not a fully-tweakable rack. This is the same "which parameters actually need a macro" discipline already documented generally on Randomized Rack Design and EffectRack.

### 4. Save as a named preset, recall instantly
Save the whole chain (routing + macro mapping) as a single preset ("Sparkle" in the source). Demoed by dragging a fresh perc loop onto a new mixer track in a different project, loading the preset, and immediately having both macros available with zero rebuild — the same "recallable instrument in your palette" payoff already documented on EffectRack.

## Usage

- **Melodic top-line / one-shot texture layer** — the source use case: a piano one-shot run through the full wet chain as a textural overlay on top of a chord progression.
- **Any percussive loop** — demoed working on a 130 BPM perc loop dragged in after the fact, proving the saved preset generalizes beyond the original source material.

## Variations

- **Warm-up build only (step 1)** — the simpler chorus-modulated-reverb chain is a complete, useful "pedal" on its own; the fully-wet 6-stage build in step 2 is the fuller expression, not a prerequisite.
- **Swap the half-time stage's automated engagement** — elsewhere on this vault, the equivalent half-time stage in a Dez Wright wash-out chain (spring reverb → Portal → half-time → EQ, see Portal) has its engagement automated to switch on only in the second half of a loop rather than running constantly; the same automation move applies here if a static Half Time macro reads as too committed.
- **As a send instead of an insert** — the video builds this as a track insert (Patcher on a one-shot's channel); nothing about the macro/chain structure prevents running it on a return if the goal is a shared texture across multiple tracks.

## Notes

- Two unowned Waves plugins named in the source (SoundShifter, and the half-time device — likely Cableguys HalfTime) already have owned-lane substitutes documented above and cross-linked on Plugin Wishlist; nothing here blocks building the chain today with owned tools.
- Plugin notes carrying this video's techniques: ValhallaVintageVerb, TAL-Chorus-LX, Portal, kHs Pitch Shifter, EQ Eight, EffectRack.
- Effect-type pages carrying this video's techniques: Reverb, Modulation, Delay, Pitch and Formant, EQ.

**Sources:** loner, [this secret plugin will change the way you process your melodies!?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xwuodd40bug) — video-derived, 2026-08-11.

chains.title: Master Chain
chains.routing: [all buses] → Master → export
chains.body:
**Role:** The final 10%. If the buses did their jobs, every move here is ±1–2 dB. Two modes: **mix-into-it** (the tonal/glue stages live on the master from early in the mix, so you're always hearing "the record" — the Disclosure/SSL-Fusion habit) and **final loudness** (the last three stages, engaged at export time).

## Chain overview
Corrective EQ → adaptive clarity → glue → tape → imaging → density → clip → limit. Corrective before compression (the comp should react to a balanced signal); limiter dead last, always.

## Session Setup
- 🎬 *From video:* a strong stated preference on which sample rate to work/master in, corroborating and adding nuance to the §3 entry below — **avoid 48 kHz** ("the most digital sounding to me, I hear it every single time... a little strident, a little hard"); **44.1 kHz or 96 kHz preferred** ("so much more musical," "it loves 96"); **88.2 kHz the weak middle option** ("kind of bland, just kind of sits there"). One engineer's consistent ear over a decade of sessions, not a measured claim — full detail on Session Templates. → Session Templates, Critical Listening for Mastering — Jack Joseph Puig (Mix with the Masters), [Listening to the details with Jack Joseph Puig](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=20CbTBdY8sk)
- 🎬 *From video:* a drums-first gain-structure checkpoint with a concrete number, from a working mix (not the mastering session itself, but the discipline that sets this chain's own input up correctly): route the drum bus through an analog-console-emulation stage into a bus compressor and set gain so it **hits the compressor at roughly −1 dB** — since drums are deliberately the loudest element, that reading confirms proper gain structure and guarantees headroom for everything layered in after. Check the 2-bus next: sweet spot **−5 to −6 dB**, leaving ~5 dB of headroom before 0. See Gain Staging for the full recipe. — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), [Mixing Summits with Jaycen Joshua](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L6xx7DWKzng)
- 🎬 *From video:* near-master every section/stem individually BEFORE it ever reaches this chain — drums, hats, instrumental, and vocals each get processed (EQ'd, compressed, limited) close to a finished level on their own, so each one barely nudges the 2-bus when it lands, and this chain's own final limiting stage has almost nothing left to do. The limiter used per-stem for this is framed as **adaptive** rather than threshold-hunting (see Limiting for the full mechanism) — reacts to whatever energy it's given rather than chasing a fixed dB number. Corroborates this chain's own "a limiter should end up doing almost nothing" philosophy (§8 below) from the stem side rather than the final-bus side. → Limiting (effect) — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), [Mixing Summits with Jaycen Joshua](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L6xx7DWKzng)
- 🎬 *From video:* import the stereo mix into a dedicated mastering session at a **minimum of 24-bit / 96 kHz** — even when the mix's own sample rate is lower, mastering at a higher rate reduces the aliasing your own processing (saturation, clipping, limiting) introduces; treat the mix's own settings as a floor, not a ceiling. Before touching any processor, pull in **~5 dB of headroom via clip gain** (not a fader) — a starting point, not a fixed rule — and roughly level-match tracks first if mastering several in one sitting. Signal routing, plainly stated: **file/waveform → inserts → any aux sends/buses → stereo output** — decide the order deliberately since each stage hits the signal in the order it's placed — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)

## Signal chain — mix-into-it stages

### 1. Pro-Q 4 — Corrective
- Natural-phase while mixing (linear-phase only at final export — it costs latency and transient smear)
- HPF 20–25 Hz gentle · fix only *whole-mix* issues (a resonance every element shares); anything else belongs on a bus.
- 🎬 *From video:* the first insert in a mastering chain is consequential — it sets the direction of everything downstream — and there are two valid candidates for it, not just one: **subtractive EQ** (attenuate parts of the spectrum you don't want amplified later — the stated preference, since it "sets me up well for having a successful chain later on," matching this stage's own subtractive-first approach) or a **mastering preamp** (unowned as a hardware/plugin category — see Plugin Wishlist). Keep the move subtle either way — it's mastering, and it's the first insert. — Sage Audio, [How to Make a Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WNkkwWh7DJg)
- 🎬 *From video:* a general ordering discipline for this stage's role — the first EQ insert in a mastering chain is typically **subtractive** (attenuate whatever shouldn't carry forward, stereo L/R or mid-side depending on where the offending content sits), saving **additive** boosts for a later EQ insert once the signal's already been cleaned up; some engineers combine both moves into one first insert instead, a valid variant on this stage's own approach — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)
- 🎬 *From video:* on a lo-fi master, keep this stage minimal on purpose — highpass everything at **20 Hz and below** ("just in case anything got caught," not expected to do much) plus a small dip around **200–250 Hz** to stop the low-mid range congesting once everything sums; explicitly framed as cleanup, not tone-shaping — the genre's whole appeal is not needing the "fancy mixing techniques" a cleaner style would call for here — Max Konyi, [Final Mix & Master | Studio One LoFi Tutorial | Part 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OKUCuyLBSg)
- 🎬 *From video:* treat any master EQ as a **bypassed guide** — do the tiny linear-phase move (mids up, −1 to −1.5 dB super-highs), then screenshot it for the mastering engineer instead of baking it in — Disclosure, [Looking For Love](https://youtu.be/NlJt0pCptGk).
- 🎬 *From video:* a general-purpose corrective-EQ recipe for this stage — linear phase at a **low-latency** setting (minimal pre-ringing, less transient smear than zero-latency), a **side-image-only HPF** (18–24 dB/oct) placed **between the source's fundamental and its 2nd-order harmonic** (makes everything below identical L/R without touching the fundamental), a small dip ~250 Hz (masking/mud), and a small dip in a resonant high-mid pocket (vocal nasal resonance, busy instruments). The source video runs a second EQ pass after dynamics (this chain doesn't have one — §5 Ozone 9 Imager plus this stage cover the same ground) that reapplies the same side-image HPF, since downstream dynamics stages reintroduce side-image lows — worth a quick recheck here if §2–§4 read wide in the lows. — Sage Audio, [The Only Music Mastering Video You'll Ever Need](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M88T8jFL2uU) → Width and Stereo
- 🎬 *From video:* this stage's own gain-staging ceiling and phase mechanism, stated as a general mastering-EQ rule rather than tied to any one move above — never move a band more than **±3 dB** here unless fixing a serious mix problem with no access to revise the mix; normal working range **0.25–2 dB**. Mechanically, this stage's **natural-phase** mode shifts the signal's phase on every boost/cut, and that shift **alters the shape of the curve itself**, not just tone — reach for linear phase (already this stage's own preference at final export, per the top of this section) when precision matters more than a natural feel. When genuinely unsure what a master needs beyond the moves already logged here: a generic starting point is a small boost **~80 Hz**, a small boost **~2 kHz**, a subtle shelf **~5 kHz and up** — louder kick, more prominent vocal, clearer master; not a fit for every mix. — Sage Audio, [How to EQ Your Master](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GF-XMVa3lW8) → EQ
- 🎬 *From video:* two SUBTRACTIVE dynamic-EQ moves that belong right here, at this stage, since dynamic-EQ subtraction is meant to run early in the chain. **Sibilance:** watch the analyzer for high-frequency spikes and match their timing against when an S is actually sung/spoken (confirms it's sibilance, not something else at the same frequency), then center a Dynamic band on the confirmed spot. **Muddiness:** a Dynamic band around **200 Hz**, using the plugin's Isolate/solo tool to pin the exact culprit frequency inside that bell's bandwidth by ear before attenuating — don't drag it too far down the spectrum chasing it, or it starts eating content unrelated to the mud. → EQ, Masking and Carving, De-essing — Sage Audio, [How to Use Dynamic Eq During Mastering](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvuBplNrYMs)
- 🎬 *From video:* a deliberately minimal two-move version of this stage, from a "keep peaks intact" personal chain — **side-image HPF at 12 dB/octave** (gentler slope than this stage's existing linear-phase side-HPF entries above, chosen specifically to keep phase rotation to a minimum while still focusing lows into the center) plus a **mid-image bell dip in the highs** for sibilance, center frequency mix-dependent. Discipline stated alongside it, worth carrying as a general rule for this whole stage: only change the spectrum where it's absolutely needed, since **all EQ types affect transients to some degree**, not just linear-phase — a reason to run this stage's cuts as sparingly as this source does. → EQ — Sage Audio, [My Favorite Mastering Chain - Why Simple is Better](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLVMsAwjRPw)
- 🎬 *From video:* a worked EDM opening mid-side EQ recipe distinct from this stage's other mid/side entries — **side image:** cut lows, boost ~**200 Hz** (where the low-order harmonics that matter sit), high shelf for width; **mid image:** amplify the kick's fundamental, dip a small amount ~**250 Hz** (declutters so higher frequencies read louder), boost ~**3 kHz** for the same reason. Followed immediately in the source by a transient/tonal split-EQ pass (almost certainly Eventide/Soundtheory Split EQ, unowned — see Plugin Wishlist) with **per-band mid-side panning**: lows centered on transients, high-mids' tonal band subtly widened, highs' transients re-centered *and* tonal band widened a good amount — a genuinely new width move beyond this chain's existing mid/side EQ recipes. → Width and Stereo, Plugin Wishlist — Sage Audio, [Creating an EDM Mastering Chain in 10 Steps](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yOJ-EtjFD34)

### 2. Soothe2 — Dynamic unmasking
- **Soft mode** · low-ish depth (this is a master — 2–4 dB of reduction max) · sharpness/selectivity moderate · **fence the low end off** (set the low band edge ~120–150 Hz so it doesn't re-decide your kick/808 balance) · delta-listen to hear only what it's removing, then back off
- Pair with **Tonal Balance Control 2** open as a *meter* (not processing) to catch the broad tonal-balance errors Gullfoss used to auto-correct — nudge those on §1 Pro-Q 4 instead.
- **Why:** Soothe2 dynamically suppresses resonances/masking as they occur (the same "unmask hidden detail, tame buildup only while the problem is present" idea), so the body returns the instant the resonance passes. *(Owned substitute for Gullfoss Master, which isn't licensed — Soothe2 covers the dynamic-unmasking half; Tonal Balance Control 2 + Pro-Q cover the tonal-balance half Gullfoss also did automatically. Note: standard Gullfoss IS owned — see the 🎬 note directly below for a way to use it here alongside/instead of Soothe2.)*
- 🎬 *From video:* run standard Gullfoss (owned, distinct from the unlicensed Gullfoss Master above) isolated to **mids and highs only** — pull the frequency-range limiters in to exclude the kick/low end, since Gullfoss's real-time analysis introduces latency that could smear a transient. Lean mainly on **Recover** to bring buried mix detail forward. (The source captions describe this as "reducing phase cancellation" — that doesn't match Gullfoss's documented mechanism; read it as the plugin's ordinary unmasking job.) — Sage Audio, [How to Master a Song Start to Finish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUygMNRx2yE) → Gullfoss
- 🎬 *From video:* resonance reduction reframed as multiband compression with a preset threshold, not a form of EQ — use the **"Bounce to the Grammy Awards"** preset here, which measures the mid and side images separately so suppression can differ between center and sides; adjust the pre-emphasis EQ bands from there to target whatever's too prevalent (commonly low-mids and the sibilance range, confirm by ear), higher-quality/oversampling settings to reduce phase cancellation, dial the final amount with the mix knob — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)

### 3. Glue Compressor — The glue
- **Ratio 2:1** (②) · **Attack 30 ms** (③ — slow, transients pass) · **Release Auto** (④ — breathes with the tempo) · **Threshold for 1.5 dB GR on the beat** (①) · **Makeup** to exact unity (⑤ — level-matched A/B or it always sounds "better") · **Soft Clip OFF** (⑧ — let the dedicated limiter cap peaks) · **Dry/Wet 100%** (⑦)
- **Why:** The SSL-bus-comp move — 1.5 dB of slow stereo compression is what makes a collection of buses sound like *a record*. More than 2–3 dB here means a bus is too hot upstream — fix it there, not with the glue comp.
- 🎬 *From video:* BPM-time the release — the actual formula, not just "match the tempo": `60,000 ÷ BPM = one quarter note in ms`, ×4 for a whole note, minus the attack time = the release (140 BPM example: 429 ms → 1,716 ms whole note, minus attack). An out-of-time release makes the return-to-unity land like a rogue transient and can mess up perceived timing. Pairs with a vari-mu character compressor for tone (not owned, see Plugin Wishlist) — this stage's Soft Clip is the closest owned stand-in for the harmonic-coloration half — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)
- 🎬 *From video:* when a kick dominates this stage's gain reduction on a kick-heavy mix, filter the compressor's own detector — a **self-sidechain highpass at ~70 Hz** — rather than reaching for an external sidechain track; the kick's dominant low end stops driving the compressor by itself while everything above 70 Hz (including the kick's own transient content) still triggers it normally. Worked settings on a gentle lo-fi glue pass: ratio 2:1, attack ~100 ms, release ~100 ms (slow enough that individual transients pass through), target only 2–3 dB GR max, landing ~2 dB with the self-sidechain filter engaged — Max Konyi, [Final Mix & Master | Studio One LoFi Tutorial | Part 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OKUCuyLBSg) → Sidechaining, Compression
- 🎬 *From video:* a mastering-specific target for this stage — **1–2 dB total, Peak/RMS switch biased toward RMS with a little Peak blended in**, tuned so it's inaudible as compression, just quieter. The point: keeping this stage this light shrinks §8's job down to a few dB, which is what keeps the limiter itself from sounding noticeable. — Sage Audio, [The Only Music Mastering Video You'll Ever Need](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M88T8jFL2uU)
- 🎬 *From video:* whether to compress at this stage at all is a real question, not a given — mastering compression is often debated and should be used **only if the master actually needs it**. When it is warranted, compressor *type* sets the character: **optical** reads smooth/gentle (good for a subtle glue pass, matching this stage's own light-touch settings above), **digital** reads more aggressive (better suited to louder/harder genres) — pick the type for the genre before dialing in the settings above — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)
- 🎬 *From video:* an alternative to this stage's plain glue setting — **mid-side processing with de-linked triggering**, so the mid image compresses more than the side (mid usually drives the detector more), reading as stereo expansion without ever isolating processing to the mid alone. Paired feature on the source unit: **"dual phase rotation"** — mild phase cancellation introduced at higher frequencies, netting a fuller-sounding low end as a side effect; worth trying on any owned M/S-capable bus compressor even without a name match (source plugin unclear from captions — see Plugin Wishlist). — Sage Audio, [How to Master a Song Start to Finish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUygMNRx2yE) → Width and Stereo
- 🎬 *From video:* glue isn't only what THIS stage does — it's also a function of which buses/groups get routed together upstream. Rafa Sardina runs a hardware SSL/summing-box hybrid where "glue you also create with your choices of summing, your choices [of] share compression, [routing] certain elements in the mix" — routing drums and bass through the same bus for a blended feel, a separate bus for a more distinct part. Ableton-native equivalent: which tracks share a Group/return, not just what sits on this master stage, is itself a glue decision — made early, at song-evaluation time. His own master-stage glue chain (SSL-style comp + a subtractive GML-style EQ cutting ~300 Hz, a small additive Sontec-style "flavor" boost ~1 kHz) runs from EARLY in the mix, the same "mix-into-it" mode this chain documents at the top of this section — not just at export. → Session Templates, Masking and Carving, EQ — Mix with the Masters (Rafa Sardina), Rafa Sardina's mixing workflow
- 🎬 *From video:* the SSL-bus-comp move taken further — as ONE of several parallel stereo buses (a "multibus" setup, not this chain's single-glue-stage default) each doing a little, summed together. Checked at the loudest chorus, GR reads "barely three [dB]" at **30 ms / 4:1 ratio / 0.1 s release** — fast enough to never audibly hold the signal — paired with a second parallel-blend compressor run mostly dry and a passive tube EQ engaged for its circuit coloration alone, no EQ move dialed in. The driving constraint: an explicit brief to avoid sounding "overly compressed." Full structure (multiple simultaneous parallel buses, doubling via a second bus, the bypassed-vs-engaged A/B demo method) on Parallel Processing. → Solid Bus Comp, UAD Pultec EQP-1A, Parallel Processing, Compression — Michael Brauer (Mix with the Masters), The power of multi-bus processing with Michael Brauer

### 4. Kramer Tape — Tape finish
- **15 ips** (④) · **Flux very low** (① — barely driven) · **Record ~+1** (②) · **Playback to unity** (③) · **Wow & Flutter off** (⑥) · **Noise off** (⑦)
- **Why:** Final rounding — top-end sweetening + gentle transient softening that reads as "expensive."
- 🎬 *From video:* a hardware validation of this exact stage — bussing several tracks to a physical tape deck together and consolidating them to a stereo pass produces glue credited specifically to "tape's compression and saturation," the same principle this plugin runs here, just done earlier and on hardware. Also worth remembering: an A/B test found an all-digital mix of the same song read as *more* characterful than the tape-printed version — most of what reads as "warmth" gets decided upstream of this stage, not created by it. See Committing and Printing — Zach Scholz, [Using Analog Tape to Glue a Mix Together](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xk0LYE7HGAI) & [Why 70's Records Sound so Warm](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6eGa5NOTYg)

### 5. Ozone 9 Imager — Imaging
- Band 1 (<120 Hz): width DOWN to 0 (mono low end — punch and vinyl/club safety) · top band: +5–10% width max if the mix needs it
- **Why:** Frequency-dependent width is the safe kind: mono where power lives, wide where sparkle lives.
- 🎬 *From video:* measured research puts a hard number on "safe" width — commercial masters keep L/R RMS within **0.8 dB** of each other, expansion above 200 Hz is fine but small at this stage, and any expansion here should be an M/S-balance/EQ move (this stage), never delay-based — a demonstrated A/B showed a delay-based expander losing focus on centered elements (lead vocal/bass/kick/snare) where an EQ-based side-image boost didn't. Amplify what's already there in the side image rather than manufacture new inter-channel differences. — Sage Audio, [Audio Mastering Science: Using Research to Make Informed Decisions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21dpmumO4So) → Width and Stereo
- 🎬 *From video:* a third additive mid-side EQ recipe for this stage, distinct from the two boost/attenuate recipes below — ear-sensitivity-driven rather than phase-driven. Amplify the **side image's highs and mid frequencies**, amplify **3–5 kHz on the mid** (the range ears are most sensitive to — reads as an overall louder mix without more gain), and optionally amplify **the kick's fundamental**. Placed after the corrective/de-essing/dynamics stages, same "additive EQ goes later" sequencing this chain already follows at §1. → EQ — Sage Audio, [How to Make a Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WNkkwWh7DJg)
- 🎬 *From video:* a mid/side EQ width recipe pairing a matched boost/attenuate move rather than boosting the side alone — boost the **mid** image at **~80 Hz** (kick) and **~2 kHz** (vocal), then **attenuate the side image at those same two frequencies** to reduce phase cancellation between the mid and side content; separately, a **high shelf on the side image** widens perceived top end "more times than not." Distinct from this stage's existing mid/side EQ entries (which pair a side HPF + mid ~2.5 kHz boost, no matching side attenuation) — a genuine alternative recipe, worth A/B'ing rather than a straight replacement. → Width and Stereo — Sage Audio, [How to EQ Your Master](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GF-XMVa3lW8)
- 🎬 *From video:* four ADDITIVE dynamic-EQ moves that belong at this point in the chain — after §3/§4's compression and saturation, per this chain's own additive-dynamic-EQ sequencing rule (§1, and see EQ). **Kick:** a Dynamic bell centered on the kick's most prominent spectrum frequency, expanded **+3 dB** above the filter. **Vocal:** the same expansion mechanism, bell at **~2 kHz** on the mid/stereo channel, triggers whenever the vocal is sung. **Width:** a Dynamic shelf on the **side image ~7 kHz+**, range ~2 dB, expanding only when high-frequency content is present — dynamic width rather than this stage's own static Imager settings above. **Mid-range power:** a Dynamic band on the mid frequencies reads differently by placement — mid image makes drums/vocal more dynamic/impressive, side image makes guitar body and reverb tails more dynamic; worth balancing both. → Pro-Q 4, Kick Design, Masking and Carving — Sage Audio, [How to Use Dynamic Eq During Mastering](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvuBplNrYMs)

## Signal chain — final loudness stages (export time)

### 6. Oxford Inflator — Density
- Effect 15–30%, Curve 0 — perceived loudness before any GR is spent.
- 🎬 *From video:* a developer-recommended operating method for this stage, distinct from its existing Effect-15–30%/Curve-0 setting above — **Effect to 100, then use Input to dial how aggressive the processing reads**, rather than a low fixed Effect amount. Framed as prioritizing signal content with a positive value over content with a negative value, raising the ratio of signal-to-silence — the same upward-processing mechanism this stage already runs, just driven from the opposite end of the Effect knob. Worth A/B'ing against the existing setting rather than a straight swap. — Sage Audio, [How to Make a Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WNkkwWh7DJg)
- 🎬 *From video:* Disclosure's current master is basically **just this + a clipper** — Inflator does the upward loudness, no EQ or comp on the bus — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).
- 🎬 *From video (optional, rare):* **if — and only if — a mix reads disjointed rather than cohesive** (elements sound like they were recorded in different rooms), a subtle reverb send can go **right here** — after this stage's upward compression, before §7's clipper and §8's peak limiter — following a mastering-reverb tip: dial the send in with the limiter engaged (its makeup gain exposes tails that seemed subtle unlimited), check both loud and sparse sections and automate the send if no one level covers both, and use a realistic convolution reverb (Hybrid Reverb) or one with EQ + early/mid/late reflection control (ValhallaRoom) to boost cohesion only in the specific bands/reflection stages that sound disjointed. Never reach for this if the mix is already too blurred/masked — it will only make that worse. — Sage Audio, [Reverb on a Master: Everything You Need to Know](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vzJSKU7kGrU) → Reverb, Depth and Space
- 🎬 *From video:* the mechanical reason this stage exists as a separate step from saturation and the §8 limiter — **upward processing reshapes the wave from its quietest points up**, preserving timbre/transient impact while adding loudness, vs. saturation (reshapes peaks) or limiting (retains peak shape, uses clean gain). Named alternatives for this exact slot, each with a different harmonic flavor: PSP Vintage Warmer 2's knee function, the Weiss MM-1 Maximizer (Softube) — neither owned, see Plugin Wishlist. — Sage Audio, [The Only Music Mastering Video You'll Ever Need](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M88T8jFL2uU) → Saturation and Distortion
- 🎬 *From video:* mechanically, this stage doesn't work like a clipper — it pushes quieter signal upward, then gradually/gently rounds the amplitude down as it nears 0 dB rather than squaring the waveform; some call it a "soft clipper" but the wave-shaping is far more gradual than a clip's flat-topped squaring — Sage Audio, [Stop Limiting Your Masters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s_LDCzWx20g) → Clipping and Loudness
- 🎬 *From video:* whichever saturation source this stage (or a parallel saturator alongside it) uses — tape, tube, transistor, or otherwise, each with its own harmonic "clarity"/character flavor — keep it **subtle** at the mastering stage specifically (overdone saturation here reads as unpleasant distortion, not glue), and if the plugin offers it, **enable 2x-or-more oversampling** so the added harmonics don't alias — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)
- 🎬 *From video:* pair this stage with a frequency-split parallel saturator for a two-tool density move — this stage does overall density (increase Effect, adjust Input to compensate), then a parallel valve/tube saturator (PSP per captions, exact model unclear, see Plugin Wishlist) split so its low section targets the **kick's fundamental** specifically and its high section targets **vocal presence** specifically, not a generic wide low/high split. Result: the whole mix reads fuller from this stage while the kick and vocal specifically get more prominent from the saturator's targeted split. — Sage Audio, [How to Master a Song Start to Finish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUygMNRx2yE) → Saturation and Distortion
- 🎬 *From video:* a direct mechanical comparison between this stage and the (unowned) Sonnox Oxford Limiter's Enhance function, answering a question the source says comes up often — **Enhance is the same processing as this stage with Curve set to 50**, but the two units land differently: this stage's harmonics run higher in amplitude in the lows and much subtler in the highs, while Enhance reads more balanced overall with extra emphasis on high-frequency harmonics that "tie the high range back in to the song's root note." Sharpens the Inflator-vs-Enhance comparison already logged on Plugin Wishlist with a concrete parameter match (Curve 50) rather than a general "similar processing" note. → Plugin Wishlist — Sage Audio, [My Favorite Mastering Chain - Why Simple is Better](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLVMsAwjRPw)

### 7. kHs Clipper — Clip the peaks
- **Hard-clip mode** (② — Hardness max) — **Input to shave 1–2 dB** of transient peak (①). Hard clip = transparent (everything under the ceiling untouched, odd harmonics only on the shaved samples); soft clip = audible rounding/warmth — a tone choice, not a headroom tool.
- Aliasing paranoia is overblown here: clipping happens on transients, which mask it completely. But **beware oversampling** — enable kHs Clipper's oversampling and **verify with a true-/sample-peak meter** that the downsampling isn't recreating overs and silently eating the headroom you just made. *(Owned substitute for Gold Clip. If you need a guaranteed true-peak ceiling over a clipper's character, Pro-L 2 in transparent mode is the owned fallback — but a limiter rounds transients where a clipper shaves them, so keep the clipper unless overs sneak through.)*
- **Why:** Clipping micro-transients (inaudible) hands the limiter a smaller job — the modern loudness recipe is clipper+limiter sharing the work, each doing what it's transparent at.
- 🎬 *From video:* lean on the clipper for loudness and let mix-wide saturation carry the rest — "enough saturation across the mix already, then clip; the clip *is* saturation." Keep tape on drums/bass, not here — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8).

### 8. Ozone 9 Maximizer — The limiter
- IRC IV · **ceiling −1.0 dBTP** (true peak — prevents streaming-codec clip) · push threshold for **2–3 dB GR max** on the loudest section
- 🎬 *From video:* this stage's role in a reactive, two-limiter stereo-bus pass — engage it only after listening confirms the bus needs it ("it's a reactive thing... I love to listen to music first and see if something needs something"), and when it's warranted, run Ozone 9 Equalizer with barely-there moves first (+0.3 dB ~80 Hz, +0.8 dB ~8 kHz) before this Maximizer module, for "a little more beef" rather than raw loudness. Paired ahead of both, an unowned Waves L2 Ultramaximizer (Threshold **−2.6** — see Plugin Wishlist) does the first light pass; A/B'd bypassed vs. engaged, the combination read as harder-hitting and clearer without sounding heavy. Full ears-first framing behind the "listen before reaching for a processor" habit: Critical Listening for Mastering. → Ozone 9 Equalizer, Plugin Wishlist — Neal Pogue (Mix with the Masters), Understanding Kaytranada's vision with Neal Pogue

- 🎬 *From video:* the mechanical reason this stage's ~50 ms release floor (below) isn't arbitrary — a frequency's period is `1 ÷ frequency`, so 20 Hz (bottom of human hearing) works out to a 50 ms period; set the release *shorter* than that and it can alter a wave's amplitude mid-cycle (audible distortion), so 50 ms is a floor for full-range accuracy, not a target to undercut. Aliasing gets the same "why" here too: exceeding the frequency ceiling a low session sample rate (44.1 kHz) can represent reflects the excess back down the spectrum as harsh distortion — the mechanism behind this stage's own oversampling note above. → Limiting, Pro-L 2 — Sage Audio, [How to Master Loud and Clear Without Sounding Harsh](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cy-S6YmVe2U)
- 🎬 *From video:* aggressive limiting is one of the more likely places in the whole chain to introduce aliasing — since this stage does the most nonlinear work of any stage here, **enable oversampling specifically at this stage** if the limiter offers it, not just as general practice elsewhere in the chain — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)
- 🎬 *From video:* a concrete release-time ladder for this stage, faster than this chain's own ">100 ms" target above — 50 ms is the sweet spot for a loud master without introducing distortion, faster mildly-to-moderately distorts, 250 ms+ for smoother, 5–10 ms for maximum loudness if some distortion is acceptable; and a mechanical note on the Attack control specifically — a limiter's true attack is always near-instant, what the Attack knob actually sets is the time before the release envelope begins (quicker = less distortion, longer = louder). *Tension flag: the 50 ms figure sits below this chain's own "release above 100 ms" target elsewhere on this stage — worth A/B'ing both, not a default swap.* → Limiting, Pro-L 2 — Sage Audio, [How to Limit Your Master](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SrFwQqDMJQM)
- 🎬 *From video:* on a simple lo-fi master with no dedicated clipper stage, push the limiter's **input gain up** until GR on the loudest hits lands ~2–3 dB (matching whatever the glue comp above already targeted), then pull the **ceiling back an extra ~1 dB** below 0 dBTP as insurance against **intersample peaks** — true-peak overs that MP3/lossy export can introduce even on a file that measures clean on a sample-peak meter. If the kick alone is still pushing the loudest reduction, trim the kick's own fader ~1–1.5 dB rather than fighting it purely at the limiter, then add a small amount back at the limiter's input (~1 dB) to recover the lost loudness — a two-knob back-and-forth (source level vs. limiter drive), not a single "crank the limiter" move — Max Konyi, [Final Mix & Master | Studio One LoFi Tutorial | Part 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OKUCuyLBSg) → Limiting, Clipping and Loudness
- 🎬 *From video:* keep channels **linked (or mostly linked)** here — the research reason, not just habit: commercial masters measure with L/R RMS within **0.8 dB** of each other, and unlinked/independent-channel limiting is exactly the kind of processing that can push a channel outside that range by attenuating one side more than the other. Same logic rules out L/R-differential EQ anywhere upstream of this stage. — Sage Audio, [Audio Mastering Science: Using Research to Make Informed Decisions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21dpmumO4So) → Width and Stereo
- 🎬 *From video:* a tool-agnostic target for this stage — **release above 100 ms, channel link ~60–80%, max 3 dB of attenuation.** If more GR than that is needed to hit an LUFS target, the fix is upstream (more upward processing at §6, more peak attenuation) rather than pushing Threshold harder here. After limiting, re-listen rather than trust a number — if the quiet detail pushed forward doesn't sound right, revisit §1/this-pass's tone EQ, not this device. — Sage Audio, [The Only Music Mastering Video You'll Ever Need](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M88T8jFL2uU)

## Monitoring
- Meter sandwich per [FX Chain System](#/chains/system) + Stereo Tool or Utility mono-flip for compatibility checks · A/B against 2–3 reference tracks **loudness-matched** (level-matched A/B is the only honest A/B).
- 🎬 *From video:* after limiting, check **LUFS and dB true peak separately** on a metering plugin — they measure different things and neither substitutes for the other; LUFS is the master's loudness, dB true peak is its actual ceiling risk. If true peak reads above 0 dBTP, go back and pull the limiter's output ceiling down rather than trusting the LUFS number alone. General streaming-safe starting range (wider than this chain's own tighter −9 to −7 LUFS-I pop/trap target above): **−14 to −8 LUFS integrated**, **−2 to −0.5 dBTP** — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)

## Export
