Favor mastering plugins with both input AND output meters so an over-hot handoff between stages gets caught immediately. Most plugins run 64-bit internally (signal can swing above 0 dB inside the plugin without clipping — it only matters at the actual output), which doesn't excuse skipping careful metering. And once §8's limiter is in the chain, go back and re-judge EQ/saturation calls made earlier (§1, §6, §7) — ears read frequency balance differently at different loudness levels, so a boost or a touch of distortion that sounded fine mastering quiet can read as harsh once the limiter makes the master louder. See §8's inline note above for this source's basic oversampling+lookahead+true-peak recipe and its −1/−2 dBTP lossy-export reminder. → Gain Staging, Limiting, Clipping and Loudness — Sage Audio, [How to Gain Stage Your Master](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WW4bnNi4DAA)
- **A rapid-fire limiter checklist covering the same §8 stage from a different angle than the chain's other limiter sources: ranked picks, attenuation ceiling, release ladder, attack-control mechanics, true-peak stance, oversampling, and a new mid-side stereo-expansion route.** Ranked limiter picks (opinion): free — Limiter No. 6; introductory — Waves L1; versatile — Pro-L 2 (owned); detail-retaining — Newfangled Audio Elevate; overall-sounding — Voxengo Elephant. Attenuation: typically stay under 5–6 dB GR, reach for pre-limiter compression instead of pushing harder if more loudness is needed — a looser number than this chain's own "max 3 dB" §8 target. Release: 50 ms sweet spot / faster distorts / 250 ms+ smoother / 5–10 ms max-loud-with-distortion — faster than this chain's own ">100 ms" §8 target (see the inline note above). Attack: always near-instant on a limiter regardless of the knob; the control actually sets time-before-release-envelope. True-peak: skip it, pull the ceiling down + oversample + short lookahead instead, restating this chain's existing contrarian stance. New here: **mid-side limiting** — attenuate the mid image harder than the side — as a second stereo-expansion route alongside the already-documented channel-unlinking/dual-mono technique. → Limiting, Pro-L 2, Width and Stereo, Plugin Wishlist — Sage Audio, [How to Limit Your Master](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SrFwQqDMJQM)
- **A from-scratch mastering-chain setup walkthrough — session prep, routing order, and the four-stage EQ → saturation → compression → limiting flow, sourced whole.** Distinct from this chain's other Sage Audio sources in being a setup/fundamentals overview rather than a deep-dive on one technique: session at **24-bit/96 kHz minimum** (reduces processing-induced aliasing) with **~5 dB of clip-gain headroom** before any processing; signal routing stated plainly as file → inserts → aux sends/buses → stereo output; first EQ insert subtractive/corrective, additive EQ later; saturation kept subtle with 2x+ oversampling; compression only if the master needs it (optical for smooth/subtle, digital for aggressive genres); limiter oversampling flagged as an aliasing-specific concern; post-limiter, LUFS and dB true peak checked separately (streaming-safe starting range −14 to −8 LUFS, −2 to −0.5 dBTP); export as three versions (archival high-res, per-service streaming spec, 320 kbps for sharing/promo). See the inline 🎬 notes on §1, §3, §6, and §8 above, plus the Session Setup, Monitoring, and Export sections. → EQ, Saturation and Distortion, Compression, Limiting, Clipping and Loudness — Sage Audio, [How to Setup Your Mastering Chain](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y-5B4kOXUoM)
- **A dedicated limiter-only breakdown gives this chain's two-limiter finish (§8's Wolfgang Gartner/Sonnox+Pro-L 2 entries) distinct, named roles per instance instead of just "split the GR."** Limiter 1's job: attenuate peaks by about 2 dB. Limiter 2's job: increase perceived loudness. Same ceiling/look-ahead/oversampling settings on both — see the concrete non-true-peak recipe on Pro-L 2 (ceiling −0.5 to −1 dB, 0.1 ms look-ahead, 4x+ oversampling) — and deliberately mix limiter *types* across the two instances to combine their distinct timbres. → Limiting, Pro-L 2 — Sage Audio, [Limiter Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LZxglknf3xA)
- **A complete, single-pass mastering-chain shape sourced whole — de-essing first, then band-linked masking EQ, dynamic-EQ-as-expander, upward processing + targeted split saturation, two optional cohesion sends, de-linked M/S bus comp, adaptive clarity, late tone EQ, then a dual-limiter finish.** Distinct from this chain's own 8-stage default and from the "minimal 5-stage" model already logged below — narrated as one continuous pass rather than a menu, useful as a sanity check on stage order. In sequence: (1) a mid-side de-esser (shelf+bell, subtle, few dB max — mid gets attenuated more than the side, with an incidental side-image width bump as a byproduct); (2) a 4-band dynamic EQ where one band's level triggers a *different* band's gain reduction (250 Hz ducked whenever a 2.5 kHz trigger band crosses threshold — 250 Hz masks 2.5 kHz) plus a second de-essing bell; (3) the same dynamic-EQ mechanism run as an *expander* — a mid-image bell over the kick's fundamental and a side-image shelf over the highs, both set to expand instead of attenuate, for more dynamic lows and wider highs; (4) Oxford Inflator for overall density paired with a frequency-split parallel saturator (kick fundamental low / vocal presence high — see this chain's own §6 note); (5)/(6) two optional aux sends — a 100%-wet "collective" reverb blended via the aux fader, and a mid-frequency upward-processing aux that *also* feeds that same reverb aux for cohesion; (7) mid-side bus compression with de-linked triggering + a "dual phase rotation" fuller-lows feature (see this chain's own §3 note); (8) Gullfoss isolated to mids/highs, Recover-led (see this chain's own §2 note); (9) late Pultec-style tone shaping — small boosts/dips only, after clarity work is already done (16 kHz air, 700 Hz dip, 3 kHz boost); (10) two limiters in series (Oxford Limiter → Pro-L 2) with true-peak mode avoided in favor of oversampling + low lookahead; (11) a loudness check landing ~−10 LUFS integrated. → De-essing, EQ, Masking and Carving, Width and Stereo, Saturation and Distortion, Reverb, Parallel Processing, Gullfoss, UAD Pultec EQP-1A, Limiting, Clipping and Loudness — Sage Audio, [How to Master a Song Start to Finish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUygMNRx2yE)
- **Mid/side saturation as a master-bus option distinct from §4's Kramer Tape stage — saturate the mid image's lows for a more centered low end, the side image's highs for expanded stereo highs.** Not currently a chain stage (§4 tape saturation isn't mid/side-routed); worth trying as an alternate/additional pass via Roar's native mid/side mode or Stereo Tool's Mid Sat/Side Sat before or after §4, when a master needs width from harmonics rather than from §5's imager. The manual routing behind this (duplicate the channel, one S1 MS Matrix/Ghz Midside Matrix 3 instance per image) is also the general mechanism for putting any non-M/S plugin — including a de-esser or transient shaper — into mid/side on this chain. → Roar, Stereo Tool, Width and Stereo, Saturation and Distortion — Sage Audio, [Mid Side Masterclass](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SHxih1xc5yM)
- **Multiband compression as dynamic EQ, and tuned to mimic how the human ear compresses loud sound.** Two mastering-EQ-shaped moves, both on Pro-MB: dynamically duck a problem band only when it's actually loud instead of statically (worked examples: 250 Hz, 1–2 dB on a muddy mix with buried vocals; 2–5 kHz on the side image only when reverb masks the vocal); and, separately, tune a band below 1 kHz to attack 40 ms/release 150 ms with a soft knee, no lookahead — reproducing how the ear's own compression response works (below 1 kHz, 1–20 dB depending on loudness, ~40 ms to engage, ~150 ms held), which reads as more naturally "compressed" than an arbitrary setting. → Pro-MB, Multiband Compression, Masking and Carving — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)
- **Mastering-stage de-essing — a stage this chain doesn't otherwise carry, since Nate's vocal chains de-ess long before mastering.** Sibilant energy at this stage usually sits 5–8 kHz (confirm by ear/spectrum). Set threshold carefully — too loose and it attenuates unrelated high end (cymbals, air) whenever it triggers, not just the sibilant; the correctness check is listening for whether attenuation fires *with* the sibilant specifically. Worth a pass here if the mix hand-off carries any residual harshness Pro-DS on individual vocal tracks didn't catch; multiband compression (Pro-MB) is a valid substitute for a dedicated de-esser at this stage too. → Pro-DS, De-essing — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)
- **A second, independent Sage Audio video runs mastering-stage de-essing as the very FIRST move in the whole chain, and specifically in mid-side mode.** Shelf + Bell filters, subtle attenuation (a few dB max); because it's mid-side, the mid image gets attenuated more than the side, giving both more accurate de-essing on centered content and an incidental, subtle expansion of the side image's highs as a byproduct. Corroborates the entry above on *why* this stage matters even though Nate's vocal chains de-ess earlier — worth running first rather than last if a hand-off still carries residual sibilance. → Pro-DS, De-essing, Width and Stereo — Sage Audio, [How to Master a Song Start to Finish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUygMNRx2yE)
- **Dynamic EQ to attenuate out-of-key frequencies — a musicality pass, distinct from §1's corrective EQ work.** In-key content reads relatively louder (and more musical) once out-of-key frequencies get gently ducked. Workflow on Pro-Q 4: a free online tuner/key analyzer finds the key, look up in-vs-out-of-key frequencies, the piano roll snaps a band's center frequency exactly to a note, enable Dynamic EQ per band, target 0.5–1 dB of attenuation, keep Q narrow so the cut lands mostly on the out-of-key note. A worthwhile final musicality check once §1–§8 are otherwise settled, not a replacement for any existing stage. → Pro-Q 4, EQ — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)
- **Mid-image-only compression as a stereo-width move — a mechanism distinct from §5 Ozone 9 Imager's EQ-based approach.** With a mid/side-capable compressor, attenuate only the mid (center) image by 0.5–1.5 dB and skip makeup gain (which would cancel the relative-loudness shift the trick depends on) — the sides read louder *relative* to the now-quieter center, expanding the stereo image without ever boosting the sides directly. Frequency-specific version on owned Pro-MB (Stereo Placement set to Mid on the target band) so only certain bands widen. A genuinely different width tool from §5's imager, worth trying when Imager alone isn't giving the width a mix needs. → Width and Stereo, Pro-MB — Sage Audio, [Mastering Compression Settings](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YUn31aE9X_8)
- **The case against brick-wall limiting as this chain's final stage, and what to reach for instead when transient impact matters more than loudness.** A limiter's look-ahead lets it see peaks coming and attenuate exactly there — its only real benefit is letting you push more input gain (amplifying quiet detail, the actual "loudness" trick), but it *always* shaves the peak, which is what reads as blurred transients no matter how good the specific algorithm is. See the Variations entry above for a parallel-compression/saturation alternative to §6–§8 built from this video. → Clipping and Loudness, Limiting, Parallel Processing — Sage Audio, [Stop Limiting Your Masters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s_LDCzWx20g)
- **A minimal 5-stage mastering-chain model, sourced whole: EQ → RMS-leaning compressor → upward processor (+ optional saturator) → tone EQ → limiter — the same shape as this chain's own corrective-EQ-first/limiter-last structure, condensed to 5 stages instead of 8.** The stated design principle behind the order: make each stage's setting *effective* on its own so a later stage never has to undo what an earlier one did — more conflicting processing compounds into more processing needed to fix it, and a more processed, unpleasant sound. Concrete targets at each stage: EQ pass 1 corrective (linear-phase low-latency, side-image HPF between fundamental and 2nd harmonic, ~250 Hz dip, high-mid resonance dip); RMS compressor 1–2 dB total, RMS-biased blend (maps onto §3 Glue Compressor's Peak/RMS switch); upward processor bringing up quiet detail without hitting the limiter hard (maps onto §6 Oxford Inflator); EQ pass 2 tonal (repeat the side-image HPF, dip/boost as needed, side-image bell for width, side/mid air-frequency choice); limiter last and light (release >100 ms, link 60–80%, max 3 dB GR — maps onto §8 Ozone 9 Maximizer/Pro-L 2). See the inline 🎬 notes on §1, §3, §6, and §8 above for the full per-stage detail. → EQ, Compression, Saturation and Distortion, Limiting, Width and Stereo — Sage Audio, [The Only Music Mastering Video You'll Ever Need](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M88T8jFL2uU)
- **A research-driven QC pass to run on a master occasionally (not every session): check dynamic range, stereo width, and reverb level against published/measured targets instead of ear-only judgment.** Dynamic range: a 2014 AES paper (Pastana & Rice, 928 commercially successful songs) measured peak:RMS crest factor per octave at ~16:1 in the lows up to ~28:1 in the highs — split the master into 3 wide bands (a free tool like Isolate), solo each with a peak+RMS meter, and compress a band that's too dynamic or expand one that's over-squashed relative to the target. Stereo width: the same measurement approach on commercial masters found L/R RMS deviates by at most 0.8 dB — keep this stage (§5) and the limiter (§8) channel-linked/non-differential to stay inside that. Reverb: a blind study (30 listeners) found −9 LU below the dry signal is the most popular reverb level — and because this chain's own dynamics stages (glue comp, clipper, limiter makeup gain) amplify quiet detail including reverb tails, reverb should be set a touch low pre-mastering rather than corrected here, since there's no reliable way to isolate and fix it from a finished stereo file. → Multiband Compression, Width and Stereo, Reverb, Clipping and Loudness — Sage Audio, [Audio Mastering Science: Using Research to Make Informed Decisions](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21dpmumO4So)
- **Reverb-on-master is a rare, conditional cohesion move — a decision spectrum, a chain-position rule, and an EQ reframe.** Only reach for reverb on the master bus when the mix reads *disjointed* (elements sound recorded in different spaces) — never when it's already too blurred/masked (more reverb there only worsens it). When it's warranted: insert it after upward compression, before peak limiting (§6/§7 boundary above), and dial the level in with the limiter engaged — its makeup gain exposes reverb tails that read as subtle unlimited; check both loud and sparse sections and automate the send if no one level covers both. Pick a reverb with an EQ section and use it to boost/cut *cohesion* per frequency band (not tone) — e.g. only the specific ranges (worked example: ~1.5 kHz and ~6 kHz) that sound disjointed — and one with controllable early/mid/late reflections to fill gaps in perceived depth rather than adding a generic wash. Keep it very subtle, same "a little goes a long way" discipline as the glue-comp stage. → Reverb, ValhallaRoom, Hybrid Reverb, Depth and Space, Automation, Limiting — Sage Audio, [Reverb on a Master: Everything You Need to Know](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vzJSKU7kGrU)
- **Automate the master volume to get subliminally louder across the song, and ride the breakdowns down.** The master fader creeps up through the song (e.g. +0.21 dB by the final drop, a further +0.3-0.5 dB bump into the last drop) so it feels quietly louder as it plays; breakdowns get pulled down (roughly −2 dB) and ramped back up in a short automation move right before the drop hits. Final limiter chain: a first limiter doing light gain reduction (~1-2 dB) feeding a second doing more (~1-2 dB more), splitting the loudness push across two limiters instead of one. → Automation, Limiting — Wolfgang Gartner (Sol State), [7 Music Producer Tricks From Wolfgang Gartner's Deleted Twitch Stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P-0vQIKHu4k)
- **Matching-EQ against a reference track as a master-chain stage, THEN adjust by feel.** Load a reference into a matching EQ, capture its curve, move your own master's curve to align with it — catches frequency gaps invisible by ear alone (worked example: the match revealed a need for more highs that hadn't been consciously noticed). A full alternate chain built around this: matching-EQ pass → low boost → steep high-pass below ~28 Hz (protects big PA systems from muddy sub-audible rumble) → Ozone Imager set mono below 110 Hz → a small (~5%) mid boost → a touch more width/highs (~1%) → a light glue/console-emulation stage last. Comfortable letting reverb tails and similar peaks push into the red if the result serves the song. → Referencing and Translation, Width and Stereo — Jay Eskar (Sol State), [Get UNSTUCK Using A "Song Theme"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HJSK_EIGNP8)
- **A minimal 3-stage lo-fi master chain, sourced whole: cleanup EQ → self-sidechain-filtered glue comp → limiter with a true-peak margin.** No imaging, no saturation, no dedicated clipper stage — deliberately less than this chain's full 8-stage default, matching the genre's own "doesn't have to be perfect" ethos. See inline 🎬 notes on §1, §3, and §8 above for the concrete settings (EQ cleanup numbers, the ~70 Hz self-sidechain filter trick, the limiter's ~1 dB true-peak safety margin for MP3 intersample peaks). → Sidechaining, Compression, Limiting, Clipping and Loudness — Max Konyi, [Final Mix & Master | Studio One LoFi Tutorial | Part 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-OKUCuyLBSg)
- **Bus-to-tape as a glue move, validated on hardware** — sending several related tracks out to a physical tape deck at once and consolidating them to a stereo pass gets tape's own compression/saturation to do bus-glue duty; the same idea this chain's own Kramer Tape stage runs, applied here earlier (at a guitar group) rather than only at the final master. → Kramer Tape, Sony TC-630 — Zach Scholz, [Using Analog Tape to Glue a Mix Together](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xk0LYE7HGAI)
- **A/B test: an all-digital mix read as MORE characterful than the same song printed through tape** — undercuts the assumption that a tape-finish stage is what makes a mix sound "warm." The traits that actually matter (track-count discipline, broad-strokes-by-ear decisions, early commitment) get set well before this chain's tape stage ever runs — treat §4 as a genuine finishing touch, not a fix for problems decided upstream. → Committing and Printing — Zach Scholz, [Why 70's Records Sound so Warm (How to Get That Character)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6eGa5NOTYg)
- **Produce INTO the limiter** — Pro-L 2 (Dubstep style, punchy) stays on the master the whole time you beatmake so drums are judged the way the finished record hits; then balance by turning everything that isn't drums DOWN — drums should be the loudest thing hitting the limiter — Lophiile, [Make Your Drums Slap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v4ZhwlhF5yE) & [All About Basslines stream](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tnruvmw_OWc)
General tips pulled from production breakdowns (via `/music-enrich`), newest-first.

- **Hybrid analog pre-master = a flavor/glue pass, do everything except limiting.** Convert the digital mix → analog through an SSL desk (comp/EQ) → back to digital → hand to mastering. It's the last 5–10%; conversion loss only bites where there's deep sub, so it's fine on midrange-heavy material and risky on full-range techno/dubstep. → Referencing and Translation — Disclosure, [SSL SIX Mixing Al Green](https://youtu.be/ZCNX8U6oZmE)
- **SSL Fusion master-bus stage order** (a template many mastering chains follow): HPF (skip on a full mix) → **Vintage Drive** (fullness/density — trim output as you drive; density = harmonics↔compression) → **Violet non-linear EQ** (boost highs+lows hard) → **HF Compressor** (sidechained high-frequency comp — controls vocal/snare top without the kick triggering it; hold 5 s for **LMC "trash-mic" mode**, great on drums, not for master) → **Space/Width imager** (space = lows, width = top) → subtle Transistor. Ideally *insert* it on the desk (needs a D-sub) rather than print-and-reconvert. → Plugin Wishlist — Disclosure, [SSL SIX Mixing Al Green](https://youtu.be/ZCNX8U6oZmE)
- **Two-bus summing: everything → Instrument bus + Vocal bus → master.** Every part hits its instrument bus → one Instrument bus; every vocal → one Vocal bus; both → master (mute one = instrumental / acapella). Nest sub-buses freely ("a bus in a bus"). **Keep headroom on the summing buses** — pre-limit the instrument bus a hair, keep a final EQ on the vocal bus — so late fixes are a quick project revisit, not a whole-mix move. → Compression Staging — Disclosure, [Birthday](https://youtu.be/b-6x_4XRwOQ)
- **A busier "production" mix bus (older Disclosure) = SSL G-bus comp → tape → Softube multiband → Saturn 2 (clean-tube for top sparkle) → Oxford Inflator → Soothe2 (low, wet/dry, catches mid-range jumps) → EQ.** Denser than the current clipper+Inflator master; note it's the *while-producing* bus, not the mastering hand-off — Disclosure, [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag)
- **Print through hardware, using a software EQ as a *visual* guide** — set a stock EQ how you want it (e.g. +dB @ 50, cut treble, high-band comp), then dial an SSL Fusion to match, send out the desk → Fusion → record ("SSL return"). The plugin is just the target picture. → Referencing and Translation — Disclosure, [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag)
- **Never bounce through a limiter before mastering** — keep the master limiter for the demo bounce only; leave it off for the engineer — Disclosure, [Never Enough](https://youtu.be/lGopQwQo9Ag)
- **Current Disclosure master = clipper + Oxford Inflator only** — no EQ, no compression; a heavily-oversampled clipper catches peaks (beats the aliasing Oxford Limiter across a full mix), Inflator does upward loudness. Bypass it all for the mastering engineer; send −10 to −6 dBFS — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8) & [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ)
- **Saturation is the loudness, not the limiter** — get enough saturation across the mix, then clip (the clip *is* saturation); keep tape on drums/bass, not the master — Disclosure, [NO CAP](https://youtu.be/kz5dmb3QdI8)
- **EQ the master as a bypassed guide** — a tiny linear-phase move (mids up, −1 to −1.5 dB super-highs), then screenshot it for the engineer rather than baking it in — Disclosure, [Looking For Love](https://youtu.be/NlJt0pCptGk) & [Waterfall](https://youtu.be/sL5CG444qwQ)
